Straight-run gasoline from fractional distillation is only about 20% of crude and of poor quality, so heavy oils are cracked to make more and better petrol.

**Thermal cracking** uses heat alone (free-radical mechanism). In **liquid-phase** thermal cracking the heavy oil is cracked at about 475-530 °C under high pressure (30-100 kg/cm²) to keep it liquid; the petrol has octane number about 65-70. In **vapour-phase** thermal cracking the oil is vaporised and cracked at 600-650 °C and low pressure (10-20 kg/cm²); it suits only oils that vaporise easily and gives more olefins and gum.

**Catalytic cracking** uses a catalyst such as artificial clay, zeolite or alumina-silica ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + SiO_2}$) at lower temperature (300-450 °C) and pressure (1-5 kg/cm²); it goes through carbocations, which rearrange to branched chains and give high-octane petrol. In **fixed-bed** cracking the preheated oil vapour (420-450 °C) passes over a stationary catalyst bed; carbon deposits on the catalyst, so the bed is taken off-line after 8-10 hours and regenerated by burning off the carbon. In **moving-bed (fluidised-bed)** cracking finely powdered catalyst is kept fluidised by the oil vapour in a reactor at about 500 °C, carried continuously to a **regenerator** where air burns off the carbon, and returned, so the process runs without interruption.
key_points: Cracking: large high-boiling molecules into smaller low-boiling ones, e.g. $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_5H_{12} + C_5H_{10}}$; products are a mixture of alkanes and alkenes.
Thermal cracking: heat only, free-radical mechanism; liquid phase (475-530 °C, 30-100 kg/cm²) or vapour phase (600-650 °C, 10-20 kg/cm²).
Liquid-phase thermal petrol has octane number about 65-70; vapour-phase petrol is richer in olefins, so higher octane but more gum.
Catalytic cracking: artificial clay, zeolite or alumina-silica ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + SiO_2}$), 300-450 °C, 1-5 kg/cm²; carbocation mechanism.
Fixed-bed: preheater, catalyst chamber (about 425-450 °C, 1.5 kg/cm²), fractionating column, stabiliser; about 40% converted to gasoline; catalyst regenerated by burning off carbon after 8-10 hours.

Fluidised (moving) bed: powdered catalyst carried with oil vapour into the reactor (about 500 °C); cyclone separator keeps catalyst back; spent catalyst burnt clean with air in the regenerator and recycled; continuous.
Catalytic over thermal: higher yield and octane number, lower temperature and pressure, less gum and sulphur, less gas and coke, better control of products.
Heat from burning the carbon in the regenerator helps supply the heat of cracking, so less external fuel is needed.
formulas: $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{22} \xrightarrow{\Delta} C_5H_{12} + C_5H_{10}}$ — cracking of decane to pentane and pentene
traps: Writing 'polymerisation' or 'reforming' for cracking: cracking breaks big molecules; reforming rearranges molecules without much change in size.
Swapping the conditions: liquid-phase thermal uses high pressure and lower temperature; vapour-phase uses higher temperature and low pressure.
Saying catalytic cracking needs higher temperature than thermal: it is lower (300-450 °C).
Forgetting the regeneration step: in fixed bed the bed is regenerated in place (process stops); in fluidised bed a separate regenerator works continuously.
Drawing the fluidised-bed diagram without the regenerator, cyclone separator and fractionating column loses most of the diagram marks.
topics.asked_as: 'What is cracking? Describe fixed-bed (or fluidised-bed) catalytic cracking with a neat diagram' (5-7 marks); 'Compare thermal and catalytic cracking' or 'Give advantages of catalytic cracking' (3-5 marks); 'Distinguish liquid-phase and vapour-phase cracking' (2-3 marks).

questions.q: What is cracking? Why is it necessary?
questions.a:
**Cracking** is the decomposition of bigger hydrocarbon molecules (high boiling point) into simpler, lower-boiling hydrocarbons by heat, with or without a catalyst:
$$\mathrm{C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_5H_{12} + C_5H_{10}}$$
(decane, b.p. 174 °C, gives pentane and pentene, b.p. about 36 °C and 30 °C).

**Need**: straight-run gasoline from fractional distillation of crude is only about 20% of the crude, and its knock rating is poor. Demand for petrol is much larger, so the heavier fractions (gas oil, fuel oil) are cracked to increase both the **quantity** and the **quality** (octane number) of gasoline.

questions.q: Describe the fixed-bed catalytic cracking process with a labelled diagram.
questions.a:
**Diagram** (label): preheater (furnace), catalyst chamber (two, used alternately), fractionating column, cooler, stabiliser; outlets for heavy oil, gases and cracked gasoline.

**Process**: (1) The heavy oil charge is vaporised and heated in a **preheater** to the cracking temperature, about 420-450 °C. (2) The vapours pass through a **catalyst chamber** packed with artificial clay or alumina-silica ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + SiO_2}$) kept at about 425-450 °C and 1.5 kg/cm². About 40% of the charge is converted into gasoline and about 2-4% of carbon is deposited on the catalyst. (3) The cracked vapours go to a **fractionating column**, where heavy oil condenses at the bottom and gasoline vapour with gases passes on. (4) The vapours are cooled and condensed; dissolved gases are removed in a **stabiliser** to give stable gasoline.

**Regeneration**: the carbon deposit deactivates the catalyst, so after 8-10 hours the chamber is switched out and the catalyst is regenerated by burning off the carbon with air; the oil is meanwhile diverted to the second chamber.

questions.q: Describe moving-bed (fluidised-bed) catalytic cracking. How is it better than fixed-bed cracking?
questions.a:
**Process**: (1) Finely powdered catalyst (artificial clay or alumina-silica) is mixed with the preheated heavy oil vapour and carried into the **reactor**, where it behaves like a boiling fluid (fluidised) and cracking takes place at about 500 °C. (2) At the top of the reactor a **cyclone separator** lets the cracked vapours go to the **fractionating column** and returns the catalyst powder to the bed. (3) The spent catalyst, coated with carbon, falls to the bottom and is blown by a current of air into the **regenerator**, where the carbon burns off. (4) The regenerated hot catalyst flows back to the incoming oil, and the cycle repeats. (5) The cracked vapours are fractionated, cooled and stabilised to give gasoline.

**Advantages over fixed bed**: the process is **continuous** (no shutdown for regeneration); very close contact of powdered catalyst and vapour gives uniform temperature and better conversion; the heat released in burning the carbon is carried back by the catalyst and supplies much of the heat of cracking.

questions.q: Give the advantages of catalytic cracking over thermal cracking.
questions.a:
1. **Higher yield** of gasoline from the same feed.
2. **Higher octane number**: the carbocation mechanism gives branched alkanes and aromatics, which resist knocking.
3. **Milder conditions**: lower temperature (300-450 °C) and pressure (1-5 kg/cm²), so cheaper plant and less fuel.
4. **Less gum**: fewer diolefins are formed, so the product is more stable on storage.
5. **Less sulphur**: much of the S is removed as $\mathrm{H_2S}$, so the petrol corrodes and pollutes less.
6. **Better control**: product composition can be steered by choice of catalyst and conditions; less gas and coke are formed.
7. Heat from regenerating the catalyst is recovered, so less external fuel is needed.

questions.q: Distinguish between liquid-phase and vapour-phase thermal cracking.
questions.a:
| Liquid-phase thermal cracking | Vapour-phase thermal cracking |
|---|---|
| Oil is kept liquid during cracking | Oil is vaporised first, then cracked |
| About 475-530 °C | About 600-650 °C |
| High pressure, 30-100 kg/cm² | Low pressure, 10-20 kg/cm² |
| Any heavy oil can be used | Only oils that vaporise easily can be used |
| Petrol of octane number about 65-70 | Petrol richer in olefins (higher octane) but more gum, needs more treatment |

questions.q: The catalyst commonly used in catalytic cracking of heavy oils is:
questions.a: Artificial clays, zeolites and alumina-silica are the cracking catalysts. Ni is a hydrogenation catalyst, $\mathrm{V_2O_5}$ is for the contact process, and Fe-Mo is for the Haber process.

questions.q: In fluidised-bed catalytic cracking, the carbon deposited on the catalyst is removed:
options: By washing the catalyst with benzene
By burning it off with air in a separate regenerator, continuously
By stopping the plant every 8-10 hours
It is not removed; fresh catalyst is used each time
questions.a: The spent catalyst is blown into a regenerator, where air burns off the carbon, and is returned to the reactor without stopping the process. Stopping every 8-10 hours is the fixed-bed method.

questions.q: Petrol from catalytic cracking has a higher octane number than petrol from thermal cracking because:
options: It contains more branched alkanes and aromatics
It is cracked at a higher temperature
questions.a: Catalytic cracking goes through carbocations, which isomerise to branched chains and also form aromatics; both resist knocking. Straight chains knock most, and catalytic cracking actually uses a lower temperature.

topics.why: Knocking with its chemical cause, octane and cetane number definitions, TEL and its drawbacks, and unleaded petrol come in almost every Fuels paper, as 5-mark questions and as MCQs.
topics.gist:
**Knocking (petrol engine)**. In a spark-ignition engine the compressed fuel-air mixture is ignited by a spark. If the compression ratio is high, the unburnt last part of the charge (end gas) ignites by itself before the flame reaches it, giving a sudden pressure rise and a sharp metallic sound: **knocking**. Its chemical cause is the formation of peroxides that decompose explosively. Effects: loss of power and efficiency, overheating, and damage to pistons, valves and bearings.

Knocking tendency with structure: **n-alkanes > branched alkanes > olefins > cycloalkanes > aromatics**. **Octane number** is the % by volume of iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane, ON 100) in a mixture with n-heptane (ON 0) that knocks like the fuel.

**Antiknock agents**: tetraethyl lead (**TEL**, $\mathrm{Pb(C_2H_5)_4}$) breaks the peroxide chains, but deposits PbO in the engine; **ethylene dibromide** is added as a scavenger to form volatile $\mathrm{PbBr_2}$, but the lead pollutes the air and poisons catalytic converters. So **unleaded petrol** is used now: high octane by blending branched and aromatic components and adding **MTBE** (methyl tertiary-butyl ether), which supplies oxygen for complete combustion.

**Diesel knock**: in a compression-ignition engine fuel is injected into hot compressed air. If the **ignition delay** is long, fuel accumulates and then burns all at once. **Cetane number** is the % of cetane (n-hexadecane, CN 100) in a mixture with α-methylnaphthalene (CN 0) with the same ignition quality. Straight chains ignite easily, so **good petrol is bad diesel and vice versa**. Dopes such as ethyl nitrite raise cetane number.
key_points: Knocking: self-ignition of the end gas before the flame front reaches it, with a sharp metallic sound; caused by peroxide formation at high compression ratio.
Effects: loss of power and efficiency, more fuel consumption, overheating, mechanical damage to pistons, cylinder heads, valves.
Knocking tendency: n-alkanes > branched alkanes > olefins > cycloalkanes (naphthenes) > aromatics; in n-alkanes it rises with chain length.
Octane number: % iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane, 100) in an iso-octane + n-heptane (0) blend matching the fuel's knocking.
TEL, $\mathrm{Pb(C_2H_5)_4}$: forms Pb/PbO that destroy chain-carrying radicals and peroxides; ethylene dibromide scavenger gives volatile $\mathrm{PbBr_2}$.
Drawbacks of TEL: toxic lead in exhaust, PbO/PbBr2 deposits, poisons the Pt/Rh catalytic converter; hence unleaded petrol with MTBE and branched/aromatic blending stocks.
Diesel knock: long ignition delay lets injected fuel accumulate, then it burns violently.
Cetane number: % n-hexadecane (cetane, 100) in a cetane + α-methylnaphthalene (0) blend of the same ignition quality.
Ignition quality: n-alkanes > cycloalkanes > olefins > branched alkanes > aromatics, the reverse of antiknock order; so good petrol is bad diesel.
Cetane improvers (dopes): ethyl nitrite, isoamyl nitrite, acetone peroxide.
formulas: $\mathrm{ON} = \%\,\text{iso-octane (by volume) in the matching iso-octane + n-heptane blend}$ — octane number
$\mathrm{CN} = \%\,\text{n-hexadecane in the matching cetane + } \alpha\text{-methylnaphthalene blend}$ — cetane number
$\mathrm{Pb + C_2H_4Br_2 \rightarrow PbBr_2 + C_2H_4}$ — ethylene dibromide as lead scavenger
traps: Calling n-heptane 100 and iso-octane 0: it is iso-octane 100, n-heptane 0.
Calling cetane 0: cetane (n-hexadecane) is 100, α-methylnaphthalene is 0.
Saying high octane fuel is a good diesel fuel: high octane (branched, aromatic) means poor ignition quality, so low cetane.
Calling ethylene dibromide an antiknock: it is only a scavenger for lead; TEL is the antiknock.
Defining knocking as 'incomplete combustion': it is premature self-ignition of the end gas (petrol) or delayed then sudden ignition (diesel).
Mixing up octane by volume with mass: the textbook definition is percentage by volume.
topics.asked_as: 'What is knocking? Explain its chemical cause and how it is prevented' (5 marks); 'Define octane number and cetane number' (2-3 marks); 'Write a note on TEL / unleaded petrol' (3 marks); 'Good petrol is a bad diesel. Explain' (2-3 marks); MCQs on reference fuels and order of knocking.

questions.q: What is knocking in a petrol engine? Explain its cause, its harmful effects, and how it depends on the structure of the hydrocarbon.
questions.a:
**Knocking**: in a spark-ignition engine, the compressed fuel-air mixture should burn smoothly as the flame front spreads from the spark plug. When the compression ratio is high, the last unburnt portion of the charge (end gas) gets heated and compressed so much that it **ignites on its own** before the flame front reaches it. The sudden, very rapid pressure rise produces a sharp metallic sound called knocking.

**Chemical cause**: during compression, hydrocarbons combine with oxygen to form **peroxides**; these unstable compounds decompose explosively, giving premature combustion.

**Effects**: loss of power and thermal efficiency, higher fuel consumption, overheating of the cylinder, and mechanical damage to pistons, cylinder head, valves and bearings.

**Structure**: knocking tendency decreases in the order
$$\text{n-alkanes} > \text{branched alkanes} > \text{olefins} > \text{cycloalkanes} > \text{aromatics}$$
Among n-alkanes, longer chains knock more. Branched and aromatic hydrocarbons are therefore good petrol components.

**Prevention**: use high-octane fuel (branched or aromatic components from catalytic cracking, reforming, alkylation), add antiknock agents (TEL formerly, MTBE now), and match the compression ratio to the fuel.

questions.q: Define octane number. A petrol sample has octane number 80. What does this mean?
questions.a:
**Octane number** of a fuel is the percentage by volume of **iso-octane** (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) in a mixture of iso-octane and **n-heptane** that has the same knocking characteristics as the fuel under the same set of conditions. Iso-octane, which knocks very little, is given ON 100; n-heptane, which knocks badly, is given ON 0.

A petrol of **ON 80** knocks like a mixture of **80% iso-octane and 20% n-heptane** by volume. The higher the octane number, the higher the compression ratio the engine can use without knocking.

questions.q: What is TEL? How does it act as an antiknock agent? Why is ethylene dibromide added with it, and why has leaded petrol been replaced by unleaded petrol?
questions.a:
**TEL** is tetraethyl lead, $\mathrm{Pb(C_2H_5)_4}$, added in small quantity to petrol to raise its octane number.

**Action**: in the cylinder TEL decomposes to Pb and ethyl radicals; Pb is oxidised to PbO. These destroy the peroxides and the free radicals that carry the chain reaction, so premature self-ignition is stopped and combustion is smooth.

**Scavenger**: PbO would deposit on spark plugs, valves and cylinder walls. **Ethylene dibromide** is added so that lead forms volatile $\mathrm{PbBr_2}$, which goes out with the exhaust:
$$\mathrm{Pb + C_2H_4Br_2 \rightarrow PbBr_2 + C_2H_4}$$

**Why unleaded petrol**: (i) lead compounds in the exhaust are toxic and pollute air; (ii) lead poisons the Pt/Rh catalyst of the **catalytic converter** that removes CO, NO and unburnt hydrocarbons. Unleaded petrol obtains its octane number from branched and aromatic blending stocks and from **MTBE** (methyl tertiary-butyl ether), whose oxygen helps complete combustion of CO to $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and reduces peroxide formation.

questions.q: What is diesel knock? Define cetane number and explain why a good petrol is a bad diesel fuel.
questions.a:
**Diesel knock**: in a compression-ignition engine only air is compressed (to about 500 °C), and fuel is injected into it. The time between injection and ignition is the **ignition delay**. If the delay is long, injected fuel accumulates in the cylinder and then ignites all at once, giving a sudden pressure rise and knocking.

**Cetane number**: the percentage of **cetane** (n-hexadecane, $\mathrm{C_{16}H_{34}}$, CN 100) in a mixture with **α-methylnaphthalene** (CN 0) that has the same ignition quality as the diesel under test. Ignition quality can be raised by dopes such as **ethyl nitrite**, isoamyl nitrite and acetone peroxide.

**Good petrol is bad diesel**: a petrol engine needs a fuel that resists self-ignition (branched alkanes, aromatics: high octane). A diesel engine needs a fuel that self-ignites quickly (straight-chain alkanes: short ignition delay, high cetane). Ignition quality follows n-alkanes > cycloalkanes > olefins > branched alkanes > aromatics, the reverse of the antiknock order. So a fuel with high octane number has a low cetane number, and vice versa.

questions.q: Write a short note on MTBE and unleaded petrol.
questions.a:
**Unleaded petrol** is petrol whose octane number is raised without lead compounds. It is needed in vehicles with catalytic converters, since lead poisons the Pt/Rh catalyst, and it avoids lead pollution.

Its octane number comes from (i) high-octane blending stocks rich in branched alkanes and aromatics (from catalytic cracking, reforming, isomerisation, alkylation), and (ii) oxygenates, chiefly **MTBE**, methyl tertiary-butyl ether, $\mathrm{CH_3\text{-}O\text{-}C(CH_3)_3}$. MTBE has a high octane number and supplies oxygen in the fuel, so combustion is more complete, CO emission falls, and peroxide formation is reduced.

questions.q: The two reference fuels for octane number are:
questions.a: Iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) is 100 and n-heptane is 0. Cetane and α-methylnaphthalene are the cetane-number references.

questions.q: Which of the following has the highest tendency to knock in a petrol engine?
questions.a: Straight-chain alkanes knock most; n-heptane is the zero point of the octane scale. Aromatics (benzene), cycloalkanes and branched alkanes (iso-octane) knock much less.

questions.q: Ethylene dibromide is added to leaded petrol to:
options: Convert lead into volatile lead bromide that leaves with the exhaust
questions.a: Ethylene dibromide is a scavenger: it converts Pb/PbO from TEL into volatile $\mathrm{PbBr_2}$ so lead does not deposit in the engine. TEL is the actual antiknock.

topics.topic: Numericals on calorific value and ultimate analysis
topics.why: A Dulong HCV/LCV numerical or a minimum-air calculation from ultimate analysis is set in nearly every Fuels paper and is the surest 5 marks in the unit.
topics.gist:
**Dulong's formula** estimates calorific value from ultimate analysis (all in %):
$$\mathrm{HCV} = \tfrac{1}{100}\left[8080\,C + 34500\left(H - \tfrac{O}{8}\right) + 2240\,S\right]\ \text{kcal/kg}$$
8080, 34500 and 2240 kcal/kg are the calorific values of C, H and S. The oxygen in the fuel is assumed to be already combined with hydrogen as water (8 parts O with 1 part H), so only $H - O/8$ is **available hydrogen**. Then $\mathrm{LCV} = \mathrm{HCV} - 0.09\,H \times 587$.

**Minimum air by mass** (per kg fuel, fractions not %):
- $\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$: 12 kg C needs 32 kg $\mathrm{O_2}$, so $32/12$ kg per kg C.
- $\mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O}$: 4 kg H needs 32 kg, so 8 kg per kg H.
- $\mathrm{S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2}$: 1 kg per kg S.

Subtract the oxygen already in the fuel. Air contains 23% $\mathrm{O_2}$ by mass, so air $= \mathrm{O_2} \times 100/23$. N, ash and moisture need no oxygen.

**Gaseous fuels by volume** (per $\mathrm{m^3}$): $\mathrm{H_2}$ and CO each need 0.5 volume, $\mathrm{CH_4}$ 2, $\mathrm{C_2H_4}$ 3, $\mathrm{C_2H_6}$ 3.5; subtract any $\mathrm{O_2}$ in the gas. Air has 21% $\mathrm{O_2}$ by volume, so air $= \mathrm{O_2} \times 100/21$. To get volume of air for a solid fuel, convert kg $\mathrm{O_2}$ to $\mathrm{m^3}$ at NTP (32 kg occupies 22.4 $\mathrm{m^3}$) first.

**Excess air**: furnaces use more than the minimum; actual air $=$ minimum air $\times (1 + \tfrac{\%\,\text{excess}}{100})$.
key_points: Dulong: $\mathrm{HCV} = \frac{1}{100}[8080C + 34500(H - O/8) + 2240S]$ kcal/kg, with C, H, O, S in %.
O/8 term: fuel oxygen is taken as already combined with H (8 g O per 1 g H), so only H − O/8 can burn.
$\mathrm{LCV} = \mathrm{HCV} - 0.09H \times 587$ kcal/kg.
O$_2$ per kg: C needs 32/12 = 2.667 kg, H needs 8 kg, S needs 1 kg; subtract O present in the fuel.
Air by mass = O2 × 100/23; air by volume = O2 × 100/21.
Gas fuels per m$^3$: $\mathrm{H_2}$ 0.5, CO 0.5, $\mathrm{CH_4}$ 2, $\mathrm{C_2H_4}$ 3, $\mathrm{C_2H_6}$ 3.5 m$^3$ of O$_2$; $\mathrm{N_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ need none.
Mass to volume: 32 kg of $\mathrm{O_2}$ occupies 22.4 m$^3$ at NTP.
Excess air: actual = minimum × (1 + x/100).
Convert % to fractions (per kg) before multiplying in air calculations; keep % in Dulong's bracket and divide by 100.
formulas: $\mathrm{O_2\ (kg/kg)} = \dfrac{32}{12}C + 8\left(H - \dfrac{O}{8}\right) + S$ — C, H, O, S as fractions; same as $\frac{32}{12}C + 8H + S - O$
$\text{Actual air} = \text{minimum air} \times \left(1 + \dfrac{x}{100}\right)$ — with x % excess air
traps: Writing H + O/8 instead of H − O/8 in Dulong's formula.
Forgetting the 1/100 in Dulong when C, H, O, S are in %.
Using 100/21 for air by mass or 100/23 for air by volume: mass uses 23, volume uses 21.
Not subtracting the oxygen already present in the fuel (or in the gas).
Counting N, ash or $\mathrm{CO_2}$ as needing oxygen.
Using 0.9H instead of 0.09H for the latent heat term.
topics.asked_as: 'Calculate HCV and LCV of a coal of given composition using Dulong's formula' (3-5 marks); 'Calculate the minimum mass/volume of air required for complete combustion of 1 kg of coal' (5 marks); 'Find the volume of air needed for 1 m³ of a gaseous fuel' with excess air (5 marks).

questions.q: A coal has the following composition by mass: C = 84%, H = 5.5%, O = 4%, S = 1.5%. Calculate its higher and lower calorific values using Dulong's formula (latent heat of steam = 587 kcal/kg).
Calculate the gross and net calorific values of a coal containing C = 78%, H = 6%, O = 8%, S = 2% by Dulong's formula (latent heat of steam = 587 kcal/kg).

A coal has C = 80%, H = 5%, O = 6%, S = 1%, N = 2% and ash = 6%. Calculate the minimum mass of air needed for complete combustion of 1 kg of the coal, and the air needed with 40% excess air. (Air contains 23% O₂ by mass.)
questions.a:
Per kg of coal: C = 0.80 kg, H = 0.05 kg, S = 0.01 kg, O = 0.06 kg. N and ash need no oxygen.

| Element | Reaction | $\mathrm{O_2}$ needed (kg) |
|---|---|---|
| C | $\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$ | $0.80 \times 32/12 = 2.1333$ |
| H | $\mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O}$ | $0.05 \times 8 = 0.4000$ |
| S | $\mathrm{S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2}$ | $0.01 \times 1 = 0.0100$ |
| | Total | $2.5433$ |

Less O in coal = 0.06 kg, so net $\mathrm{O_2}$ = 2.5433 − 0.06 = **2.4833 kg**.

$$\text{Minimum air} = 2.4833 \times \frac{100}{23} = 10.80\ \text{kg}$$

$$\text{Air with 40\% excess} = 10.797 \times 1.40 = 15.12\ \text{kg}$$

**Minimum air ≈ 10.80 kg per kg coal; with 40% excess ≈ 15.12 kg.**

questions.q: For the coal of the previous question (net O₂ required = 2.4833 kg per kg of coal), calculate the minimum volume of air at NTP needed to burn 1 kg of it. (Air contains 21% O₂ by volume.)
questions.a:
32 kg of $\mathrm{O_2}$ occupies 22.4 $\mathrm{m^3}$ at NTP.

$$\text{Volume of } \mathrm{O_2} = \frac{2.4833 \times 22.4}{32} = 1.738\ \mathrm{m^3}$$

$$\text{Volume of air} = 1.738 \times \frac{100}{21} = 8.28\ \mathrm{m^3}$$

**Minimum air ≈ 8.28 m³ at NTP per kg of coal.**

questions.q: A gaseous fuel has the composition by volume: H₂ = 50%, CH₄ = 30%, CO = 10%, N₂ = 5%, CO₂ = 5%. Calculate the volume of air needed for complete combustion of 1 m³ of the gas, (a) minimum, (b) with 20% excess air. (Air contains 21% O₂ by volume.)
questions.a:
Per $\mathrm{m^3}$ of gas:

| Constituent | Reaction | $\mathrm{O_2}$ ($\mathrm{m^3}$) |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{H_2}$ 0.50 | $\mathrm{H_2 + \tfrac12 O_2 \rightarrow H_2O}$ | $0.50 \times 0.5 = 0.25$ |
| $\mathrm{CH_4}$ 0.30 | $\mathrm{CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O}$ | $0.30 \times 2 = 0.60$ |
| CO 0.10 | $\mathrm{CO + \tfrac12 O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$ | $0.10 \times 0.5 = 0.05$ |
| $\mathrm{N_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | do not burn | 0 |
| | Total | $0.90$ |

(a) $$\text{Minimum air} = 0.90 \times \frac{100}{21} = 4.29\ \mathrm{m^3}$$

(b) $$\text{Air with 20\% excess} = 4.286 \times 1.20 = 5.14\ \mathrm{m^3}$$

**Minimum air ≈ 4.29 m³; with 20% excess ≈ 5.14 m³ per m³ of gas.**

questions.q: In Dulong's formula, why is the hydrogen term written as (H − O/8)?
questions.a: Dulong assumed that all the oxygen in the fuel is already combined with hydrogen in the form of water ($\mathrm{H_2O}$: 2 parts H with 16 parts O, i.e. 1 part H with 8 parts O). That hydrogen is already 'burnt' and gives no heat. So O parts of oxygen lock up O/8 parts of hydrogen, and only the **available (free) hydrogen** $H - O/8$ is counted with the calorific value of hydrogen, 34500 kcal/kg.

questions.q: The minimum mass of oxygen needed for complete combustion of 1 kg of carbon is:
questions.a: $\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$: 12 kg C needs 32 kg $\mathrm{O_2}$, so 1 kg needs 32/12 = 2.67 kg. (1.33 kg is for C to CO; 8 kg is for 1 kg H; 11.59 kg is the air, 2.67 × 100/23.)

questions.q: To convert the mass of oxygen required into the mass of air required, it is multiplied by:
questions.a: Air contains 23% oxygen by mass, so mass of air = mass of O2 × 100/23. The factor 100/21 is used for volumes, since air is 21% oxygen by volume.

topics.topic: Sources and specifications of drinking water
topics.why: A 2-3 mark question on sources and impurities, or a list of potable water standards, opens most Water questions and is easy marks.
topics.gist:
Water reaches us from two kinds of source.

**Surface water**: (i) **rain water**, the purest natural water, but it dissolves $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and dust from the air; (ii) **river water**, which picks up dissolved salts (chlorides, sulphates, bicarbonates of Ca, Mg, Na) and suspended silt and organic matter from the land it flows over; (iii) **lake water**, fairly constant in composition, with less dissolved mineral but more organic matter; (iv) **sea water**, the most impure, about 3.5% dissolved salts, mostly $\mathrm{NaCl}$.

**Underground water**: **springs and wells** (shallow and deep). Filtration through soil removes suspended matter and microbes, so it is clear and often free of organisms, but it dissolves more minerals and is usually **harder** than surface water.

**Impurities** fall into four classes: **dissolved** salts and gases ($\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{O_2}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$); **suspended** (sand, clay, silt, organic debris); **colloidal** (finely divided clay, $\mathrm{SiO_2}$, organic colloids that cause colour and turbidity); and **biological** (bacteria, algae, fungi, viruses, protozoa).

**Potable water** (WHO / BIS IS 10500) must be clear, colourless, odourless and pleasant to taste; pH 6.5-8.5; TDS below 500 ppm; total hardness below 300 ppm as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (common textbook figure; IS 10500 acceptable limit is 200 mg/L); turbidity below 10 ppm; chloride below 250 ppm; fluoride about 1-1.5 ppm (more causes fluorosis, less causes dental caries); free from pathogens, toxic metals ($\mathrm{Pb}$, $\mathrm{As}$, $\mathrm{Hg}$) and $\mathrm{H_2S}$.
key_points: Surface sources: rain (purest), river, lake, sea (most impure, ~3.5% salts).
Underground sources: springs and wells; clear and low in microbes but high in dissolved minerals (harder).
Four classes of impurity: dissolved (salts, gases), suspended, colloidal, biological.
Colloidal impurities cause colour and turbidity and do not settle on standing.
Potable pH 6.5-8.5; TDS < 500 ppm; hardness < 300 ppm as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (textbook figure).
Turbidity < 10 ppm; chloride < 250 ppm; fluoride ~1-1.5 ppm.
Must be free from pathogens, toxic heavy metals and objectionable gases like $\mathrm{H_2S}$.
Fluoride above ~1.5 ppm causes fluorosis; too little causes dental caries.
traps: Calling rain water perfectly pure: it dissolves $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and dust.
Saying well water is softer than river water: underground water is usually harder (more contact with minerals).
Confusing suspended and colloidal impurities: colloidal ones do not settle and need coagulation.
Quoting pH 7 exactly as the standard: the permissible range is 6.5-8.5.
Stating zero fluoride as ideal: about 1 ppm is beneficial for teeth.
Textbooks differ on the hardness limit (300 ppm in Jain & Jain, 200 mg/L acceptable in IS 10500:2012); name the source you quote.
topics.asked_as: 'What are the sources of water? Classify impurities present in natural water' (3-5 marks); 'Give the specifications/characteristics of potable water' (2-3 marks); MCQs on pH range, fluoride or TDS limits.

questions.q: Name the sources of water and compare surface and underground water.
questions.a:
**Surface water**: rain water, river water, lake water, sea water.
**Underground water**: spring water, well water (shallow and deep).

| Surface water | Underground water |
|---|---|
| Contains suspended matter, organic matter and microbes | Clear; soil filters out suspended matter and most microbes |
| Fewer dissolved salts (except sea water) | More dissolved salts, so usually harder |
| Exposed to air, dissolves $\mathrm{O_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | May contain $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, Fe |
| Composition varies with season | Composition fairly constant |

questions.q: Classify the impurities present in natural water with examples.
questions.a:
1. **Dissolved impurities**: (a) inorganic salts: bicarbonates, chlorides, sulphates, nitrates of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Na^+}$, $\mathrm{K^+}$, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$; (b) gases: $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{O_2}$, $\mathrm{N_2}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, $\mathrm{SO_2}$; (c) organic matter from decaying vegetation.
2. **Suspended impurities**: sand, clay, silt, plant debris; they settle on standing and make water turbid.
3. **Colloidal impurities**: finely divided clay, $\mathrm{SiO_2}$, $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$, organic colloids (size 1-1000 nm); they do not settle, give colour and turbidity, and need coagulation.
4. **Biological impurities**: bacteria, algae, fungi, protozoa, viruses; pathogens cause water-borne diseases (cholera, typhoid, dysentery).

questions.q: List the specifications (characteristics) of potable water as per WHO / BIS IS 10500.
questions.a:
1. Clear, colourless, odourless and pleasant in taste.
2. pH 6.5-8.5.
3. Total dissolved solids below 500 ppm.
4. Total hardness below 300 ppm as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (Jain & Jain figure; IS 10500:2012 acceptable limit 200 mg/L).
5. Turbidity below 10 ppm.
6. Chloride below 250 ppm; sulphate below about 200 ppm.
7. Fluoride about 1-1.5 ppm.
8. Free from pathogenic bacteria (coliform count nil in 100 mL).
9. Free from toxic metals ($\mathrm{Pb}$, $\mathrm{As}$, $\mathrm{Hg}$, $\mathrm{Cr}$) and dissolved gases like $\mathrm{H_2S}$.
10. Should not be corrosive and should not deposit scale in pipes.

questions.q: Why is underground water generally harder than surface water?
questions.a:
Underground water percolates through soil and rock layers containing limestone ($\mathrm{CaCO_3}$), dolomite ($\mathrm{MgCO_3\cdot CaCO_3}$), gypsum ($\mathrm{CaSO_4}$) and other minerals for a long time. Dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$ converts the carbonates into soluble bicarbonates:
$$\mathrm{CaCO_3 + H_2O + CO_2 \rightarrow Ca(HCO_3)_2}$$
So it carries more $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, and is harder, though clearer, than surface water.

questions.q: What is the significance of fluoride in drinking water?
questions.a: About **1 ppm** (up to 1.5 ppm) fluoride in drinking water protects teeth by forming fluorapatite in enamel, which resists acid attack. Below about 0.5 ppm, dental caries become common. Above 1.5 ppm it causes **dental fluorosis** (mottled teeth) and at higher levels **skeletal fluorosis** (stiff, brittle bones). Excess fluoride is removed by the Nalgonda technique (alum and lime).

questions.q: The permissible pH range of drinking water is:
questions.a: WHO and BIS IS 10500 prescribe pH 6.5-8.5 for potable water.

questions.q: Which natural water contains the highest amount of dissolved salts?
questions.a: Sea water has about 3.5% dissolved salts, mainly $\mathrm{NaCl}$, with $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ and $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$.

questions.q: Colour and turbidity in natural water that do not settle on standing are mainly due to:
questions.a: Colloidal particles (1-1000 nm) stay dispersed, scatter light and impart colour; they need a coagulant to settle.

topics.topic: Purification of water step by step
topics.why: 'Describe the treatment of water for municipal supply' with a flow sheet is a regular 5-7 mark question, and the alum reaction is asked on its own.
topics.gist:
Municipal water is purified in a fixed sequence, each step removing a different class of impurity.

1. **Screening**: water passes through screens (bar or mesh) that hold back floating matter: leaves, wood, plastics.
2. **Sedimentation (plain settling)**: water stands in large tanks for 2-6 hours; heavy suspended particles settle by gravity. About 70-75% of suspended matter is removed.
3. **Coagulation (sedimentation with coagulant)**: fine and colloidal particles carry negative charge and will not settle. A coagulant is added and mixed. **Alum** reacts with the natural bicarbonate alkalinity:
$\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3 + 3Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3\downarrow + 3CaSO_4 + 6CO_2}$
The gelatinous $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ **floc** (and $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$, which neutralises the charge on colloids) entraps the fine particles and bacteria and settles. Alum works best at pH 6.5-8.5. **Ferrous sulphate** with lime gives $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$ floc and works at higher pH; **sodium aluminate** suits acidic water.
4. **Filtration**: the clarified water passes through a **slow or rapid sand gravity filter**: fine sand on top, then coarse sand, then gravel, with an under-drain. Remaining floc, colloids and many bacteria are retained. When the top layer clogs it is scraped (slow filter) or back-washed (rapid filter).
5. **Disinfection (sterilisation)**: pathogens left are killed by chlorine, bleaching powder, chloramine, ozone or UV. Chlorine is dosed up to the **break-point** so that a small free residual chlorine stays in the mains (covered in the next topic).
key_points: Order: screening → sedimentation → coagulation → filtration → disinfection.
Screening removes floating matter; plain sedimentation removes heavy suspended particles (70-75%).
Colloids are negatively charged and need a coagulant; $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ neutralises the charge.
Alum + bicarbonate alkalinity gives gelatinous $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ floc that entraps fine particles.
Alum works at pH 6.5-8.5; ferrous sulphate (with lime) at higher pH; sodium aluminate for acidic water.
Sand gravity filter: fine sand / coarse sand / gravel layers; cleaned by scraping or back-washing.
Filtration removes floc, colloids and part of the bacteria but not dissolved salts.
Disinfection kills pathogens; chlorine dosed to break-point leaves a free residual in the mains.
formulas: $\mathrm{FeSO_4 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2 + CaSO_4}$ — ferrous sulphate with lime
traps: Putting filtration before coagulation: floc must form and settle first, or the filter clogs at once.
Saying filtration or coagulation removes hardness: dissolved $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ salts pass through.
Writing the alum reaction with $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ instead of $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$; the floc forms from the bicarbonate alkalinity.
Forgetting the 6 $\mathrm{CO_2}$ when balancing the alum equation.
Calling the $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ floc a disinfectant: it entraps bacteria mechanically but does not kill them.
topics.asked_as: 'Describe the various steps in the purification of water for municipal supply with a flow diagram' (5-7 marks); 'What is coagulation? Explain the action of alum with equation' (3 marks); 'Draw a sand gravity filter' (3 marks).

questions.q: Describe the steps involved in the purification of water for domestic (municipal) supply.
questions.a:
Flow sheet: **Raw water → Screening → Sedimentation → Coagulation → Filtration → Disinfection → Storage and supply.**

1. **Screening**: bar/mesh screens remove floating matter (leaves, wood, plastic).
2. **Sedimentation**: water is held in large tanks for 2-6 h; heavy suspended particles settle (70-75% removal).
3. **Coagulation**: colloidal and fine particles do not settle. Alum is added:
$$\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3 + 3Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3\downarrow + 3CaSO_4 + 6CO_2}$$
The gelatinous $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ floc entraps fine particles and bacteria and settles in the coagulation tank.
4. **Filtration**: water passes through a sand gravity filter (fine sand, coarse sand, gravel, under-drain); remaining floc, colloids and many bacteria are retained.
5. **Disinfection**: pathogens are killed by chlorine (or bleaching powder, chloramine, ozone, UV); chlorine is added to the break-point so that 0.1-0.2 ppm free residual chlorine remains in the supply.

questions.q: What is coagulation? Explain the role of alum in water treatment with the chemical reaction.
questions.a:
**Coagulation** is the addition of a chemical (coagulant) that makes finely divided and colloidal particles, which will not settle by themselves, combine into larger flocs that settle quickly.

Colloidal particles in natural water carry negative charge and repel each other. **Alum** ionises to give $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$, which neutralises this charge, and reacts with the bicarbonate alkalinity of water:
$$\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3 + 3Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3\downarrow + 3CaSO_4 + 6CO_2}$$
The gelatinous $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ floc sweeps down the neutralised colloids, suspended particles and many bacteria as it settles. Alum is effective in the pH range 6.5-8.5; if the water lacks alkalinity, lime or soda is added.

questions.q: Describe a sand gravity filter with a labelled sketch.
questions.a:
A rectangular tank of masonry/concrete containing, from top to bottom: (i) **fine sand** layer (about 1 m), (ii) **coarse sand** layer, (iii) **fine gravel**, (iv) **coarse gravel**, resting on (v) a perforated **under-drain** system that collects filtered water.

**Working**: coagulated, settled water enters at the top and flows down under gravity. Suspended floc, colloids and some bacteria are retained in the fine sand; in slow sand filters a slimy biological layer (*schmutzdecke*) forms on the sand and helps hold bacteria. Filtered water is drawn off at the bottom.

**Cleaning**: when the rate of filtration falls, the top 2-3 cm of sand is scraped off and replaced (slow filter) or the bed is **back-washed** with water and air from below (rapid filter).

questions.q: Why is ferrous sulphate preferred over alum for some waters? Give the reactions.
questions.a:
Alum works only in the pH range about 6.5-8.5. **Ferrous sulphate** (with lime) is effective at a higher pH (around 8.5 and above) and gives a heavier floc that settles faster; it is also cheaper. Reactions:
$$\mathrm{FeSO_4 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2 + CaSO_4}$$
$$\mathrm{4Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4Fe(OH)_3\downarrow}$$
The $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$ floc entraps colloidal matter. (It is not used for coloured waters, which may retain iron.)

questions.q: Does filtration remove hardness from water? Explain.
questions.a: No. Filtration removes only **suspended and colloidal** matter (and some bacteria) by a physical straining action. Hardness is due to **dissolved** salts of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ (bicarbonates, chlorides, sulphates) which are in true solution and pass through the sand bed. Hardness needs chemical softening (lime-soda, zeolite, ion exchange) or boiling (for temporary hardness).

questions.q: The gelatinous precipitate formed when alum is added to natural water is:
questions.a: Alum reacts with bicarbonate alkalinity to give $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ floc; $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ stays dissolved.

questions.q: The correct sequence of municipal water treatment is:
questions.a: Coarse matter first (screening), then settleable solids, then colloids (coagulation), then filtration and finally disinfection.

questions.q: Alum is most effective as a coagulant in the pH range:
questions.a: $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ is least soluble around pH 6.5-8.5; outside this range it dissolves as $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ or aluminate.

topics.why: Chlorination mechanism, bleaching powder reaction and the break-point chlorination curve are asked almost every year for 3-7 marks.
topics.gist:
**Sterilization** destroys **all** micro-organisms, pathogenic or not, including spores. **Disinfection** destroys only the **disease-causing (pathogenic)** organisms, making water safe to drink; it is what municipal treatment actually does, though many texts loosely call it sterilization.

**Methods**:
1. **Boiling** for 10-15 min kills germs; fine for a household, impossible on a city scale, and leaves no protection.
2. **Bleaching powder**: about 1 kg per 1000 kL. $\mathrm{CaOCl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow Ca(OH)_2 + Cl_2}$; $\mathrm{Cl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow HOCl + HCl}$. Cheap, but adds Ca (hardness), deteriorates on storage and dosing is uncertain.
3. **Chlorine** (gas or solution) is the most common. $\mathrm{HOCl}$ is the real germicide: being neutral and small, it enters the cell and **inactivates its enzymes** by oxidation, killing it. HOCl dominates below about pH 6.5; at high pH $\mathrm{OCl^-}$ (weaker) predominates.
4. **Chloramine** ($\mathrm{NH_3 + HOCl \rightarrow NH_2Cl + H_2O}$): slower but longer-lasting residual, no chlorinous taste.
5. **Ozone**: $\mathrm{O_3 \rightarrow O_2 + [O]}$; nascent oxygen kills bacteria and removes colour, odour and taste; costly and leaves no residual.
6. **UV light**: kills germs in clear water with no chemicals; costly, no residual, fails in turbid water.

**Break-point chlorination**: as chlorine dose rises, it is first consumed by reducing agents, then forms chloramines, which are then oxidised (residual falls) until the **break-point**. Beyond it, residual **free chlorine** rises in proportion to the dose. Dosing just past the break-point kills all germs, oxidises organics and leaves 0.1-0.2 ppm residual that protects water in the mains.
key_points: Sterilization: kills all micro-organisms; disinfection: kills only pathogens.
Bleaching powder: $\mathrm{CaOCl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow Ca(OH)_2 + Cl_2}$; dose about 1 kg per 1000 kL.
$\mathrm{Cl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow HOCl + HCl}$; HOCl is the active germicide (enzyme inactivation).
HOCl predominates at low pH (below ~6.5); $\mathrm{OCl^-}$, a weaker disinfectant, at high pH.
Chloramine: longer-lasting residual, no taste; slower acting.
Ozone: nascent oxygen; removes colour, odour, taste; costly, no residual.
UV: no chemicals, no residual, needs clear water.
Break-point: dose at which chloramines and organics are fully oxidised and free residual chlorine starts to appear.
Residual chlorine 0.1-0.2 ppm protects water against recontamination in the distribution pipes.
formulas: $\mathrm{CaOCl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow Ca(OH)_2 + Cl_2}$ — bleaching powder in water
$\mathrm{Cl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow HOCl + HCl}$ — hydrolysis of chlorine
traps: Using 'sterilization' and 'disinfection' as exact synonyms: sterilization kills all organisms, disinfection only pathogens.
Saying $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ or $\mathrm{HCl}$ kills the germs: the active species is HOCl.
Saying high pH improves chlorination: at high pH weaker $\mathrm{OCl^-}$ predominates.
Drawing the break-point curve as rising continuously: residual first rises (chloramines), falls to a minimum (break-point), then rises linearly.
Calling ozone and UV better in every respect: they leave no residual protection in the mains.
Overdosing beyond break-point: excess chlorine gives unpleasant taste and odour and is harmful; it is removed by dechlorination ($\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{Na_2S_2O_3}$).
topics.asked_as: 'What is break-point chlorination? Explain with a curve and give its advantages' (5 marks); 'Distinguish sterilization and disinfection' (2 marks); 'Explain the disinfecting action of chlorine / bleaching powder with equations' (3 marks); short numerical on bleaching powder dose.

questions.q: Distinguish between sterilization and disinfection of water.
questions.a:
| Sterilization | Disinfection |
|---|---|
| Destroys **all** micro-organisms, pathogenic and non-pathogenic, including spores | Destroys only **pathogenic** (disease-causing) organisms |
| Needs severe treatment (autoclave, prolonged boiling, high doses) | Moderate chemical/physical treatment (chlorine, ozone, UV) |
| Not required, and uneconomical, for drinking water | The aim of municipal water treatment |

In water chemistry texts the two words are often used loosely for the same step; the exam expects the distinction above.

questions.q: Explain the disinfecting action of bleaching powder and of chlorine. Why does pH matter?
questions.a:
**Bleaching powder** in water liberates chlorine:
$$\mathrm{CaOCl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow Ca(OH)_2 + Cl_2}$$
**Chlorine** (from bleaching powder or added as gas) hydrolyses to hypochlorous acid:
$$\mathrm{Cl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow HOCl + HCl}$$
**HOCl** is the real germicide. Being small and uncharged it penetrates the cell wall of bacteria and destroys them by inactivating (oxidising) their essential enzymes:
$$\mathrm{HOCl + Germs \rightarrow Germs\ killed}$$
**pH**: $\mathrm{HOCl \rightleftharpoons H^+ + OCl^-}$. Below about pH 6.5 most chlorine is present as HOCl, which is roughly 80 times more effective than $\mathrm{OCl^-}$; at high pH $\mathrm{OCl^-}$ predominates and disinfection is slower. Hence chlorination is most effective in slightly acidic to neutral water.

questions.q: What is break-point chlorination? Explain with the help of a curve and state its advantages.
questions.a:
**Break-point chlorination** is the addition of chlorine just beyond the dose at which all reducing substances, ammonia/chloramines and organic matter have been oxidised, so that any further chlorine appears as **free residual chlorine**.

**Curve** (chlorine applied on x-axis, residual chlorine on y-axis):
- **A to B**: added chlorine is consumed by reducing agents ($\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, $\mathrm{NO_2^-}$, organics); little or no residual.
- **B to C**: chlorine combines with $\mathrm{NH_3}$ and organics to form **chloramines** and chloro-organic compounds; combined residual rises.
- **C to D**: further chlorine oxidises the chloramines and chloro-organics to $\mathrm{N_2}$, $\mathrm{N_2O}$, $\mathrm{NCl_3}$; residual **falls** to a minimum at D, the **break-point**.
- **Beyond D**: no demand remains; free residual chlorine rises in proportion to the dose added.

**Advantages**: (i) complete destruction of pathogens; (ii) oxidises organic matter, $\mathrm{NH_3}$ and other reducing substances; (iii) removes colour, odour and taste; (iv) a small free residual (0.1-0.2 ppm) protects water against recontamination in the distribution system; (v) prevents growth of weeds and algae in mains.

questions.q: Give the advantages and disadvantages of chlorine, ozone and UV as disinfectants.
questions.a:
**Chlorine**: *Advantages*: cheap, effective in small doses, easy to dose, stable, leaves residual that protects mains. *Disadvantages*: excess gives taste and odour and irritates mucous membranes; forms trihalomethanes with organics; less effective at high pH; toxic gas to handle.

**Ozone**: *Advantages*: powerful germicide (nascent oxygen, $\mathrm{O_3 \rightarrow O_2 + [O]}$), also removes colour, odour and taste, short contact time, no harmful taste. *Disadvantages*: costly, must be generated on site, unstable, leaves no residual.

**UV light**: *Advantages*: no chemicals added, no taste or odour, fast, kills bacteria and viruses. *Disadvantages*: needs clear water (turbidity shields microbes), costly for large volumes, leaves no residual.

questions.q: Bleaching powder contains 30% available chlorine. How much bleaching powder is needed to give 1 ppm of chlorine to 1,000,000 L of water?
questions.a:
1 ppm = 1 mg per litre.
Chlorine required $= 1\ \text{mg/L} \times 1{,}000{,}000\ \text{L} = 10^6\ \text{mg} = 1\ \text{kg}$.
Bleaching powder supplies 30 g of available chlorine per 100 g, so
$$\text{Bleaching powder} = \frac{1\ \text{kg} \times 100}{30} = 3.33\ \text{kg}$$
**About 3.33 kg of bleaching powder.**

questions.q: Why is residual chlorine maintained in water supplied to towns? What is the usual value?
questions.a: After treatment, water travels a long way through pipes where it can be recontaminated through leaks, joints and back-siphonage. A small **free residual chlorine**, about **0.1-0.2 ppm** at the consumer's tap, continues to kill any pathogens that enter, prevents growth of algae and slime in mains, and its presence is a check that the water was adequately disinfected. It is kept low so it causes no taste or health problem.

questions.q: The active disinfecting species when chlorine is added to water is:
questions.a: $\mathrm{Cl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow HOCl + HCl}$; HOCl penetrates the cell and inactivates enzymes.

questions.q: In break-point chlorination, the break-point is the dose at which:
options: Residual chlorine is at its minimum after chloramines are destroyed, and free residual begins to appear
questions.a: After the chloramines are oxidised, residual falls to a minimum (break-point); beyond it free chlorine rises with dose.

topics.why: Hardness numericals (from salt analysis or EDTA titres) and the EDTA method are in essentially every CY1107-type paper for 5-10 marks.
topics.gist:
**Hardness** is the soap-destroying property of water, caused mainly by dissolved $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ salts: $\mathrm{2C_{17}H_{35}COONa + Ca^{2+} \rightarrow (C_{17}H_{35}COO)_2Ca\downarrow + 2Na^+}$.

**Temporary (carbonate) hardness**: due to bicarbonates of Ca and Mg; removed by **boiling**:
$\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + H_2O + CO_2}$; $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + 2CO_2}$.
**Permanent (non-carbonate) hardness**: due to chlorides, sulphates (and nitrates) of Ca and Mg; not removed by boiling. Total = temporary + permanent.

Hardness is expressed as **$\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalents** because $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ has molar mass 100 (equivalent mass 50), making calculation easy, and it is insoluble so it is the usual precipitate:
$$\text{Hardness as CaCO}_3 = \frac{\text{mass of salt (mg/L)} \times 100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$$
Units: **ppm** (parts per $10^6$) = **mg/L**; **degree Clark** (1 part per 70,000); **degree French** (1 part per $10^5$). $1\ \text{ppm} = 0.07\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{Cl} = 0.1\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{Fr}$.

**Disadvantages**: *domestic*: wastes soap, curdy scum, poor cooking of pulses, scale in kettles. *Industrial*: textile (spots, uneven dyeing), sugar (deliquescent sugar, poor crystallisation), paper (reacts with sizing chemicals, poor gloss), laundry (wastes soap, discoloured fabrics). *Boilers*: **scale and sludge** (heat loss, overheating, explosion risk), **caustic embrittlement**, **corrosion**, **priming and foaming**.

**EDTA method**: $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$/$\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ with **EBT** at pH 10 ($\mathrm{NH_3}$-$\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$ buffer) give a **wine-red** complex; EDTA, a stronger chelator, takes the metal, and the end point is **blue** (free EBT). Titrate before (total) and after boiling (permanent).
key_points: Temporary hardness: $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$, $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$; removed by boiling.
Permanent hardness: chlorides, sulphates, nitrates of Ca and Mg; not removed by boiling.
Expressed as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalents: molar mass 100, equivalent mass 50.

Multiplying factor = 100 / molar mass: $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ 162, $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ 146, $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ 136, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ 111, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ 120, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ 95, $\mathrm{MgCO_3}$ 84, $\mathrm{Mg(NO_3)_2}$ 148.
$\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$ (61): factor 100/122 (two $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$ per $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$); $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (44): factor 100/44.
Boiler troubles: scale, sludge, caustic embrittlement, corrosion, priming and foaming.
EDTA titration: EBT indicator, $\mathrm{NH_3}$-$\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$ buffer pH 10, wine-red to blue.
Total hardness from raw water titre; permanent from boiled, filtered water; temporary = total − permanent.
formulas: $\text{Hardness (ppm as CaCO}_3) = \dfrac{\text{salt (mg/L)} \times 100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$ — $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent
$\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} CaCO_3\downarrow + H_2O + CO_2}$ — removal of temporary hardness
$\mathrm{M^{2+} + EBT \rightarrow [M\text{-}EBT]}$ (wine red); $\mathrm{[M\text{-}EBT] + EDTA \rightarrow [M\text{-}EDTA] + EBT}$ (blue) — EDTA end point
$\text{Hardness (ppm)} = \dfrac{V_{\text{EDTA}} \times (\text{mg CaCO}_3 \text{ per mL EDTA}) \times 1000}{V_{\text{water}}}$ — EDTA calculation
traps: Using 100/61 for $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$: the factor is 100/122, since two $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$ correspond to one $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$.
Counting $\mathrm{NaCl}$, $\mathrm{KCl}$ or $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ in hardness: only Ca, Mg (and Fe, Al) salts cause hardness.
Putting $\mathrm{MgCO_3}$ or $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ in permanent hardness: dissolved carbonates are counted as temporary.
Swapping Clark and French: Clark is per 70,000 (1 ppm = 0.07 °Cl), French per $10^5$ (1 ppm = 0.1 °Fr).
Forgetting the ×1000/V(sample) step in EDTA calculations: hardness is per litre.
Running EDTA titration without the pH 10 buffer: EBT does not give a sharp colour change and the Mg complex is unstable at low pH.
Saying boiling removes all hardness: permanent hardness remains.
topics.asked_as: 'What is hardness? Distinguish temporary and permanent hardness' (3 marks); numerical from salt analysis giving temporary, permanent and total hardness in ppm, °Cl, °Fr (5 marks); 'Describe the EDTA method for estimating hardness' with calculation (5-7 marks); 'Disadvantages of hard water in boilers / industry' (3-5 marks).

questions.q: Distinguish between temporary and permanent hardness. Why is hardness expressed in terms of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalents?
questions.a:
| Temporary (carbonate) hardness | Permanent (non-carbonate) hardness |
|---|---|
| Due to bicarbonates of Ca and Mg | Due to chlorides, sulphates, nitrates of Ca and Mg |
| Removed by boiling: $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + H_2O + CO_2}$; $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + 2CO_2}$ | Not removed by boiling; needs lime-soda, zeolite or ion exchange |

**Why $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$**: (i) its molar mass is 100 and equivalent mass 50, whole numbers that make the conversion simple; (ii) it is the most common insoluble salt precipitated in softening; so different salts can be added on a common basis:
$$\text{Hardness as CaCO}_3 = \frac{\text{mass of salt} \times 100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$$

questions.q: A water sample contains $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ = 32.4 mg/L, $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ = 29.2 mg/L, $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ = 27.2 mg/L and $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ = 9.5 mg/L. Calculate the temporary, permanent and total hardness in ppm, °Cl and °Fr.
questions.a:
Convert each salt to $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent: $\dfrac{\text{mg/L} \times 100}{\text{molar mass}}$

| Salt | mg/L | Molar mass | As $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (ppm) |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ | 32.4 | 162 | $32.4 \times 100/162 = 20$ |
| $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ | 29.2 | 146 | $29.2 \times 100/146 = 20$ |
| $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ | 27.2 | 136 | $27.2 \times 100/136 = 20$ |
| $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ | 9.5 | 95 | $9.5 \times 100/95 = 10$ |

**Temporary hardness** (bicarbonates) $= 20 + 20 = 40$ ppm $= 40 \times 0.07 = 2.8\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{Cl} = 4.0\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{Fr}$

**Permanent hardness** (sulphate, chloride) $= 20 + 10 = 30$ ppm $= 2.1\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{Cl} = 3.0\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{Fr}$

**Total hardness** $= 40 + 30 = 70$ ppm $= 4.9\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{Cl} = 7.0\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{Fr}$

questions.q: 50 mL of a water sample required 25.0 mL of EDTA solution for titration using EBT indicator at pH 10. Another 50 mL of the same sample, after boiling, filtering and making up, required 15.0 mL of the same EDTA. 1 mL of the EDTA is equivalent to 0.5 mg of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$. Calculate total, permanent and temporary hardness.
questions.a:
**Total hardness**: 25.0 mL EDTA $\equiv 25.0 \times 0.5 = 12.5$ mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ in 50 mL water.
$$\text{Total} = \frac{12.5 \times 1000}{50} = 250\ \text{mg/L} = 250\ \text{ppm}$$

**Permanent hardness** (boiled sample): 15.0 mL EDTA $\equiv 15.0 \times 0.5 = 7.5$ mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ in 50 mL.
$$\text{Permanent} = \frac{7.5 \times 1000}{50} = 150\ \text{ppm}$$

**Temporary hardness** $= 250 - 150 = 100$ ppm.

(1 mL EDTA = 0.5 mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ corresponds to 0.005 M EDTA, since 1 mL × 0.005 mmol/mL × 100 mg/mmol = 0.5 mg.)

**Total 250 ppm, permanent 150 ppm, temporary 100 ppm.**

questions.q: Describe the EDTA method for the estimation of hardness of water, giving the principle and the reactions involved.
questions.a:
**Principle**: EDTA (as its disodium salt) forms stable, colourless 1:1 chelates with $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$. The indicator **Eriochrome Black T (EBT)** is blue at pH 10 and forms a less stable **wine-red** complex with these ions. At the end point EDTA takes the metal from the indicator and the colour turns **blue**.
$$\mathrm{M^{2+} + EBT \rightarrow [M\text{-}EBT]}\ \text{(wine red)}$$
$$\mathrm{[M\text{-}EBT] + EDTA \rightarrow [M\text{-}EDTA] + EBT}\ \text{(blue)}$$
**pH 10 buffer** ($\mathrm{NH_4OH}$-$\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$) is used because the metal-EDTA complexes (especially Mg) are stable and EBT shows its blue colour only around this pH.

**Procedure**:
1. **Standardise EDTA** against standard hard water (1 mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ per mL): 50 mL standard hard water + 10 mL buffer + 2-3 drops EBT, titrate to blue: $V_1$ mL.
2. **Total hardness**: 50 mL sample + buffer + EBT, titrate: $V_2$ mL.
3. **Permanent hardness**: boil 250 mL sample to about 50 mL, filter, make up to 250 mL; titrate 50 mL: $V_3$ mL.

**Calculation**: 1 mL EDTA $\equiv 50/V_1$ mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$.
Total $= \dfrac{V_2}{V_1} \times 1000$ ppm; Permanent $= \dfrac{V_3}{V_1} \times 1000$ ppm; Temporary = Total − Permanent.

questions.q: Discuss the disadvantages of hard water in boilers.
questions.a:
1. **Scale and sludge**: on evaporation, salts deposit. Loose, slimy precipitates ($\mathrm{MgCO_3}$, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$) form **sludge** in cooler parts; hard adherent coatings ($\mathrm{CaSO_4}$, $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$, $\mathrm{CaSiO_3}$, $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$) form **scale** on hot surfaces. Scale is a poor conductor, so fuel is wasted, the metal overheats and weakens, and cracks in scale can let water hit the red-hot plate, causing sudden steam generation and **explosion**; sludge chokes pipes.
2. **Caustic embrittlement**: $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ from softening hydrolyses at high pressure ($\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + CO_2}$); concentrated NaOH in fine cracks and rivets attacks the iron (forming sodium ferroate), making the boiler brittle.
3. **Boiler corrosion**: dissolved $\mathrm{O_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and acids from hydrolysis of $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ ($\mathrm{MgCl_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2 + 2HCl}$) corrode the boiler metal.
4. **Priming and foaming**: dissolved salts, oils and suspended matter cause foam; water droplets are carried with steam (priming), giving wet steam and damaging turbines.

questions.q: Give two disadvantages each of hard water in domestic use and in the textile, sugar and paper industries.
questions.a:
**Domestic**: (i) wastes soap, forms insoluble curdy scum; (ii) pulses cook poorly and food tastes bad; scale forms in kettles and geysers (fuel wastage).
**Laundry/textile**: soap is wasted; insoluble Ca/Mg soaps stick to fabric, causing spots, uneven dyeing and loss of brightness; Fe salts give stains.
**Sugar**: sulphates and other salts cause deliquescent sugar and poor crystallisation, lowering yield.
**Paper**: Ca and Mg salts react with sizing chemicals (rosin, alum), giving poor gloss and smoothness; Fe salts change colour.

questions.q: The multiplying factor to convert $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ into $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent is:
questions.a: Molar mass of $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ = 146, so factor = 100/146. (100/162 is for $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$, 100/84 for $\mathrm{MgCO_3}$.)

questions.q: In the EDTA titration of hard water using EBT indicator at pH 10, the colour change at the end point is:
questions.a: The metal-EBT complex is wine red; when EDTA has taken all $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$/$\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, free EBT appears blue.

topics.why: A favourite 5-mark 'explain the mechanism and prevention' question; the concentration cell and the $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4 : NaOH}$ ratios are what the marker looks for.
topics.gist:
**Caustic embrittlement** is a type of boiler corrosion (a form of **stress corrosion**) caused by a high concentration of **free alkali (NaOH)** in boiler water. It makes the boiler metal **brittle**, and fine **intercrystalline cracks** appear at points of high local stress: **rivets, bends and joints**.

**Cause.** Water softened by the lime-soda process carries some residual $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$. At high pressure it hydrolyses:
$$\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + CO_2}$$
The water then turns caustic. It seeps into hair cracks and crevices, where it evaporates and the NaOH **concentrates** to a high value.

**Mechanism (concentration cell).** The cell is
$$\text{Iron at rivets, bends, joints (under stress)} \mid \text{conc. NaOH} \mid \text{dil. NaOH} \mid \text{Iron at plane surfaces}$$
Iron in contact with **concentrated NaOH** (in the cracks, under stress) is **anodic** and dissolves as **sodium ferroate**, $\mathrm{Na_2FeO_2}$. Iron in contact with **dilute NaOH** (the main body) is cathodic. Sodium ferroate decomposes to $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ (magnetite) and **regenerates NaOH**, so the attack continues and the cracks grow until the metal fails.

**Prevention.** (1) Soften with **sodium phosphate** instead of $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$. (2) Add **tannin or lignin**, which block the hair cracks so NaOH cannot seep in. (3) Add **$\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$**, which also blocks the cracks, keeping $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4 : NaOH}$ at **1:1, 2:1 and 3:1** for working pressures up to 10, up to 20 and above 20 atm.
key_points: Caustic embrittlement: brittleness and intercrystalline cracking of boiler metal due to high concentration of NaOH; a form of stress corrosion.
Source of NaOH: residual $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ from lime-soda softening hydrolyses at high pressure: $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + CO_2}$.
NaOH seeps into hair cracks, water evaporates, NaOH concentrates there.
Concentration cell: iron under stress in conc. NaOH (rivets, bends, joints) is the anode; iron in dil. NaOH (plane surfaces) is the cathode.
Anodic iron dissolves as sodium ferroate $\mathrm{Na_2FeO_2}$.
$\mathrm{Na_2FeO_2}$ decomposes to $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ and regenerates NaOH, so a small amount of NaOH keeps the attack going.
Prevention: sodium phosphate instead of sodium carbonate as softening reagent.
Prevention: tannin or lignin to block hair cracks.
Prevention: $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ in ratio $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4 : NaOH}$ = 1:1 (up to 10 atm), 2:1 (up to 20 atm), 3:1 (above 20 atm).
formulas: $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + CO_2}$ — hydrolysis of residual soda at high pressure
$\mathrm{Fe + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2FeO_2 + H_2}$ — anodic iron dissolves as sodium ferroate
$\mathrm{3Na_2FeO_2 + 4H_2O \rightarrow 6NaOH + Fe_3O_4 + H_2}$ — ferroate decomposes, NaOH regenerated
$\mathrm{Na_2SO_4 : NaOH} = 1:1,\ 2:1,\ 3:1$ — for pressures up to 10, up to 20, above 20 atm
traps: Calling the stressed iron in concentrated NaOH the cathode: it is the **anode** (it dissolves).
Writing sodium ferrate ($\mathrm{Na_2FeO_4}$) instead of sodium **ferroate** $\mathrm{Na_2FeO_2}$.
Missing the regeneration of NaOH, which is why the attack is continuous.
Mixing up the $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4 : NaOH}$ ratios: the ratio rises with pressure (1:1, 2:1, 3:1).
Saying the cause is $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ attacking iron directly: it is the NaOH formed by its hydrolysis.
Recommending more $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ for softening: replace it with sodium phosphate.
