questions.q: What is caustic embrittlement? Explain its mechanism and the methods of prevention.
questions.a:
**Caustic embrittlement** is a type of boiler corrosion in which the boiler material becomes brittle and develops fine intercrystalline cracks at stressed parts (rivets, bends, joints) because of a high concentration of free NaOH in the boiler water.

**Cause**: water softened by the lime-soda process contains residual $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$, which hydrolyses at high pressure:
$$\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + CO_2}$$
The caustic water flows into minute hair cracks; the water evaporates and NaOH concentrates there.

**Mechanism**: a concentration cell is set up:
$$\text{Iron at rivets, bends, joints} \mid \text{conc. NaOH} \mid \text{dil. NaOH} \mid \text{Iron at plane surfaces}$$
Iron under stress in contact with concentrated NaOH is anodic and dissolves as sodium ferroate:
$$\mathrm{Fe + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2FeO_2 + H_2}$$
Sodium ferroate decomposes, depositing magnetite and regenerating NaOH:
$$\mathrm{3Na_2FeO_2 + 4H_2O \rightarrow 6NaOH + Fe_3O_4 + H_2}$$
The regenerated NaOH continues the attack, so the cracks deepen and the metal becomes brittle.

**Prevention**:
1. Use sodium phosphate instead of sodium carbonate as the softening reagent.
2. Add tannin or lignin to boiler water; they block the hair cracks and pits.
3. Add $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$, which also blocks the cracks; $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4 : NaOH}$ is kept at 1:1, 2:1 and 3:1 for pressures up to 10, up to 20 and above 20 atm respectively.

questions.q: Why is caustic embrittlement called a form of stress corrosion? Where in a boiler does it occur?
questions.a: The attack is concentrated where the metal is under **stress**: rivets, bends and joints. Stressed iron in contact with concentrated NaOH becomes anodic relative to unstressed iron in dilute NaOH and dissolves along the grain boundaries, giving intercrystalline cracks. Corrosion that needs both a corrosive medium and tensile stress is stress corrosion; caustic embrittlement is that with NaOH as the medium.

questions.q: Why is sodium phosphate preferred to sodium carbonate for softening water for high-pressure boilers?
questions.a: Residual $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ hydrolyses at high pressure, $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + CO_2}$, making the water caustic; the NaOH concentrates in cracks and causes caustic embrittlement, while the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ released makes the steam corrosive. Sodium phosphate does not produce free NaOH this way, and it precipitates $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ as soft phosphate sludge, so it softens without causing embrittlement.

questions.q: A boiler works at 15 atm and its water contains 40 ppm of NaOH. How much $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ should be present to prevent caustic embrittlement? What would it be if the boiler worked at 25 atm?
questions.a:
For pressures up to 20 atm, $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4 : NaOH} = 2:1$:
$$\mathrm{Na_2SO_4} = 2 \times 40 = 80\ \text{ppm}$$
Above 20 atm the ratio is $3:1$:
$$\mathrm{Na_2SO_4} = 3 \times 40 = 120\ \text{ppm}$$
**80 ppm at 15 atm; 120 ppm at 25 atm.**

questions.q: Write the cell set up during caustic embrittlement and identify the anode and the cathode.
questions.a:
$$\text{Iron at rivets, bends, joints} \mid \text{conc. NaOH} \mid \text{dil. NaOH} \mid \text{Iron at plane surfaces}$$
**Anode**: iron at the stressed parts (rivets, bends, joints) in contact with concentrated NaOH; it dissolves as $\mathrm{Na_2FeO_2}$.
**Cathode**: iron at plane surfaces in contact with dilute NaOH; it is protected.

questions.q: In caustic embrittlement, the anodic iron dissolves as:
questions.a: Iron dissolves in concentrated NaOH as sodium ferroate $\mathrm{Na_2FeO_2}$, which then decomposes to $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ and regenerates NaOH.

questions.q: To prevent caustic embrittlement in a boiler working above 20 atm, the ratio $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4 : NaOH}$ is kept at:
questions.a: 1:1 up to 10 atm, 2:1 up to 20 atm, 3:1 above 20 atm.

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT help prevent caustic embrittlement?
questions.a: Excess $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ is the cause: it hydrolyses to NaOH at high pressure. The other three are the standard remedies.

topics.why: The three causes with their equations, and the removal of oxygen by sulphite, hydrazine and deaeration, are asked as a 5-mark question in nearly every paper.
topics.gist:
**Boiler corrosion** is the decay or disintegration of boiler material by chemical or electrochemical attack of its environment. Its three main causes:

**1. Dissolved oxygen** (the chief cause). Water holds about 8 ppm $\mathrm{O_2}$ at room temperature; on heating it is released and attacks iron:
$$\mathrm{2Fe + 2H_2O + O_2 \rightarrow 2Fe(OH)_2}$$
$$\mathrm{4Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2[Fe_2O_3 \cdot 2H_2O]}\ \text{(rust)}$$
Removal: **sodium sulphite**, $\mathrm{2Na_2SO_3 + O_2 \rightarrow 2Na_2SO_4}$; **hydrazine**, $\mathrm{N_2H_4 + O_2 \rightarrow N_2 + 2H_2O}$, which is **ideal** because its products are nitrogen and water, so it adds **no dissolved solids**; or **mechanical deaeration**, spraying water over perforated plates at **high temperature and low pressure** (vacuum), which lowers the solubility of gases.

**2. Dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$.** It forms carbonic acid, $\mathrm{CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3}$, which slowly attacks the metal. It also comes from bicarbonates on heating: $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow MgCO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}$. Removed by **ammonia**, $\mathrm{2NH_4OH + CO_2 \rightarrow (NH_4)_2CO_3 + H_2O}$, or by mechanical deaeration along with $\mathrm{O_2}$.

**3. Acids from dissolved salts.** $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ hydrolyses at high temperature:
$$\mathrm{MgCl_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2 + 2HCl}$$
The HCl attacks iron, $\mathrm{Fe + 2HCl \rightarrow FeCl_2 + H_2}$, and $\mathrm{FeCl_2}$ hydrolyses to give the HCl back, so the acid works in a **chain**: a small amount of $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ causes extensive corrosion. Remedy: neutralise the acid with **alkali**.
key_points: Boiler corrosion: decay of boiler material by chemical or electrochemical attack of its environment.
Three causes: dissolved $\mathrm{O_2}$, dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$, acids from hydrolysis of dissolved salts (chiefly $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$).
Dissolved oxygen: $\mathrm{2Fe + 2H_2O + O_2 \rightarrow 2Fe(OH)_2}$, then $\mathrm{4Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2[Fe_2O_3 \cdot 2H_2O]}$ (rust).
$\mathrm{O_2}$ removal by sodium sulphite: $\mathrm{2Na_2SO_3 + O_2 \rightarrow 2Na_2SO_4}$ (but the sulphate adds dissolved solids).
$\mathrm{O_2}$ removal by hydrazine: $\mathrm{N_2H_4 + O_2 \rightarrow N_2 + 2H_2O}$; ideal because no salts are added.
Mechanical deaeration: water sprayed over perforated plates in a tower, heated, under vacuum; high temperature and low pressure expel $\mathrm{O_2}$ and $\mathrm{CO_2}$.
$\mathrm{CO_2}$ forms carbonic acid; also released from bicarbonates: $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow MgCO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}$.
$\mathrm{CO_2}$ removal by ammonia: $\mathrm{2NH_4OH + CO_2 \rightarrow (NH_4)_2CO_3 + H_2O}$, or by deaeration.
$\mathrm{MgCl_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2 + 2HCl}$; HCl attacks iron and is regenerated from $\mathrm{FeCl_2}$, so a little $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ does a lot of damage; neutralise with alkali.
traps: Calling sodium sulphite the ideal deoxidiser: it adds $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ to the water; **hydrazine** is ideal because it gives only $\mathrm{N_2}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$.
Saying deaeration works at low temperature and high pressure: gas solubility falls at **high temperature and low pressure**.
Writing the rust equation unbalanced; check 4 : 1 : 2.
Forgetting that HCl is **regenerated**, which is why a little $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ is so harmful.
Treating $\mathrm{CO_2}$ only as dissolved from air: bicarbonate decomposition in the boiler is a major source.
Confusing boiler corrosion with caustic embrittlement: the latter is a separate, NaOH-driven stress corrosion.
topics.asked_as: 'What is boiler corrosion? Discuss its causes and prevention with equations' (5-7 marks); 'Why is hydrazine an ideal deoxidiser?' (2 marks); 'How does a small amount of $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ cause extensive corrosion?' (2-3 marks); MCQs on reagents.

questions.q: What is boiler corrosion? Discuss the causes of boiler corrosion and how each is prevented, with equations.
questions.a:
**Boiler corrosion** is the decay or disintegration of boiler material by chemical or electrochemical attack of its environment.

**1. Dissolved oxygen.** Released on heating, it attacks iron:
$$\mathrm{2Fe + 2H_2O + O_2 \rightarrow 2Fe(OH)_2}$$
$$\mathrm{4Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2[Fe_2O_3 \cdot 2H_2O]}\ (\text{rust})$$
*Removal*: (a) sodium sulphite, $\mathrm{2Na_2SO_3 + O_2 \rightarrow 2Na_2SO_4}$; (b) hydrazine, $\mathrm{N_2H_4 + O_2 \rightarrow N_2 + 2H_2O}$, ideal since it adds no dissolved solids; (c) mechanical deaeration: water is sprayed over perforated plates in a tower, heated from the sides and connected to a vacuum pump; high temperature and low pressure expel dissolved gases.

**2. Dissolved carbon dioxide.** Forms carbonic acid, $\mathrm{CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3}$, which corrodes the metal slowly. It is also released from bicarbonates: $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow MgCO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}$.
*Removal*: (a) ammonia, $\mathrm{2NH_4OH + CO_2 \rightarrow (NH_4)_2CO_3 + H_2O}$; (b) mechanical deaeration along with oxygen.

**3. Acids from dissolved salts.** $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ hydrolyses at high temperature:
$$\mathrm{MgCl_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2 + 2HCl}$$
HCl attacks iron and is regenerated:
$$\mathrm{Fe + 2HCl \rightarrow FeCl_2 + H_2}$$
$$\mathrm{FeCl_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2 + 2HCl}$$
So a small amount of $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ causes extensive corrosion.
*Prevention*: neutralise the acid by adding a calculated amount of alkali.

questions.q: Why is hydrazine considered an ideal reagent for removing dissolved oxygen from boiler feed water?
questions.a:
$$\mathrm{N_2H_4 + O_2 \rightarrow N_2 + 2H_2O}$$
The products are nitrogen (a harmless gas that escapes) and water. Unlike sodium sulphite, which leaves $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ in the water, hydrazine adds **no dissolved salts**, so it does not raise the dissolved solids or contribute to scale, priming or foaming.

questions.q: Explain how a small amount of $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ in boiler water can cause a large amount of corrosion.
questions.a:
At boiler temperature $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ hydrolyses, liberating HCl:
$$\mathrm{MgCl_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2 + 2HCl}$$
HCl attacks the iron:
$$\mathrm{Fe + 2HCl \rightarrow FeCl_2 + H_2}$$
$\mathrm{FeCl_2}$ hydrolyses and gives back the HCl:
$$\mathrm{FeCl_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2 + 2HCl}$$
The HCl is not consumed; it is regenerated each cycle and keeps attacking fresh iron. Hence a little $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ produces extensive corrosion. It is prevented by neutralising the acid with alkali.

questions.q: A boiler feed water contains 8 ppm of dissolved oxygen. Calculate the amount (in ppm) of (a) sodium sulphite and (b) hydrazine needed to remove it. (Na = 23, S = 32, O = 16, N = 14, H = 1)
questions.a:
(a) $\mathrm{2Na_2SO_3 + O_2 \rightarrow 2Na_2SO_4}$

Molar mass of $\mathrm{Na_2SO_3} = 2(23) + 32 + 3(16) = 126$; 32 parts of $\mathrm{O_2}$ need $2 \times 126 = 252$ parts of $\mathrm{Na_2SO_3}$.
$$\mathrm{Na_2SO_3} = \frac{252}{32} \times 8 = 63\ \text{ppm}$$

(b) $\mathrm{N_2H_4 + O_2 \rightarrow N_2 + 2H_2O}$

Molar mass of $\mathrm{N_2H_4} = 2(14) + 4(1) = 32$; 32 parts of $\mathrm{O_2}$ need 32 parts of $\mathrm{N_2H_4}$.
$$\mathrm{N_2H_4} = \frac{32}{32} \times 8 = 8\ \text{ppm}$$

**Sodium sulphite 63 ppm; hydrazine 8 ppm.**

questions.q: Describe mechanical deaeration of boiler feed water.
questions.a: Water is sprayed from the top of a tall steel tower fitted with **perforated plates**, which spread it into thin films with large surface area. The tower is **heated** from the sides (steam jacket) and connected to a **vacuum pump**. At high temperature and low pressure the solubility of gases is low, so dissolved $\mathrm{O_2}$ and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ are expelled and pumped out. Deaerated water is drawn from the bottom. It removes both corrosive gases without adding chemicals.

questions.q: The ideal chemical for removing dissolved oxygen from boiler water is:
questions.a: Hydrazine gives only $\mathrm{N_2}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$, adding no salts. Sodium sulphite works but leaves $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$; ammonia removes $\mathrm{CO_2}$, not $\mathrm{O_2}$.

questions.q: Dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$ in boiler water is removed by adding:
questions.a: $\mathrm{2NH_4OH + CO_2 \rightarrow (NH_4)_2CO_3 + H_2O}$. Mechanical deaeration also removes it.

questions.q: Mechanical deaeration removes dissolved gases most effectively at:
questions.a: Solubility of gases decreases with rise of temperature and fall of pressure, so the tower is heated and kept under vacuum.

topics.why: 'Distinguish priming and foaming; give causes and prevention' is a standard 3-5 mark question, often paired with carry-over.
key_points: Priming: water droplets carried with steam; the steam is wet.
Causes of priming: high steam velocity, very high water level, sudden boiling, improper boiler design, high dissolved solids.
Prevention of priming: mechanical steam purifiers, low water level, avoiding rapid change in steaming rate, efficient softening, blow-down.
Foaming: formation of persistent bubbles that do not break easily.
Cause of foaming: oils and alkalis that lower the surface tension of water.
Prevention of foaming: antifoams such as castor oil; remove oil with sodium aluminate; replace concentrated water with fresh water.
Priming and foaming together are called carry-over.
Effects: deposits on superheaters and turbine blades, loss of efficiency, wrong water-level readings, possible damage to machinery.
formulas: $\mathrm{NaAlO_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow NaOH + Al(OH)_3}$ — sodium aluminate gives the floc that entraps oil
traps: Defining priming as foam: priming is **wet steam** (droplets carried over); foaming is **persistent bubbles**.
Saying antifoams raise surface tension: oils and alkalis lower it, and castor oil acts by spreading over the bubble film and breaking it.
Saying more castor oil is always better: excess castor oil itself causes foaming.
Giving a high water level as prevention: a high water level is a cause of priming.
Forgetting the collective term carry-over.
topics.asked_as: 'What are priming and foaming? Give their causes and methods of prevention' (5 marks); 'Distinguish between priming and foaming' (2-3 marks); 'What is carry-over?' (2 marks); MCQs on causes and antifoams.

questions.q: What are priming and foaming? Discuss their causes, prevention and harmful effects.
questions.a:
**Priming**: the process in which some particles of liquid water are carried along with the steam, producing **wet steam**.
*Causes*: (i) high steam velocity; (ii) very high water level in the boiler; (iii) sudden boiling or sudden increase in steam demand; (iv) improper boiler design with too little steam space; (v) high concentration of dissolved solids.
*Prevention*: fitting mechanical steam purifiers, keeping the water level low, avoiding rapid change in steaming rate, efficient softening and filtration of feed water, and blow-down of concentrated water.

**Foaming**: the formation of small but **persistent bubbles** at the water surface which do not break easily.
*Cause*: oils and alkalis in the boiler water, which lower its surface tension.
*Prevention*: adding antifoaming agents like castor oil; removing oil by adding sodium aluminate (its $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ floc entraps the oil); replacing concentrated boiler water with fresh feed water.

Priming and foaming generally occur together and are collectively called **carry-over**.

**Harmful effects**: (i) dissolved salts carried in wet steam deposit on superheater tubes and turbine blades, lowering their efficiency and life; (ii) the useful heat and efficiency of the boiler fall; (iii) the water-level gauge gives false readings, which can lead to overheating; (iv) wet steam can damage engine parts.

questions.q: Distinguish between priming and foaming.
questions.a:
| Priming | Foaming |
|---|---|
| Water droplets are carried with the steam (wet steam). | Persistent bubbles form at the water surface. |
| Caused by high steam velocity, high water level, sudden boiling, faulty design, high dissolved solids. | Caused by oils and alkalis that lower surface tension. |
| Prevented by steam purifiers, low water level, steady steaming, blow-down. | Prevented by antifoams (castor oil), removing oil with sodium aluminate. |

questions.q: What is carry-over? Why is it harmful to turbines?
questions.a: **Carry-over** is the collective term for priming and foaming, in which water and the salts dissolved in it are carried over with the steam. When the wet steam reaches the superheater and turbine, the water evaporates and the salts **deposit on superheater tubes and turbine blades**, reducing their efficiency, unbalancing the blades and shortening their life.

questions.q: How is foaming prevented? Explain the role of sodium aluminate.
questions.a:
Foaming is prevented by (i) adding antifoaming agents such as castor oil in small amount, which spread over the bubble film and break the foam; (ii) removing the oil responsible for foaming; (iii) replacing the concentrated boiler water with fresh feed water.

**Sodium aluminate** hydrolyses to give a gelatinous floc of aluminium hydroxide:
$$\mathrm{NaAlO_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow NaOH + Al(OH)_3}$$
The $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ entraps the oil droplets and settles, so the oil that lowers surface tension is removed.

questions.q: Why does a high water level in the boiler favour priming?
questions.a: With a high water level the **steam space** above the water is small, so the steam leaves close to the boiling surface at high velocity and easily drags water droplets with it, giving wet steam.

questions.q: Foaming in boilers is mainly caused by:
questions.a: Oils and alkalis lower the surface tension of water and stabilise bubbles. High steam velocity causes priming.

questions.q: A commonly used antifoaming agent for boiler water is:
questions.a: Castor oil, added in small amount, breaks the foam. Excess castor oil itself causes foaming.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of priming?
questions.a: Priming is caused by **high** steam velocity, not low.

topics.topic: Scale and sludge: internal and external treatment
topics.why: Scale vs sludge, the disadvantages of scale, and internal conditioning (phosphate, carbonate, calgon) are among the most repeated 5-10 mark questions in the Water unit.
topics.gist:
When hard water evaporates in a boiler, salts concentrate and precipitate.

**Sludge** is a **soft, loose, slimy, non-adherent** precipitate formed in the **colder parts** of the boiler, by salts more soluble in hot water than cold: $\mathrm{MgCO_3}$, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$. It is a poor conductor of heat and can choke pipes, but is easily removed by **blow-down** (draining part of the concentrated water).

**Scale** is a **hard, adherent coating** on the inner walls, hard to remove. Causes: (i) $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}$ in **low-pressure** boilers; (ii) $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$, whose solubility **falls with rising temperature**, the main scale former in **high-pressure** boilers; (iii) $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ from $\mathrm{MgCl_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2 + 2HCl}$; (iv) **silica**, giving calcium or magnesium silicate deposits.

**Disadvantages of scale**: **waste of fuel** (a 0.325 mm scale wastes about 10% fuel, 12 mm about 150%); **overheating** and lowered strength of the plates; **danger of explosion** when the scale cracks and water meets the red-hot metal; **lowered safety**.

**Removal**: mechanical (scraper, wire brush), **thermal shocks**, chemical ($\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ by 5-10% HCl, $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ by **EDTA**).

**Internal treatment** (conditioning inside the boiler): colloidal (kerosene, tannin, agar-agar); **phosphate** ($\mathrm{NaH_2PO_4}$, $\mathrm{Na_2HPO_4}$ or $\mathrm{Na_3PO_4}$ chosen by alkalinity); **carbonate** ($\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$, low-pressure only, turns $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ into $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ sludge); **calgon** (soluble complex); sodium aluminate; EDTA.

**External treatment** softens water **before** it enters the boiler: lime-soda, zeolite and ion exchange processes.
key_points: Sludge: soft, loose, slimy, non-adherent; from $\mathrm{MgCO_3}$, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$; forms in colder parts; removed by blow-down.
Scale: hard, adherent coating; difficult to remove.

Scale formers: $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ from $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ (low-pressure boilers), $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ (high-pressure boilers, solubility falls with temperature), $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ from $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ hydrolysis, silica deposits.
Disadvantages of scale: fuel wastage (0.325 mm scale ~10%, 12 mm ~150% fuel wasted), overheating and weakening of plates, explosion risk, lowered safety.
Scale removal: scraper or wire brush (soft scale), thermal shocks (brittle scale), 5-10% HCl for $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, EDTA for $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$, blow-down for loose scale.
Internal treatment: conditioning inside the boiler by colloidal, phosphate, carbonate, calgon, sodium aluminate or EDTA conditioning.

Phosphate conditioning (high-pressure boilers): $\mathrm{NaH_2PO_4}$ (acidic) for too-alkaline water, $\mathrm{Na_2HPO_4}$ (weakly alkaline) for nearly right alkalinity, $\mathrm{Na_3PO_4}$ (alkaline) for too-acidic water.
Carbonate conditioning only for low-pressure boilers: $\mathrm{CaSO_4 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + Na_2SO_4}$.
Calgon $\mathrm{Na_2[Na_4(PO_3)_6]}$ forms a soluble complex with $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, so neither scale nor sludge forms.
External treatment: softening before the water enters the boiler by lime-soda, zeolite or ion exchange.
formulas: $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}$ — scale in low-pressure boilers
$\mathrm{CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2}$ — chemical removal of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ scale
$\mathrm{MgCl_2 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2 + 2NaCl}$ — NaOH from aluminate precipitates Mg
traps: Swapping scale and sludge: sludge is **soft and loose** (blow-down removes it); scale is **hard and adherent**.

Saying $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ is the main scale in high-pressure boilers: in high-pressure boilers $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ is fairly soluble (as $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$) and **$\mathrm{CaSO_4}$** is the main scale former.
Saying $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ is more soluble in hot water: its solubility **decreases** as temperature rises.
Using carbonate conditioning in high-pressure boilers: residual $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ hydrolyses to NaOH and $\mathrm{CO_2}$, causing caustic embrittlement and corrosion.
Choosing $\mathrm{Na_3PO_4}$ for highly alkaline water: it is for too-acidic water; $\mathrm{NaH_2PO_4}$ is for too-alkaline water.
Saying calgon precipitates calcium: it forms a **soluble** complex.
Confusing internal treatment (inside the boiler) with external treatment (softening before entry).

(5 marks); 'Explain internal treatment of boiler water: phosphate, carbonate and calgon conditioning' (5-7 marks); 'Why is $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ scale more troublesome in high-pressure boilers?' (2 marks); MCQs on reagents and definitions.

questions.q: Distinguish between scale and sludge. Give the causes of each.
questions.a:
| Sludge | Scale |
|---|---|
| Soft, loose, slimy, non-adherent precipitate. | Hard, adherent coating on the inner walls. |
| Forms in the colder parts of the boiler and where flow is slow. | Forms on the heating surfaces. |
| Formed by salts more soluble in hot water than cold: $\mathrm{MgCO_3}$, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$. | Formed by $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (from $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$), $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$, $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ (from $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ hydrolysis), silica. |
| Easily removed by blow-down or a wire brush. | Difficult to remove; needs thermal shocks, scraping or chemicals. |
| Less harmful, though a poor conductor and can choke pipes. | Very harmful: fuel wastage, overheating, explosion risk. |

**Causes of scale**: $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}$ in low-pressure boilers; $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$, whose solubility falls with temperature, in high-pressure boilers; $\mathrm{MgCl_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2 + 2HCl}$; silica forming silicate deposits.

questions.q: What are the disadvantages of scale formation in boilers? How are scales removed?
questions.a:
**Disadvantages**:
1. **Wastage of fuel**: scale is a poor conductor of heat, so more fuel is needed to heat the water. By Jain & Jain's figures, a scale 0.325 mm thick wastes about 10% fuel and one 12 mm thick about 150%.
2. **Lowering of boiler safety**: the plates are overheated, become weak and may deform.
3. **Decrease in efficiency**: deposits in valves and condensers choke them partially.
4. **Danger of explosion**: when a thick scale cracks because of uneven expansion, water suddenly reaches the overheated metal, generates a large amount of steam at once and the high pressure can burst the boiler.

**Removal**:
- Soft scale: scraper, wire brush, or blow-down.
- Brittle scale: **thermal shocks** (heating and suddenly cooling).
- Chemical: $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ scale with 5-10% HCl, $\mathrm{CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2}$; $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ scale with EDTA, which forms a soluble complex.

questions.q: What is internal treatment of boiler water? Explain phosphate, carbonate and calgon conditioning.
questions.a:
**Internal treatment (conditioning)**: the scale-forming impurities are treated **inside the boiler** so that they either stay in solution or form a loose sludge removable by blow-down.

**1. Phosphate conditioning** (high-pressure boilers): sodium phosphate precipitates calcium as soft calcium phosphate sludge:
$$\mathrm{3CaCl_2 + 2Na_3PO_4 \rightarrow Ca_3(PO_4)_2 + 6NaCl}$$
The phosphate is chosen by the alkalinity of the water: $\mathrm{NaH_2PO_4}$ (acidic) if the water is too alkaline, $\mathrm{Na_2HPO_4}$ (weakly alkaline) if the alkalinity is nearly right, $\mathrm{Na_3PO_4}$ (alkaline) if the water is too acidic.

**2. Carbonate conditioning** (low-pressure boilers only): $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ converts $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ to loose $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ sludge:
$$\mathrm{CaSO_4 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + Na_2SO_4}$$
Not used in high-pressure boilers, since excess $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ hydrolyses to NaOH and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (caustic embrittlement, corrosion).

**3. Calgon conditioning**: sodium hexametaphosphate (calgon), $\mathrm{Na_2[Na_4(PO_3)_6]}$, forms a **soluble complex** with $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$:
$$\mathrm{2CaSO_4 + Na_2[Na_4(PO_3)_6] \rightarrow Na_2[Ca_2(PO_3)_6] + 2Na_2SO_4}$$
So neither scale nor sludge forms.

Other methods: colloidal conditioning (kerosene, tannin, agar-agar coat the particles so they form loose sludge), sodium aluminate, EDTA.

questions.q: Why is $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ the main scale former in high-pressure boilers, and why is carbonate conditioning not used there?
questions.a: The solubility of $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ **decreases as the temperature rises** (it is very low at the temperatures of high-pressure boilers), so $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ separates as a hard, adherent scale on the hot surfaces; it is hard to remove even with acid. Carbonate conditioning would convert it to $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, but at high pressure the excess $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ hydrolyses, $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + CO_2}$, causing caustic embrittlement and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ corrosion. Hence phosphate or calgon conditioning is used instead.

questions.q: A boiler water contains 272 mg/L of $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$. Calculate the mass of $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ needed per litre for carbonate conditioning and the mass of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ sludge formed. (Ca = 40, S = 32, O = 16, Na = 23, C = 12)
questions.a:
$$\mathrm{CaSO_4 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + Na_2SO_4}$$
Molar masses: $\mathrm{CaSO_4} = 136$, $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3} = 106$, $\mathrm{CaCO_3} = 100$.

$$\mathrm{Na_2CO_3} = \frac{106}{136} \times 272 = 212\ \text{mg/L}$$
$$\mathrm{CaCO_3} = \frac{100}{136} \times 272 = 200\ \text{mg/L}$$

**212 mg of $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ per litre; 200 mg of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ sludge per litre.**

questions.q: Distinguish between internal and external treatment of boiler water.
questions.a:
**Internal treatment (conditioning)**: carried out **inside the boiler**; the scale-forming salts are converted into loose sludge (removed by blow-down) or kept in solution as complexes. Examples: colloidal, phosphate, carbonate, calgon, sodium aluminate, EDTA conditioning. It is a corrective method.

**External treatment**: the hardness is removed **before** the water enters the boiler. Examples: lime-soda process, zeolite (permutit) process, ion exchange (demineralisation) process. It is a preventive method.

questions.q: Which of the following forms a loose, non-adherent sludge rather than a scale?
questions.a: $\mathrm{MgCO_3}$ (with $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$) forms sludge. $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$, $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and silica form hard scale.

questions.q: Calgon conditioning prevents scale formation because calgon:
questions.a: Sodium hexametaphosphate gives the soluble complex $\mathrm{Na_2[Ca_2(PO_3)_6]}$, so neither scale nor sludge forms.

topics.why: The lime-soda reactions, the hot vs cold comparison and above all the lime and soda requirement numerical appear in almost every first-year water paper.
topics.gist:
**Lime-soda process** is an external softening method: the soluble hardness salts are converted into insoluble $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$, which settle and are filtered off.

**Lime** $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ removes temporary hardness (Ca and Mg bicarbonates), all $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ permanent hardness, free acids, dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$. Note that removing $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ permanent hardness with lime puts an equal amount of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ into the water. **Soda** $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ then removes the calcium permanent hardness, both what was present originally and what lime produced.

Requirements are worked in $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalents: lime $= \tfrac{74}{100}[\ldots]$, soda $= \tfrac{106}{100}[\ldots]$, where 74, 100 and 106 are the molar masses of $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$, $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$. Temporary Mg needs **two** lime (it gives $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$); $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ consumes lime but produces soda, so it is added in lime and subtracted in soda.

**Cold process** (room temperature): the precipitate is finely divided, so a **coagulant** (alum, $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$, sodium aluminate) is added; done in a conical sedimentation tank with a central stirrer and wood-fibre filter; residual hardness 50-60 ppm.

**Hot process** (80-150 °C, using exhaust steam): faster reaction, no coagulant needed, the sludge settles quickly, dissolved gases are expelled, residual hardness 15-30 ppm. Plant: reaction tank, conical sedimentation tank, sand filter.

**Merits**: cheap, raises pH (less corrosion, kills pathogens), removes Fe and Mn. **Demerits**: large sludge disposal, needs skilled control, residual hardness unfit for high-pressure boilers.
key_points: Lime removes temporary hardness, permanent $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$, free acids and $\mathrm{CO_2}$; soda removes permanent $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$.
Lime on permanent $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ and acids produces an equivalent amount of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, so these also appear in the soda bracket.
Temporary Mg hardness counts twice in lime: $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 + 2Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2CaCO_3 + Mg(OH)_2 + 2H_2O}$.
$\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ ($\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$ term): + in lime, − in soda; $\mathrm{NaAlO_2}$ supplies $\mathrm{OH^-}$ and is subtracted from lime.
Convert each salt to $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalents first: mg/L × 100 / molar mass (for 2 mol of a monovalent salt per $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, use twice the molar mass).
Divide by purity fraction: required = pure amount × 100/% purity.
Cold process: room temperature, coagulant needed, slow, residual 50-60 ppm.
Hot process: 80-150 °C, no coagulant, fast, removes dissolved gases, residual 15-30 ppm.
Hot plant: reaction tank (steam + lime + soda + water), conical sedimentation tank, sand filter.
Merits: cheap, raises pH, removes Fe and Mn, reduces pathogens; demerits: sludge, skilled control, residual hardness.
formulas: $\mathrm{L} = \dfrac{74}{100}\left[\text{Temp }\mathrm{Ca^{2+}} + 2\times\text{Temp }\mathrm{Mg^{2+}} + \text{Perm }(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}} + \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + \mathrm{Al^{3+}}) + \mathrm{CO_2} + \mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{HCO_3^-} - \mathrm{NaAlO_2}\right] \times \dfrac{V}{10^6} \times \dfrac{100}{\%\text{ purity}}$ kg — lime requirement (Jain & Jain), V in litres, all terms as ppm $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent
$\text{ppm } \mathrm{CaCO_3}\text{ eq} = \dfrac{\text{mg/L of salt} \times 100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$ — $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent
$\mathrm{MgSO_4 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2 \downarrow + CaSO_4}$; $\mathrm{CaSO_4 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CaCO_3 \downarrow + Na_2SO_4}$ — permanent Mg needs lime and soda
traps: Taking temporary Mg once in lime: it is 2 × temporary Mg.
Putting permanent $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ only in lime: it needs soda too, because lime converts it to an equal amount of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$.
Putting temporary hardness in soda: bicarbonates of Ca and Mg need no soda.
Adding $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ in soda: it is subtracted there, since $\mathrm{2NaHCO_3 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + Na_2CO_3 + 2H_2O}$ makes soda.
Forgetting the purity correction or multiplying instead of dividing by the purity fraction.
Leaving the answer in mg/L when the question asks for kg for a given volume: × V(L) / $10^6$.
Saying hot process needs a coagulant: only the cold process does.
topics.asked_as: 'Describe the hot lime-soda process with a neat diagram' (5-7 marks); 'Compare hot and cold lime-soda processes' (3-4 marks); 'Calculate the lime and soda needed for V litres of water' (5-7 marks, often with impure lime and soda).

questions.q: Calculate the quantities of lime and soda required to soften 10,000 L of water containing: $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ = 162 mg/L, $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ = 73 mg/L, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ = 120 mg/L, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ = 222 mg/L. (Assume lime and soda are 100% pure.)
Describe the hot lime-soda process with a labelled diagram. What are its advantages over the cold process?
questions.a:
**Principle**: hard water is treated with calculated amounts of lime and soda at 80-150 °C, so the hardness salts precipitate as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$.

**Plant** (draw and label): (1) **reaction tank**, where raw water, lime, soda and superheated/exhaust steam are fed and mixed; (2) **conical sedimentation tank**, where the sludge settles to the bottom and is drawn off through a sludge outlet; (3) **sand filter** (fine sand over coarse sand and gravel) that removes the last traces of precipitate; softened water is drawn from the filter.

**Main reactions**
$$\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2CaCO_3\downarrow + 2H_2O}$$
$$\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 + 2Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2CaCO_3\downarrow + Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + 2H_2O}$$
$$\mathrm{MgCl_2 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + CaCl_2}$$
$$\mathrm{CaCl_2 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + 2NaCl}$$

**Advantages over cold process**: reaction is much faster (minutes instead of hours), so capacity is higher; precipitate is coarse and settles fast, so **no coagulant** is needed; dissolved gases ($\mathrm{CO_2}$, air) are driven out; viscosity is lower, so filtration is easier; residual hardness is **15-30 ppm** instead of 50-60 ppm; less excess chemical is needed.

questions.q: Compare the hot and cold lime-soda processes.
questions.a:
| Cold lime-soda | Hot lime-soda |
|---|---|
| Room temperature | 80-150 °C (steam) |
| Slow reaction | Fast reaction |
| Coagulant (alum, $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$, $\mathrm{NaAlO_2}$) needed | No coagulant needed |
| Precipitate fine, settles slowly; filtration difficult | Precipitate coarse, settles fast; easy filtration |
| Residual hardness 50-60 ppm | Residual hardness 15-30 ppm |
| Dissolved gases not removed | Dissolved gases largely removed |
| Low capacity | High capacity |

questions.q: Why is a coagulant needed in the cold lime-soda process? Name two coagulants and give one reaction.
questions.a:
At room temperature the $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ formed are very finely divided; they settle slowly and pass through filters, and the reactions do not go to completion. A coagulant forms a gelatinous floc which entrains the fine particles and makes them settle quickly. Coagulants: alum $\mathrm{K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot 24H_2O}$ or aluminium sulphate, ferrous sulphate, sodium aluminate.
$$\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3 + 3Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3\downarrow + 3CaSO_4 + 6CO_2}$$
$$\mathrm{NaAlO_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Al(OH)_3\downarrow + NaOH}$$

questions.q: Explain why temporary magnesium hardness requires two equivalents of lime and why permanent magnesium hardness requires both lime and soda.
questions.a:
**Temporary Mg**: lime must first remove the bicarbonate as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and then precipitate Mg as $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ (since $\mathrm{MgCO_3}$ is fairly soluble):
$$\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 + 2Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2CaCO_3\downarrow + Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + 2H_2O}$$
One mole of $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ consumes two moles of lime, so it is counted 2× in the lime bracket.

**Permanent Mg**: lime precipitates $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ but leaves an equal amount of calcium salt in solution:
$$\mathrm{MgSO_4 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + CaSO_4}$$
This $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ is calcium permanent hardness, which soda removes:
$$\mathrm{CaSO_4 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + Na_2SO_4}$$
So permanent Mg appears in both brackets.

questions.q: Give the advantages and disadvantages of the lime-soda process.
questions.a:
**Advantages**: (1) very economical; (2) the treated water is alkaline, which reduces corrosion and kills pathogenic bacteria; (3) iron and manganese are also removed; (4) mineral content is reduced to some extent; (5) with coagulant, suspended matter is removed too.

**Disadvantages**: (1) large quantity of sludge, which is difficult to dispose of; (2) needs skilled supervision and careful calculation of chemicals; (3) residual hardness (15-60 ppm) makes the water unfit for high-pressure boilers; (4) excess soda in treated water can cause caustic embrittlement.

questions.q: In the lime-soda process, soda $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ is required to remove:
options: Permanent calcium hardness (original plus that produced by lime)
questions.a: Soda precipitates $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ of permanent hardness as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, including $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ produced when lime removes permanent $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ and acids. Temporary hardness and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ need lime only.

questions.q: Residual hardness of water softened by the hot lime-soda process is about:
questions.a: Hot process: 15-30 ppm; cold process: 50-60 ppm; zeolite about 10 ppm; ion exchange about 0-2 ppm.

topics.why: Zeolite softening with exchange and regeneration reactions, its limitations and the comparison with lime-soda is a near-certain 5-mark question, often with a regeneration numerical.
topics.gist:
**Zeolite (permutit) process** softens water by **cation exchange**. Zeolites are hydrated sodium aluminosilicates, $\mathrm{Na_2O\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot xSiO_2\cdot yH_2O}$ ($x$ = 2-10, $y$ = 2-6), written $\mathrm{Na_2Ze}$. **Natural** zeolites (natrolite, $\mathrm{Na_2O\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 3SiO_2\cdot 2H_2O}$) are non-porous and durable; **synthetic** zeolite (permutit), made by heating sodium carbonate, alumina and silica together, is porous, gel-like and has higher exchange capacity.

Hard water percolates through a bed of zeolite; $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ are retained and an equivalent amount of $\mathrm{Na^+}$ is released:
$$\mathrm{Na_2Ze + Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow CaZe + 2NaHCO_3}$$
$$\mathrm{Na_2Ze + MgSO_4 \rightarrow MgZe + Na_2SO_4}$$

When the bed is exhausted it is **regenerated** with 10% brine: $\mathrm{CaZe + 2NaCl \rightarrow Na_2Ze + CaCl_2}$; the washings are drained. NaCl needed is 117 parts per 100 parts of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent of hardness removed.

**Plant**: a steel cylinder holding the zeolite bed on gravel, with hard-water inlet, soft-water outlet, brine tank and wash-water drain.

**Advantages**: residual hardness about 10 ppm, no sludge, compact, automatic and easy to operate, adjusts itself to varying hardness. **Limitations**: turbid water clogs the pores; acidic water destroys zeolite; $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ form zeolites that cannot be regenerated; treated water carries more sodium salts; anions are untouched, so $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ decomposes in the boiler giving $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (corrosion) and NaOH (caustic embrittlement).
key_points: Zeolite = hydrated sodium aluminosilicate $\mathrm{Na_2O\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot xSiO_2\cdot yH_2O}$, written $\mathrm{Na_2Ze}$.
Natural (natrolite, non-porous, durable) vs synthetic (permutit, porous, higher capacity).
Only cations exchange: $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ are replaced by $\mathrm{Na^+}$; anions stay in the water.
Regeneration with 10% NaCl brine: $\mathrm{CaZe + 2NaCl \rightarrow Na_2Ze + CaCl_2}$.
NaCl for regeneration = $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent of hardness × 117/100.
Residual hardness about 10 ppm (better than lime-soda's 15-60 ppm).
No sludge, compact, easy and automatic operation.
Limitations: turbidity, acidity, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$/$\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$, sodium salts in treated water, bicarbonate left as $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$.
Not suitable for high-pressure boilers because of the sodium bicarbonate and carbonate it leaves.
traps: Using 58.5 instead of 117: one $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent (100 g) needs two NaCl (2 × 58.5 = 117 g).
Saying zeolite removes all ions: it removes only hardness cations; the treated water has the same anions and more sodium.
Saying zeolite-softened water is fine for high-pressure boilers: $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ gives $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and NaOH.
Writing regeneration with HCl or NaOH: that is ion-exchange resin, zeolite uses brine.
Forgetting that $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ zeolites are not regenerated by brine.
topics.asked_as: 'Describe the zeolite process of softening water with reactions and diagram' (5-7 marks); 'Give limitations of the zeolite process' or 'Compare zeolite and lime-soda processes' (3-4 marks); regeneration numerical (3-5 marks).

questions.q: A zeolite softener was exhausted after softening 10,000 L of water of total hardness 182.65 ppm (as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$). Calculate the NaCl needed to regenerate it, per litre of water softened and in total.
questions.a:
Regeneration: $\mathrm{CaZe + 2NaCl \rightarrow Na_2Ze + CaCl_2}$, so 100 g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent needs $2\times 58.5 = 117$ g NaCl.

**Per litre**: hardness = 182.65 mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ eq per litre.
$$\text{NaCl per litre} = 182.65 \times \frac{117}{100} = 213.7\ \text{mg/L}\ (\text{i.e. } 213.7\ \text{ppm})$$

**Total for 10,000 L**: hardness removed $= 182.65 \times 10{,}000 = 1{,}826{,}500$ mg = 1826.5 g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ eq.
$$\text{NaCl} = 1826.5 \times \frac{117}{100} = 2137\ \text{g} \approx 2.137\ \text{kg}$$

**NaCl = 213.7 mg per litre; 2.137 kg in total.**

questions.q: Describe the zeolite process of water softening with the reactions involved and a diagram.
questions.a:
**Zeolite**: hydrated sodium aluminosilicate $\mathrm{Na_2O\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot xSiO_2\cdot yH_2O}$, written $\mathrm{Na_2Ze}$; natural (natrolite) or synthetic (permutit).

**Plant** (draw): a closed steel cylinder containing a bed of zeolite supported on coarse sand/gravel; hard-water inlet at top, softened-water outlet at bottom, brine tank connected at top, drain for washings.

**Softening**: hard water percolates through the bed; $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ are exchanged for $\mathrm{Na^+}$:
$$\mathrm{Na_2Ze + Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow CaZe + 2NaHCO_3}$$
$$\mathrm{Na_2Ze + Mg(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow MgZe + 2NaHCO_3}$$
$$\mathrm{Na_2Ze + CaCl_2 \rightarrow CaZe + 2NaCl}$$
$$\mathrm{Na_2Ze + MgSO_4 \rightarrow MgZe + Na_2SO_4}$$

**Regeneration**: when exhausted, the supply is stopped and 10% NaCl brine is passed:
$$\mathrm{CaZe + 2NaCl \rightarrow Na_2Ze + CaCl_2}\qquad \mathrm{MgZe + 2NaCl \rightarrow Na_2Ze + MgCl_2}$$
The $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$/$\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ washings are drained and the bed is rinsed and reused.

Residual hardness of the soft water is about 10 ppm.

questions.q: Give the limitations of the zeolite process.
questions.a:
1. **Turbid water**: suspended matter clogs the pores of the zeolite, so water must be filtered first.
2. **Acidic water**: mineral acids decompose (destroy) the zeolite.
3. **$\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$**: form iron and manganese zeolites that cannot be regenerated by brine.
4. **Sodium salts**: the softened water contains more sodium salts than the raw water.
5. **Anions not removed**: bicarbonates remain as $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$; in the boiler $\mathrm{2NaHCO_3 \rightarrow Na_2CO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + CO_2}$. $\mathrm{CO_2}$ causes corrosion and NaOH causes caustic embrittlement, so the water is not fit for high-pressure boilers.
6. Hot water cannot be used, since zeolite tends to dissolve.

questions.q: Compare the zeolite process with the lime-soda process.
questions.a:
| Zeolite process | Lime-soda process |
|---|---|
| Residual hardness about 10 ppm | 15-30 ppm (hot), 50-60 ppm (cold) |
| No sludge | Large amount of sludge |
| Compact, easy, automatic operation | Bulky plant, needs skilled control |
| Turbid or acidic water cannot be used | Turbid and acidic water can be treated |
| Treated water has more sodium salts | Treated water has less dissolved solids |
| Bicarbonates remain (as $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$) | Bicarbonates removed |
| Higher capital cost | Cheaper |
| Adjusts automatically to varying hardness | Chemical doses must be recalculated |

questions.q: Why is zeolite-softened water unsuitable for high-pressure boilers?
questions.a:
Zeolite exchanges only cations. The bicarbonate of temporary hardness remains as $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$. In the boiler:
$$\mathrm{2NaHCO_3 \rightarrow Na_2CO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}\qquad \mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + CO_2}$$
$\mathrm{CO_2}$ forms carbonic acid and corrodes the boiler and condensate lines; NaOH concentrates in hair-line cracks and causes **caustic embrittlement**. The high sodium content also raises dissolved solids, causing priming and foaming.

questions.q: The exhausted zeolite bed is regenerated by passing:
questions.a: Brine (about 10% NaCl) replaces $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ by $\mathrm{Na^+}$: $\mathrm{CaZe + 2NaCl \rightarrow Na_2Ze + CaCl_2}$. HCl and NaOH regenerate ion-exchange resins.

questions.q: Which of the following permanently damages a zeolite bed?
questions.a: Iron and manganese zeolites cannot be converted back to $\mathrm{Na_2Ze}$ by brine, so $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$/$\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ must be removed before zeolite treatment.

topics.why: Demineralisation by cation and anion exchange resins, with reactions, regeneration, diagram and mixed bed, is the standard high-pressure boiler water question.
topics.gist:
**Ion-exchange (demineralisation, deionisation)** removes **all** ions, cations and anions, from water using insoluble cross-linked organic **resins**, usually styrene-divinylbenzene copolymers.

**Cation exchange resin** $\mathrm{RH^+}$ carries acidic groups, $\mathrm{-SO_3H}$ or $\mathrm{-COOH}$; it exchanges $\mathrm{H^+}$ for metal ions:
$$\mathrm{2RH^+ + Ca^{2+} \rightarrow R_2Ca^{2+} + 2H^+}$$
**Anion exchange resin** $\mathrm{R'OH^-}$ carries basic groups, quaternary ammonium or amine; it exchanges $\mathrm{OH^-}$ for anions:
$$\mathrm{R'OH^- + Cl^- \rightarrow R'Cl^- + OH^-}$$
The released ions neutralise each other: $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$.

**Plant**: hard water passes first through the **cation column** (water becomes acidic), then the **anion column**, then a **degasser** that removes $\mathrm{CO_2}$ from the carbonic acid formed from bicarbonates. Water from the cation column must go to the anion column, never the reverse, because $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ or $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ would precipitate in an alkaline anion bed.

**Regeneration**: cation resin with dilute HCl or $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, $\mathrm{R_2Ca^{2+} + 2H^+ \rightarrow 2RH^+ + Ca^{2+}}$; anion resin with dilute NaOH, $\mathrm{R'Cl^- + OH^- \rightarrow R'OH^- + Cl^-}$.

A **mixed-bed deioniser** holds both resins in one column; water meets many cation-anion stages in series and comes out as **conductivity water** (residual about 1 ppm or less).

**Advantages**: treats acidic and alkaline water, very low residual hardness (0-2 ppm), suitable for high-pressure boilers. **Disadvantages**: costly resins and chemicals, turbid water must be filtered first.
key_points: Ion exchange removes both cations and anions: demineralised (deionised) water.
Resins: styrene-divinylbenzene copolymer; cation resin $\mathrm{-SO_3H}$/$\mathrm{-COOH}$, anion resin quaternary ammonium/amine groups.
Cation: $\mathrm{2RH^+ + Ca^{2+} \rightarrow R_2Ca^{2+} + 2H^+}$; anion: $\mathrm{R'OH^- + Cl^- \rightarrow R'Cl^- + OH^-}$; then $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$.
Order: cation column, anion column, degasser.
Regenerate cation resin with dilute HCl/$\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$; anion resin with dilute NaOH.
HCl for regeneration = $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ eq × 73/100; NaOH = $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ eq × 80/100.
Mixed-bed deioniser gives conductivity water, residual about 1 ppm.
Advantages: handles acidic/alkaline water, residual 0-2 ppm, fit for high-pressure boilers.
Disadvantages: expensive, turbid water must be filtered before treatment.
formulas: $\text{HCl (g)} = \dfrac{73}{100}\times \mathrm{CaCO_3}\text{ eq (g)}$; $\text{NaOH (g)} = \dfrac{80}{100}\times \mathrm{CaCO_3}\text{ eq (g)}$ — 2 HCl or 2 NaOH per $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$
traps: Regenerating the cation resin with NaCl: that gives a sodium (zeolite-type) softener, not demineralisation; use acid.
Placing the anion column first: alkaline water would precipitate $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$/$\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ in the bed.
Using 36.5 per 100 g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent: one $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent needs two HCl (73 g).
Calling it softening only: it removes all ions, including $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$.
Forgetting the degasser: the carbonic acid from bicarbonates leaves $\mathrm{CO_2}$ in the water.
topics.asked_as: 'Describe the ion-exchange (demineralisation) process with a diagram and reactions' (5-7 marks); 'What is a mixed-bed deioniser?' (2-3 marks); 'Compare ion-exchange and zeolite processes' (3 marks); regeneration numerical (3-5 marks).

questions.q: A cation exchanger was exhausted after demineralising 10,000 L of water of hardness 200 ppm (as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$). Calculate the mass of HCl needed to regenerate it. If the anion load is equal in equivalents, how much NaOH regenerates the anion exchanger?
questions.a:
Hardness removed $= 200\ \text{mg/L} \times 10{,}000\ \text{L} = 2{,}000{,}000\ \text{mg} = 2000\ \text{g}\ \mathrm{CaCO_3}$ eq.

Regeneration: $\mathrm{R_2Ca + 2HCl \rightarrow 2RH + CaCl_2}$, so 100 g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ eq needs $2\times 36.5 = 73$ g HCl.
$$\text{HCl} = 2000 \times \frac{73}{100} = 1460\ \text{g}$$

Anion resin: $\mathrm{R'Cl + NaOH \rightarrow R'OH + NaCl}$; 100 g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ eq needs $2\times 40 = 80$ g NaOH.
$$\text{NaOH} = 2000 \times \frac{80}{100} = 1600\ \text{g}$$

**HCl = 1460 g (1.46 kg); NaOH = 1600 g (1.6 kg).**

questions.q: Describe the ion-exchange (demineralisation) process of water treatment with a diagram, reactions and regeneration.
questions.a:
**Resins**: cross-linked styrene-divinylbenzene polymers. Cation exchange resin $\mathrm{RH^+}$ has $\mathrm{-SO_3H}$ or $\mathrm{-COOH}$ groups; anion exchange resin $\mathrm{R'OH^-}$ has quaternary ammonium or amine groups.

**Plant** (draw): hard water inlet → **cation exchange column** → **anion exchange column** → **degasser** → demineralised water to storage; acid tank connected to the cation column and alkali tank to the anion column, with drains for washings.

**Cation column**:
$$\mathrm{2RH^+ + Ca^{2+} \rightarrow R_2Ca^{2+} + 2H^+}\qquad \mathrm{2RH^+ + Mg^{2+} \rightarrow R_2Mg^{2+} + 2H^+}$$
**Anion column**:
$$\mathrm{R'OH^- + Cl^- \rightarrow R'Cl^- + OH^-}\qquad \mathrm{2R'OH^- + SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow R'_2SO_4^{2-} + 2OH^-}$$
$$\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$$
Bicarbonates form $\mathrm{H_2CO_3 \rightarrow H_2O + CO_2}$; the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is removed in the degasser.

**Regeneration**: cation resin with dilute HCl or $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$: $\mathrm{R_2Ca^{2+} + 2H^+ \rightarrow 2RH^+ + Ca^{2+}}$; anion resin with dilute NaOH: $\mathrm{R'Cl^- + OH^- \rightarrow R'OH^- + Cl^-}$. Columns are then rinsed.

**Result**: water free of almost all ions, residual hardness 0-2 ppm, fit for high-pressure boilers.

questions.q: What is a mixed-bed deioniser? What is its advantage?
questions.a:
A **mixed-bed deioniser** is a single column containing an intimate mixture of cation exchange resin and anion exchange resin. As water flows down, it meets cation and anion resin particles alternately, which is equivalent to passing through a very large number of cation-anion pairs in series. The product is very pure **conductivity water** with residual dissolved solids about 1 ppm or less.

**Regeneration**: backwashing separates the lighter anion resin (top) from the heavier cation resin (bottom); each layer is regenerated separately (NaOH for the top, acid for the bottom) and the resins are then remixed with compressed air.

questions.q: Give the advantages and disadvantages of the ion-exchange process.
questions.a:
**Advantages**: (1) water of very low hardness (0-2 ppm) and low conductivity is obtained; (2) highly acidic or alkaline water can be treated; (3) both cations and anions are removed, so the water suits high-pressure boilers; (4) resins are regenerated and reused for a long time; (5) no sludge.

**Disadvantages**: (1) equipment, resins and regenerating chemicals are costly; (2) turbid water reduces efficiency and must be filtered (coagulated) first; (3) $\mathrm{Fe}$ and $\mathrm{Mn}$ and organic matter foul the resins.

questions.q: Why is the water passed through the cation exchanger before the anion exchanger, and why is a degasser used?
questions.a:
Hard water contains $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$. If it entered the anion exchanger first, the $\mathrm{OH^-}$ released would precipitate $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ and $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ inside the resin bed and choke it. In the cation exchanger these cations are removed first and the water becomes acidic; the acids are then neutralised in the anion column ($\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$).

Bicarbonates give carbonic acid in the cation column, $\mathrm{H_2CO_3 \rightarrow H_2O + CO_2}$; the dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is weakly held by the anion resin and is removed by the **degasser** (spraying the water against a counter-current of air or heating under vacuum), since $\mathrm{CO_2}$ would cause boiler corrosion.

questions.q: The exhausted anion exchange resin is regenerated by treating it with:
questions.a: $\mathrm{R'Cl^- + OH^- \rightarrow R'OH^- + Cl^-}$: dilute NaOH restores the $\mathrm{OH^-}$ form. Cation resin uses dilute HCl or $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$; zeolite uses brine.

questions.q: The functional group present in a strongly acidic cation exchange resin is:
questions.a: Sulphonic acid groups ($\mathrm{-SO_3H}$) give strongly acidic cation resins; $\mathrm{-COOH}$ gives weakly acidic ones. Amine and quaternary ammonium groups are on anion resins.

topics.why: A 5-7 mark numerical on hardness, EDTA, lime-soda, zeolite or ion exchange is set in nearly every paper and is pure marks if the method is followed.
topics.gist:
Every water numerical runs on **$\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalents**: hardness (ppm) = mg/L of salt × 100 / molar mass of salt. Use 100 for $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (molar mass), with the full molar mass of each divalent salt, e.g. $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ 120, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ 111. Where two moles of a salt match one $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ ($\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$, HCl), use twice the molar mass (168, 73).

**Salt analysis**: bicarbonates of Ca and Mg are temporary; chlorides, sulphates and nitrates of Ca and Mg are permanent; Na and K salts give no hardness.

**EDTA**: standardise EDTA with standard hard water (1 mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ per mL); then total hardness from the sample titre, permanent hardness from the titre after boiling, temporary = total − permanent.

**Lime-soda**: classify each constituent, take lime = 74/100 [...], soda = 106/100 [...], multiply by volume, divide by purity.

**Zeolite**: NaCl = $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ eq × 117/100, or work backwards from brine used to hardness.

**Ion exchange**: HCl = $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ eq × 73/100; $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ × 98/100; NaOH × 80/100; or use normality × volume = equivalents, and 1 equivalent = 50 g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$.

**Units**: 1 ppm = 1 mg/L = 0.1 °Fr = 0.07 °Cl; 1 °Cl = 14.3 ppm; 1 °Fr = 10 ppm. Always end with the unit asked: ppm, mg/L, or kg for the given volume.
key_points: Step 1: convert every constituent to ppm $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent (× 100 / molar mass).
Step 2: classify as temporary, permanent, or no hardness (Na and K salts).
EDTA: 1 mL EDTA = (mL of SHW × mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$/mL) / $V_1$; hardness = $V_2$ × (mg per mL EDTA) × 1000 / sample volume.

Lime bracket: temp Ca + 2 × temp Mg + perm (Mg + Fe + Al) + $\mathrm{CO_2}$ + $\mathrm{H^+}$ + $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$ − $\mathrm{NaAlO_2}$; soda bracket: perm (Ca + Mg + Fe + Al) + $\mathrm{H^+}$ − $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$.
Multiply mg/L by volume in litres, divide by $10^6$ for kg; divide by purity fraction.
Zeolite: 117 g NaCl per 100 g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent.
Ion exchange: 73 g HCl, 98 g $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, 80 g NaOH per 100 g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent; 1 equivalent = 50 g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$.
Degrees: 1 ppm = 0.07 °Cl = 0.1 °Fr.
formulas: $\text{ppm } \mathrm{CaCO_3}\text{ eq} = \dfrac{\text{mg/L of salt} \times 100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$ — hardness from salt analysis
$\text{Hardness (ppm)} = \dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\times 1000$ — EDTA, when 50 mL SHW (1 mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$/mL) takes $V_1$ mL and 50 mL sample takes $V_2$ mL
traps: Using 50 instead of 100 in × 100/M: 50 is the equivalent weight of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and must pair with equivalent weights of the salts, not molar masses.
Forgetting ×2 for temporary Mg in lime.
Forgetting the purity correction, or multiplying by 0.9 instead of dividing.
Mixing ppm, mg/L and kg: ppm and mg/L are per litre; multiply by volume for the total.
Counting NaCl or $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ as hardness: neither is hardness, but $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ consumes lime and reduces soda.
Using molar mass 84 for $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ against 100: two $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ (168) equal one $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$.
Putting $\mathrm{CO_2}$ in soda: dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$ needs lime only.
topics.asked_as: 'Calculate temporary, permanent and total hardness from the analysis' (3-5 marks); 'Calculate hardness by EDTA from the titre values' (3-5 marks); 'Calculate lime and soda for V litres, lime x% and soda y% pure' (5-7 marks); zeolite or ion-exchange regeneration problems (3-5 marks).

questions.q: A water sample contains (mg/L): $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ 32.4, $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ 29.2, $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ 13.6, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ 9.5, NaCl 58.5. Calculate temporary, permanent and total hardness in ppm, °Clark and °French.
questions.a:
| Salt | mg/L | M | ppm $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ eq | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ | 32.4 | 162 | 32.4 × 100/162 = 20 | Temporary |
| $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ | 29.2 | 146 | 29.2 × 100/146 = 20 | Temporary |
| $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ | 13.6 | 136 | 13.6 × 100/136 = 10 | Permanent |
| $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ | 9.5 | 95 | 9.5 × 100/95 = 10 | Permanent |
| NaCl | 58.5 | - | no hardness | - |

Temporary = 20 + 20 = **40 ppm**; permanent = 10 + 10 = **20 ppm**; total = **60 ppm**.

In °Clark (× 0.07): temporary 2.8 °Cl, permanent 1.4 °Cl, total **4.2 °Cl**.
In °French (× 0.1): temporary 4.0 °Fr, permanent 2.0 °Fr, total **6.0 °Fr**.

questions.q: 50 mL of standard hard water (1 mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ per mL) required 40 mL of EDTA. 50 mL of a water sample required 24 mL of the same EDTA, and 50 mL of the sample after boiling and filtering required 16 mL. Calculate total, permanent and temporary hardness.
questions.a:
**Standardisation**: 50 mL SHW contains 50 mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and takes 40 mL EDTA, so
$$1\ \text{mL EDTA} = \frac{50}{40} = 1.25\ \text{mg } \mathrm{CaCO_3}$$

**Total hardness**: 50 mL sample ≡ 24 × 1.25 = 30 mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$
$$\text{Total} = \frac{30}{50}\times 1000 = 600\ \text{ppm}$$

**Permanent hardness**: 50 mL boiled sample ≡ 16 × 1.25 = 20 mg $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$
$$\text{Permanent} = \frac{20}{50}\times 1000 = 400\ \text{ppm}$$

**Temporary** = 600 − 400 = **200 ppm**.

(Check with the short formula: $\frac{V_2}{V_1}\times 1000 = \frac{24}{40}\times 1000 = 600$ ppm.)

questions.q: Calculate the lime (90% pure) and soda (95% pure) needed to soften 1,00,000 L of water containing (mg/L): $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ 81, $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ 146, $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ 68, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ 95.

Calculate the lime and soda (both 100% pure) needed for 50,000 L of water containing (mg/L): $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ 40.5, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ 60, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ 55.5, $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$ 15.2, dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$ 22, $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ 16.8, HCl 7.3, NaCl 23.4.
questions.a:
| Constituent | mg/L | Factor | ppm $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ eq | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ | 40.5 | 100/162 | 25 | L |
| $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ | 60 | 100/120 | 50 | L + S |
| $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ | 55.5 | 100/111 | 50 | S |
| $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$ | 15.2 | 100/152 | 10 | L + S |
| $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | 22 | 100/44 | 50 | L |
| $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ | 16.8 | 100/168 | 10 | + L, − S |
| HCl | 7.3 | 100/73 | 10 | L + S |
| NaCl | 23.4 | - | - | none |

**Lime** $= \frac{74}{100}[25 + 50 + 10 + 50 + 10 + 10] = \frac{74}{100}\times 155 = 114.7$ mg/L.
For 50,000 L: $114.7 \times 50{,}000 = 5{,}735{,}000$ mg = **5.735 kg lime**.

**Soda** $= \frac{106}{100}[50 + 50 + 10 + 10 - 10] = \frac{106}{100}\times 110 = 116.6$ mg/L.
For 50,000 L: $116.6 \times 50{,}000 = 5{,}830{,}000$ mg = **5.83 kg soda**.

Reasons: $\mathrm{FeSO_4 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2 + CaSO_4}$ (lime, then soda for the $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$); $\mathrm{2NaHCO_3 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + Na_2CO_3 + 2H_2O}$ (uses lime, produces soda); NaCl plays no part.

questions.q: A zeolite softener was completely exhausted after softening 4000 L of hard water. It was regenerated by passing 10 L of NaCl solution containing 117 g/L of NaCl. Calculate the hardness of the water.
questions.a:
NaCl used $= 10\ \text{L} \times 117\ \text{g/L} = 1170$ g.

117 g NaCl ≡ 100 g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (from $\mathrm{CaZe + 2NaCl \rightarrow Na_2Ze + CaCl_2}$), so
$$\mathrm{CaCO_3}\text{ eq} = 1170 \times \frac{100}{117} = 1000\ \text{g} = 1{,}000{,}000\ \text{mg}$$
This hardness was in 4000 L:
$$\text{Hardness} = \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{4000} = 250\ \text{mg/L} = 250\ \text{ppm}$$

questions.q: The cation exchanger of a demineralising plant, exhausted after treating 3000 L of water, required 45 L of 0.2 N HCl for regeneration. Calculate the hardness of the water.
questions.a:
Equivalents of HCl $= N \times V = 0.2 \times 45 = 9$ equivalents.

These equal the equivalents of hardness removed; 1 equivalent of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ = 50 g:
$$\mathrm{CaCO_3}\text{ eq} = 9 \times 50 = 450\ \text{g} = 450{,}000\ \text{mg}$$
$$\text{Hardness} = \frac{450{,}000}{3000} = 150\ \text{ppm}$$

(Check by mass: HCl = 9 × 36.5 = 328.5 g; $328.5 \times \frac{100}{73} = 450$ g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$.)

questions.q: A water sample has a hardness of 1 °Clark. Its hardness in ppm is about:
questions.a: 1 °Clark = 1 grain $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ per imperial gallon = 1 part in 70,000 = 14.3 ppm (and 1 ppm = 0.07 °Cl).

questions.q: The hardness, as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent, of water containing 136 mg/L of $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ is:
questions.a: $136 \times 100/136 = 100$ ppm ($\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ molar mass 136, $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ 100).

topics.why: Definitions plus a classification with one equation each is a near-certain 2-5 mark question, and the rest of the polymer topics build on it.
topics.gist:
A **polymer** is a macromolecule built by joining many small units (**monomers**); the number of repeat units in a chain is the **degree of polymerisation (DP)**.

Whether a monomer can polymerise at all depends on its **functionality**, the number of bonding sites it has. A bifunctional monomer (ethylene, where the C=C opens to give two sites; or a diol, diacid, diamine) gives **linear** chains; a tri- or polyfunctional monomer (glycerol, phenol towards HCHO) gives **branched or cross-linked** networks.

By mechanism there are two main types:

- **Addition (chain-growth)** polymerisation: unsaturated monomers add to each other with no loss of atoms, so the polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer and $M = n \times M_0$. It is fast, needs an initiator, and the chain grows at an active end (free radical, ion or metal centre). Examples: polyethylene, PVC, polystyrene, Teflon.
- **Condensation (step-growth)** polymerisation: two different functional groups react with **elimination of a small molecule** ($\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{HCl}$, $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$). It is slow and stepwise; the repeat unit is not the monomer formula. Examples: nylon 6,6, terylene, bakelite.

**Copolymerisation** joins two or more different monomers in the same chain (Buna-S from butadiene + styrene). Copolymers can be random, alternating, block or graft. Coordination (Ziegler-Natta) polymerisation is a special kind of addition polymerisation.
key_points: Define monomer, polymer, degree of polymerisation and functionality
Bifunctional monomers give linear polymers; tri/polyfunctional give branched or 3-D cross-linked ones
Addition: no by-product, same empirical formula as monomer, fast chain reaction, needs initiator, monomer has C=C
Condensation: small molecule eliminated, stepwise and slow, monomers carry two reactive functional groups
One equation each: polyethylene (addition), nylon 6,6 or terylene (condensation)
Copolymer types: random, alternating, block, graft, with Buna-S / Buna-N as examples
Homopolymer has one kind of monomer; copolymer has two or more
formulas: $\mathrm{DP} = \dfrac{\text{molecular weight of polymer}}{\text{molecular weight of repeat unit}}$ — degree of polymerisation
traps: Calling bakelite or nylon an addition polymer; both are condensation polymers
Saying condensation always releases water: HCl and $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$ are also eliminated in some cases
Giving ethylene a functionality of 1: the double bond counts as two bonding sites
Writing a polymer equation without the 'n' coefficients or the repeat-unit brackets loses marks
Confusing a copolymer (one chain, two monomers) with a polymer blend (physical mixture)
topics.asked_as: 'Differentiate between addition and condensation polymerisation with one example each' (3-5 marks); 'Define functionality / degree of polymerisation' (2 marks); 'What is copolymerisation? Give its types' (3 marks); MCQs on identifying the type of a named polymer.

questions.q: Which of the following is a condensation polymer?
questions.a: Nylon 6,6 is formed from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid with elimination of water, so it is a condensation polymer. PVC, polystyrene and Teflon are formed by addition across C=C with no by-product.

questions.q: The functionality of ethylene ($\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2}$) in polymerisation is:
questions.a: When the $\pi$ bond opens, each carbon gets one free valency, giving two bonding sites, so ethylene is bifunctional and gives linear chains.

questions.q: Glycerol (three -OH groups) condensed with phthalic anhydride gives a polymer that is:
options: Linear with a few side groups
questions.a: Glycerol is trifunctional, so chains can grow in three directions and link to each other, giving a 3-D cross-linked network (glyptal, an alkyd resin). Trifunctional monomers always allow cross-linking.

questions.q: Differentiate between addition and condensation polymerisation (any five points) with one example of each.
questions.a:
| Addition (chain-growth) | Condensation (step-growth) |
|---|---|
| Monomers must have a C=C or C≡C | Monomers have two reactive functional groups (-OH, -COOH, -NH$_2$) |
| No by-product is formed | A small molecule ($\mathrm{H_2O}$, HCl, $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$) is eliminated |
| Polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer; $M = nM_0$ | Repeat unit differs from the monomers |
| Fast chain reaction through initiation, propagation, termination | Slow, stepwise; molecular weight builds up gradually |
| Needs an initiator (peroxide, Lewis acid, Ziegler-Natta catalyst) | Usually needs heat and/or acid-base catalyst |
| Mostly gives thermoplastics | Gives both thermoplastics (nylon) and thermosets (bakelite) |

Examples: $\mathrm{n\,CH_2{=}CH_2 \rightarrow {-}[CH_2{-}CH_2]_n{-}}$ (polyethylene); $\mathrm{n\,H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2 + n\,HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH \rightarrow {-}[NH(CH_2)_6NHCO(CH_2)_4CO]_n{-} + 2n\,H_2O}$ (nylon 6,6).

questions.q: Define functionality of a monomer. How does it decide the structure of the polymer?
questions.a:
**Functionality** is the number of bonding sites (reactive groups or bonds that can open) in a monomer molecule.

- Functionality 2 (ethylene, ethylene glycol, adipic acid): each unit can link to two others, so **linear** chains form (thermoplastics).
- Functionality 3 or more (glycerol, phenol towards formaldehyde at o- and p-positions): chains branch and link to one another, giving **branched or 3-D cross-linked** networks (thermosets such as bakelite, glyptal).
- A monofunctional compound cannot form a polymer; it only stops a chain.

questions.q: What is copolymerisation? Name its types and give one example.
questions.a:
**Copolymerisation** is the polymerisation of two or more different monomers so that both units are present in the **same chain**.

If A and B are the monomer units:
- **Random**: -A-B-B-A-B-A-A-
- **Alternating**: -A-B-A-B-A-B-
- **Block**: -A-A-A-A-B-B-B-B-
- **Graft**: a main chain of A with side branches of B

Example: **Buna-S (SBR)**, about 75% 1,3-butadiene + 25% styrene: $\mathrm{n\,CH_2{=}CH{-}CH{=}CH_2 + n\,C_6H_5CH{=}CH_2 \rightarrow {-}[CH_2{-}CH{=}CH{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH(C_6H_5)]_n{-}}$. Copolymerisation lets us combine properties: styrene adds strength and abrasion resistance to the elasticity of butadiene.

topics.why: The free-radical mechanism with initiation-propagation-termination equations is the single most repeated polymer question; ionic and Ziegler-Natta mechanisms are the standard alternatives.
topics.gist:
Addition polymerisation is a **chain reaction** with three stages: **initiation** (an active species is made and adds to one monomer), **propagation** (monomers add one after another to the active end), and **termination** (the active end is destroyed). What changes from one type to another is the active species.

1. **Free-radical**: an initiator such as benzoyl peroxide or $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$ splits on heating into radicals. The radical adds to $\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2}$ and the chain grows. Termination is by **coupling** (two radicals join) or **disproportionation** (one H atom is transferred, giving one saturated and one unsaturated chain). Examples: LDPE, PVC, PS.
2. **Cationic**: a Lewis acid ($\mathrm{BF_3}$, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$) with a trace of water gives $\mathrm{H^+}$, which makes a carbocation. It suits monomers with **electron-donating** groups (isobutylene, vinyl ethers).
3. **Anionic**: a base ($\mathrm{KNH_2}$, n-butyllithium) makes a carbanion. It suits monomers with **electron-withdrawing** groups (acrylonitrile, styrene, methyl methacrylate). With no impurities there is no natural termination: these are **living polymers**.
4. **Coordination (Ziegler-Natta)**: $\mathrm{TiCl_4 + Al(C_2H_5)_3}$ gives a Ti-alkyl centre with a vacant site. The monomer coordinates to Ti through its $\pi$ bond and **inserts** into the Ti-C bond, so the chain grows from the metal. Because the monomer always enters with the same orientation, the polymer is **stereoregular** (isotactic polypropylene), and linear HDPE forms at low pressure and temperature.
key_points: Three steps of chain polymerisation with equations: initiation, propagation, termination
Free radical initiators: benzoyl peroxide, $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$, AIBN; termination by coupling and by disproportionation
Cationic: Lewis acid + co-catalyst ($\mathrm{BF_3}$/$\mathrm{H_2O}$); monomers with electron-donating groups; isobutylene to polyisobutylene / butyl rubber
Anionic: $\mathrm{KNH_2}$ in liquid $\mathrm{NH_3}$ or n-BuLi; monomers with electron-withdrawing groups; living polymers
Ziegler-Natta catalyst = $\mathrm{TiCl_4}$ (or $\mathrm{TiCl_3}$) + $\mathrm{Al(C_2H_5)_3}$; mechanism is coordination then insertion at a vacant site
Ziegler-Natta advantages: stereoregular (isotactic) polymers, linear HDPE, low pressure and temperature, high density and crystallinity
Tacticity: isotactic (all side groups on one side), syndiotactic (alternating), atactic (random)
formulas: $\mathrm{BF_3 + H_2O \rightarrow H^+[BF_3OH]^-;\; H^+ + CH_2{=}C(CH_3)_2 \rightarrow (CH_3)_3C^+}$ — cationic initiation
$\mathrm{KNH_2 \rightarrow K^+ + NH_2^-;\; NH_2^- + CH_2{=}CHCN \rightarrow H_2N{-}CH_2{-}CH(CN)^-}$ — anionic initiation
traps: Writing termination as just 'chain stops': the examiner wants the coupling and/or disproportionation equation
Swapping the substituent rule: electron-donating groups favour cationic, electron-withdrawing groups favour anionic
Forgetting the co-catalyst (water) for $\mathrm{BF_3}$ or $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ in cationic polymerisation
Saying Ziegler-Natta needs high pressure; LDPE needs high pressure (about 1000-2000 atm), Ziegler-Natta HDPE does not
Describing the Ziegler-Natta step as radical addition instead of coordination followed by insertion into the metal-carbon bond
topics.asked_as: 'Explain the mechanism of free-radical polymerisation of ethylene/vinyl chloride with equations' (5 marks); 'Discuss the Ziegler-Natta (coordination) polymerisation mechanism and its advantages' (5 marks); 'Write short notes on cationic/anionic polymerisation' (3-5 marks); MCQs on initiators and tacticity.

questions.q: Which initiator system is used for cationic polymerisation of isobutylene?
questions.a: $\mathrm{BF_3 + H_2O \rightarrow H^+[BF_3OH]^-}$ supplies $\mathrm{H^+}$, which adds to isobutylene to give the stable tertiary carbocation $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C^+}$. Peroxide is a radical initiator, BuLi anionic, and $\mathrm{TiCl_4/AlEt_3}$ is Ziegler-Natta.

questions.q: Isotactic polypropylene is obtained by:
options: Coordination polymerisation with a Ziegler-Natta catalyst
questions.a: Each propylene inserts into the Ti-C bond with the same orientation at the catalyst surface, so all the methyl groups end up on the same side of the chain (isotactic). Free-radical routes give atactic material.

questions.q: 'Living polymers' are associated with:
questions.a: In anionic polymerisation, carbanion chain ends cannot combine with each other (like charges repel). In a pure system with no proton donor they stay active indefinitely and resume growth when more monomer is added.

questions.q: Explain the mechanism of free-radical polymerisation of ethylene using benzoyl peroxide as initiator.
questions.a:
**1. Initiation**: benzoyl peroxide splits homolytically on heating, and the radical adds to a monomer:
$\mathrm{(C_6H_5COO)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\,C_6H_5COO^{\bullet} \rightarrow 2\,C_6H_5^{\bullet} + 2\,CO_2}$
$\mathrm{C_6H_5^{\bullet} + CH_2{=}CH_2 \rightarrow C_6H_5{-}CH_2{-}CH_2^{\bullet}}$

**2. Propagation**: the new radical adds monomer after monomer and the chain grows:
$\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2CH_2^{\bullet} + n\,CH_2{=}CH_2 \rightarrow C_6H_5{-}(CH_2CH_2)_n{-}CH_2CH_2^{\bullet}}$

**3. Termination**: two growing radicals meet.
- *Coupling*: $\mathrm{R(CH_2CH_2)_m^{\bullet} + {}^{\bullet}(CH_2CH_2)_nR \rightarrow R(CH_2CH_2)_{m+n}R}$
- *Disproportionation*: one radical takes an H atom from the other, giving one saturated end ($\mathrm{{-}CH_2CH_3}$) and one unsaturated end ($\mathrm{{-}CH{=}CH_2}$).

This route at high pressure (about 1000-2000 atm, 150-250 °C) gives branched **LDPE**.

questions.q: Describe the mechanism of coordination (Ziegler-Natta) polymerisation. State its advantages.
questions.a:
**Catalyst**: $\mathrm{TiCl_4}$ (or $\mathrm{TiCl_3}$) + triethylaluminium $\mathrm{Al(C_2H_5)_3}$. The aluminium alkyl alkylates titanium, giving an active centre $\mathrm{[Ti]{-}C_2H_5}$ with a **vacant coordination site** (□).

**Mechanism**:
1. *Coordination*: the alkene ($\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCH_3}$) binds to the vacant site of Ti through its $\pi$ electrons.
2. *Insertion (migration)*: the alkyl group on Ti migrates to the coordinated alkene, so the monomer is inserted into the Ti-C bond: $\mathrm{[Ti]{-}C_2H_5 + CH_2{=}CHCH_3 \rightarrow [Ti]{-}CH_2{-}CH(CH_3){-}C_2H_5}$. A vacant site is created again.
3. *Propagation*: steps 1-2 repeat; the chain grows from the metal end.
4. *Termination*: by chain transfer to $\mathrm{H_2}$ (used to control molecular weight), or by $\beta$-hydride elimination.

**Advantages**: stereoregular (isotactic or syndiotactic) polymers; linear, highly crystalline **HDPE** with higher density, melting point and strength; works at low pressure (a few atm) and moderate temperature (about 60-70 °C); molecular weight can be controlled.

questions.q: Why do vinyl monomers with electron-donating groups polymerise by the cationic route while those with electron-withdrawing groups prefer the anionic route?
questions.a:
Cationic propagation goes through a **carbocation**. Electron-donating groups (alkyl, -OR) stabilise the positive charge by +I/+R effects, as in $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C^+}$ from isobutylene, so these monomers polymerise readily with $\mathrm{BF_3/H_2O}$.

Anionic propagation goes through a **carbanion**. Electron-withdrawing groups (-CN, -COOCH$_3$, phenyl) stabilise the negative charge by -I/-R effects, as in acrylonitrile and methyl methacrylate, so these polymerise with $\mathrm{KNH_2}$ or BuLi. Each group stabilises the intermediate of matching charge.

questions.q: Define tacticity. Distinguish isotactic, syndiotactic and atactic polymers.
questions.a:
**Tacticity** is the arrangement in space of the side groups (R) along the main chain of a polymer such as polypropylene.

- **Isotactic**: all R groups on the **same side** of the chain. Highly crystalline and strong (Ziegler-Natta PP).
- **Syndiotactic**: R groups **alternate** regularly from side to side.
- **Atactic**: R groups placed **randomly**. Amorphous, soft and weak (free-radical PP).

Regular (iso/syndio) chains pack better, so they have higher crystallinity, melting point and tensile strength.

topics.why: It is the main numerical in the polymer unit: number- and weight-average molecular weight and PDI from given data are quick, sure marks.
topics.gist:
A polymer sample is never made of chains of one length; it is **polydisperse**. So its molecular weight is an **average**, and the answer depends on how you average.
