- **Number-average** $\overline{M}_n$: every molecule counts equally. It is measured by methods that count molecules: colligative properties (osmometry) and end-group analysis.
- **Weight-average** $\overline{M}_w$: each molecule counts in proportion to its mass, so heavy chains weigh more in the average. It is measured by light scattering and ultracentrifugation.
- **Viscosity-average** $\overline{M}_v$: from intrinsic viscosity by the Mark-Houwink equation; it lies between $\overline{M}_n$ and $\overline{M}_w$.

Always $\overline{M}_w \ge \overline{M}_v \ge \overline{M}_n$. The ratio $\overline{M}_w/\overline{M}_n$ is the **polydispersity index (PDI)**; it is 1 only for a monodisperse sample (some natural proteins) and typically 1.5-3 or more for synthetic polymers.

In a numerical, first decide whether the data give **numbers of molecules** ($N_i$) or **mass/weight fractions** ($w_i$), then use the matching formula. Tensile strength, melt viscosity and softening point all rise with molecular weight. Too low gives a weak material; too high makes it hard to process.
key_points: Polymers are polydisperse, so molecular weight is an average
Formulas for $\overline{M}_n$ and $\overline{M}_w$ in terms of $N_i$ and in terms of weight fractions $w_i$
PDI = $\overline{M}_w/\overline{M}_n \ge 1$; equal to 1 only for a monodisperse sample
Methods: osmometry/end-group for $\overline{M}_n$, light scattering for $\overline{M}_w$, viscometry for $\overline{M}_v$
Order: $\overline{M}_z \ge \overline{M}_w \ge \overline{M}_v \ge \overline{M}_n$
Degree of polymerisation = $\overline{M}_n$ / molar mass of repeat unit
Effect of molecular weight on strength, viscosity and processability
formulas: $\overline{M}_w = \dfrac{\sum N_i M_i^2}{\sum N_i M_i}$ — weight average
$\overline{M}_w = \sum w_i M_i,\quad \overline{M}_n = \dfrac{1}{\sum (w_i/M_i)}$ — from weight fractions ($\sum w_i = 1$)
traps: Using the number formula when the data are weight fractions (or the other way round)
Getting PDI less than 1: that always means an arithmetic slip, because $\overline{M}_w \ge \overline{M}_n$
Dividing by $\sum N_i$ in the $\overline{M}_w$ formula instead of by $\sum N_i M_i$
Using the molar mass of the monomer pair instead of the repeat unit when finding DP of a condensation polymer
Leaving out units (g/mol) in the final answer
topics.asked_as: 'Calculate the number-average and weight-average molecular weight and PDI of a polymer sample containing ...' (3-5 marks numerical); 'Define $\overline{M}_n$ and $\overline{M}_w$; why is $\overline{M}_w \ge \overline{M}_n$?' (2-3 marks); 'Find the degree of polymerisation of PVC of molecular weight ...' (2 marks).

questions.q: A polymer sample contains 30 molecules of molecular weight 20,000, 40 molecules of molecular weight 30,000 and 30 molecules of molecular weight 60,000. Calculate $\overline{M}_n$, $\overline{M}_w$ and PDI.
A polymer sample consists of 50% by weight of chains of molecular weight 10,000 and 50% by weight of chains of molecular weight 1,00,000. Find $\overline{M}_n$, $\overline{M}_w$ and PDI.
questions.a:
The data are **weight fractions**: $w_1 = w_2 = 0.5$.

$\overline{M}_w = \sum w_iM_i = 0.5(10^4) + 0.5(10^5) = 5{,}000 + 50{,}000 = 55{,}000$ g/mol

$\overline{M}_n = \dfrac{1}{\sum w_i/M_i} = \dfrac{1}{0.5/10^4 + 0.5/10^5} = \dfrac{1}{5\times10^{-5} + 5\times10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{5.5\times10^{-5}} = 18{,}182$ g/mol

$\mathrm{PDI} = 55{,}000/18{,}182 = 3.03$

(Equal weights mean there are 10 times as many short chains by number, so $\overline{M}_n$ is pulled down towards 10,000.)

questions.q: A sample of PVC has $\overline{M}_n = 1{,}25{,}000$ g/mol. Find its degree of polymerisation. (C = 12, H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
questions.a:
Repeat unit $\mathrm{{-}CH_2{-}CHCl{-}}$ = $\mathrm{C_2H_3Cl}$: $M_0 = 2(12) + 3(1) + 35.5 = 62.5$ g/mol

$\mathrm{DP} = \dfrac{\overline{M}_n}{M_0} = \dfrac{125000}{62.5} = 2000$

questions.q: A sample contains equal numbers of molecules of molecular weight 10,000 and 1,00,000. Its number-average molecular weight is:
questions.a: With equal numbers, $\overline{M}_n$ is the simple mean: $(10^4 + 10^5)/2 = 55{,}000$. (18,182 would be $\overline{M}_n$ for equal *weights*; 91,818 is $\overline{M}_w$ for equal numbers: $(10^8 + 10^{10})/(1.1\times10^5)$.)

questions.q: For a perfectly monodisperse polymer, the polydispersity index is:
questions.a: When every chain has the same mass, $\overline{M}_w = \overline{M}_n$, so PDI = 1. For real synthetic polymers PDI > 1.

questions.q: Light-scattering measurements give which average molecular weight?
questions.a: The intensity of scattered light depends on the size (mass) of each particle, so heavier molecules contribute more; the method gives $\overline{M}_w$. Osmometry, a colligative method, gives $\overline{M}_n$.

questions.q: Why is $\overline{M}_w$ always greater than or equal to $\overline{M}_n$? What does a high PDI indicate?
questions.a:
$\overline{M}_n$ gives every molecule the same weight in the average, while $\overline{M}_w$ weights each molecule by its mass ($N_iM_i$). The heavy chains therefore pull $\overline{M}_w$ upwards, so $\overline{M}_w \ge \overline{M}_n$. The two are equal only when all chains are the same length.

A **high PDI** means a broad distribution of chain lengths: the sample has many short chains along with very long ones. This affects processing (melt flow) and mechanical properties. A PDI close to 1 means uniform chains.

topics.why: 'Differentiate between thermoplastic and thermosetting polymers' is one of the most predictable questions in the whole paper.
topics.gist:
The difference comes from **structure**, and every property in the comparison table follows from it.

**Thermoplastics** are made of **linear or slightly branched chains** held together only by weak van der Waals forces (or hydrogen bonds). Heating lets the chains slide past each other, so the material **softens and can be reshaped**; on cooling it hardens again. The change is physical and reversible, so thermoplastics can be remoulded and recycled, and many dissolve or swell in suitable solvents. Most are made by addition polymerisation: polyethylene, PVC, polystyrene, PTFE, PMMA. Some condensation polymers with linear chains, such as nylon 6,6 and PET, are also thermoplastics.

**Thermosetting** polymers start as low-molecular-weight resins that, on heating (**curing**), form strong **covalent cross-links** in three dimensions. Once set, the network cannot soften again: reheating only chars or decomposes it. They are hard, rigid, strong, brittle, insoluble and heat resistant, and cannot be recycled by melting. Most are made by condensation: bakelite, urea-formaldehyde, epoxy resins, glyptal, unsaturated polyester.

To answer: write a 6-8 point table (structure, bonding, effect of heat, reprocessing, solubility, mechanical nature, type of polymerisation, examples), then add one line on why the structure explains it.
key_points: Structure: linear/branched chains (thermoplastic) vs 3-D cross-linked network (thermoset)
Bonding between chains: weak secondary forces vs strong covalent cross-links
Effect of heat: soften reversibly vs set permanently, then char
Reprocessing and recycling: possible vs not possible
Solubility: soluble/swell in organic solvents vs insoluble
Properties: softer, tougher, less brittle vs hard, rigid, brittle, more heat resistant
Mostly addition vs mostly condensation polymerisation; examples of each
traps: Saying all condensation polymers are thermosets: nylon 6,6 and PET are condensation thermoplastics
Writing that thermosets 'melt at a higher temperature': they do not melt, they decompose
Giving a table without any examples, or with PVC listed as a thermoset
Not explaining the structural reason; the table alone may not get full marks for a 5-mark question
topics.asked_as: 'Differentiate between thermoplastic and thermosetting resins with examples' (3-5 marks); 'Why can thermoplastics be remoulded but thermosets cannot?' (2 marks); MCQs: 'Which of the following is a thermosetting polymer?'

questions.q: Which of the following is a thermosetting polymer?
questions.a: Bakelite (phenol-formaldehyde) forms a 3-D cross-linked network on curing and cannot be remelted. The others are linear thermoplastics.

questions.q: Nylon 6,6 is best described as:
questions.a: Nylon 6,6 is made by condensation of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, but both monomers are bifunctional, so the chains are linear. Linear chains soften on heating (it is melt-spun into fibres), so it is a thermoplastic.

questions.q: Differentiate between thermoplastic and thermosetting polymers (six points) with two examples of each.
questions.a:
| Property | Thermoplastic | Thermosetting |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | Linear or slightly branched chains | 3-D cross-linked network |
| Forces between chains | Weak van der Waals / H-bonds | Strong covalent cross-links |
| Effect of heat | Soften on heating, harden on cooling (reversible) | Set permanently on curing; char on reheating |
| Reshaping / recycling | Can be remoulded and recycled | Cannot be remoulded |
| Solubility | Soluble or swell in some organic solvents | Insoluble |
| Mechanical | Softer, weaker, less brittle | Hard, rigid, strong, brittle |
| Usual mode of formation | Mostly addition polymerisation | Mostly condensation polymerisation |
| Examples | Polyethylene, PVC, polystyrene, Teflon, nylon | Bakelite, urea-formaldehyde, epoxy, glyptal |

Reason: in thermoplastics heat only overcomes weak intermolecular forces, so chains can slide. In thermosets the chains are tied by covalent bonds, which break only at decomposition temperatures.

questions.q: Explain on the basis of structure why thermoplastics can be recycled but thermosetting plastics cannot.
questions.a:
Thermoplastic chains are linear and held only by weak secondary forces. Heating supplies enough energy to overcome these forces, so the chains slide and the material flows. It can be reshaped, and cooling restores it with no chemical change, so the cycle can be repeated (recycling).

In thermosets, curing has joined the chains by covalent cross-links into one giant network. Heating cannot make the chains slide without breaking covalent bonds, and at that temperature the polymer decomposes (chars) instead of flowing. So it cannot be remoulded.

questions.q: Classify the following as thermoplastic or thermosetting: PVC, urea-formaldehyde resin, Teflon, epoxy resin, polystyrene, glyptal, PET.
questions.a:
**Thermoplastic**: PVC, Teflon (PTFE), polystyrene, PET (terylene); all linear chains.

**Thermosetting**: urea-formaldehyde resin, epoxy resin (after curing with amine), glyptal (glycerol + phthalic anhydride); all cross-linked networks.

questions.q: Which statement about thermosetting polymers is correct?
options: They soften every time they are heated
They are generally soluble in organic solvents
They become permanently hard on heating due to cross-linking
They are always made by addition polymerisation
questions.a: Curing creates covalent cross-links, so the polymer sets irreversibly. It does not resoften, is insoluble, and is usually made by condensation.

topics.why: It is usually asked as one method with a diagram or as compounding ingredients; a steady 3-5 mark short note but less frequent than the polymer chemistry.
topics.gist:
A raw resin is rarely moulded alone. First it is **compounded**, which means mixing it with additives:

- **Resin (binder)**: holds everything together.
- **Plasticisers** (dioctyl phthalate, tricresyl phosphate): get between the chains, lower the glass transition temperature, and make the plastic flexible (soft PVC).
- **Fillers** (wood flour, mica, china clay, carbon black): reduce cost and improve hardness, strength or heat resistance.
- **Stabilisers** (lead or barium-cadmium soaps for PVC): stop degradation by heat and light.
- **Colorants/pigments**, **lubricants** (waxes, stearates) for easy mould release, and **catalysts/accelerators** (hexamine, peroxides) to cure thermosets.

The compounded material is then shaped:

- **Compression moulding**: a charge is placed in a heated mould and pressed. Used mainly for **thermosets** (bakelite, UF).
- **Injection moulding**: thermoplastic granules are melted in a heated cylinder and forced by a ram or screw into a **cold** closed mould. It is fast and suits mass production of thermoplastic parts (buckets, caps).
- **Transfer moulding**: a thermoset is softened in a separate chamber, then pushed into the mould. It suits intricate parts with metal inserts.
- **Extrusion**: a continuous process where molten plastic is pushed through a die (pipes, rods, sheets, wire insulation).
- **Blow moulding**: a hot tube (parison) is inflated inside a mould (bottles).

Other methods include calendering (sheets) and thermoforming.
key_points: Compounding ingredients and the function of each (resin, plasticiser, filler, stabiliser, pigment, lubricant, catalyst)
Compression moulding: heat + pressure in a closed mould; thermosets
Injection moulding: melt in heated cylinder, inject into cold mould; thermoplastics; fast, cheap per piece
Transfer moulding: thermoset softened in a pot and transferred; intricate shapes and inserts
Extrusion: continuous products of constant cross-section; pipes, rods, films, cable sheathing
Blow moulding: hollow articles such as bottles
Match the method to the polymer type and the product
traps: Recommending injection moulding with a cold mould for a thermoset: thermosets need a hot mould to cure
Calling a plasticiser a filler; a plasticiser increases flexibility, a filler adds bulk or strength
Writing the process steps with no labelled diagram when the question says 'with diagram'
Mixing up transfer and compression moulding: in transfer moulding the charge is softened outside the mould cavity
topics.asked_as: 'Describe injection / compression moulding with a neat diagram' (5 marks); 'What is compounding of plastics? Explain the role of various ingredients' (5 marks); 'Write short notes on extrusion moulding' (3 marks).

questions.q: The most suitable method for making continuous PVC pipes is:
questions.a: Extrusion forces molten plastic continuously through a die of the required cross-section, which is how pipes, rods and cable sheathing are made.

questions.q: The main role of a plasticiser in a plastic is to:
options: Increase flexibility by lowering intermolecular forces
Act as a catalyst for curing
questions.a: Plasticiser molecules (for example dioctyl phthalate) get between the polymer chains, weaken chain-chain attraction and lower $T_g$, so the plastic becomes soft and flexible. Soft PVC is the standard example.

questions.q: What is compounding of plastics? Explain the role of the various ingredients.
questions.a:
**Compounding** is mixing the raw resin with additives so that the product has the required properties and can be moulded.

1. **Resin (binder)**: the main polymer that binds the other ingredients (PVC, phenol-formaldehyde).
2. **Plasticisers**: dioctyl phthalate, tricresyl phosphate. They lower intermolecular forces and $T_g$ and increase flexibility.
3. **Fillers**: wood flour, mica, china clay, carbon black. They lower cost and improve hardness, tensile strength, heat resistance and opacity.
4. **Stabilisers**: lead, barium or cadmium salts, especially for PVC. They prevent heat- and light-induced degradation.
5. **Colouring agents**: dyes and pigments give colour.
6. **Lubricants**: waxes, oils, stearates. They help flow and easy release from the mould and give a glossy finish.
7. **Catalysts / accelerators**: hexamine, $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$, benzoyl peroxide. They speed up curing of thermosetting resins.

questions.q: Describe injection moulding with a labelled sketch description. Why is it preferred for thermoplastics?
questions.a:
**Equipment**: a hopper feeds granules into a heated cylinder containing a ram or reciprocating screw; a nozzle connects the cylinder to a split mould kept **cold** by circulating water.

**Process**:
1. Granules fall from the hopper into the heated cylinder (about 150-300 °C) and melt.
2. The ram or screw forces the melt through the nozzle into the closed mould cavity under high pressure.
3. The plastic cools and solidifies in the cold mould.
4. The mould opens, the article is ejected and the cycle repeats.

**Labelled sketch**: hopper, heater bands, ram/screw, cylinder, nozzle, mould halves with cooling channels, moulded article.

**Why for thermoplastics**: it relies on melting and then solidifying on cooling, which is reversible for thermoplastics. Cycle times are short and precision is high, so it suits mass production (buckets, bottle caps, toys).

questions.q: Differentiate compression moulding and injection moulding.
questions.a:
| Compression moulding | Injection moulding |
|---|---|
| Mainly for thermosetting resins | Mainly for thermoplastics |
| Charge placed directly in an open heated mould, then pressed | Melt injected into a closed mould from a heated cylinder |
| Mould is **hot**; curing occurs in the mould | Mould is **cold**; plastic solidifies by cooling |
| Slower cycle | Fast cycle, suits mass production |
| Examples: bakelite switches, UF crockery | Buckets, caps, toys |

questions.q: What advantage does transfer moulding have over compression moulding?
questions.a: In transfer moulding the thermosetting charge is first softened in a separate heated chamber (pot) and then forced through a sprue into the closed mould. Because the material arrives already fluid, it flows evenly round **delicate inserts and intricate shapes** without displacing or damaging them. It also gives more uniform curing, less flash and better dimensional accuracy than compression moulding.

topics.why: 'Preparation, properties and uses of bakelite / PVC / Teflon / nylon' is a standard 3-5 mark question; bakelite in particular recurs.
topics.gist:
For each named resin the examiner wants three things: **preparation with equation**, **two or three properties**, and **uses**.

**Thermoplastic resins**
- **Polyethylene**: LDPE by free-radical polymerisation at high pressure (about 1000-2000 atm), branched, soft (films, bags); HDPE by Ziegler-Natta at low pressure, linear, rigid (pipes, crates).
- **PVC**: from vinyl chloride with peroxide. Rigid; becomes flexible with plasticiser. Used for pipes, cable insulation, raincoats.
- **Teflon (PTFE)**: from tetrafluoroethylene. Very strong C-F bonds make it extremely chemically inert, heat-stable (melts about 327 °C) and non-stick with low friction. Used for non-stick cookware, gaskets, insulation.
- **Polystyrene**: transparent, brittle; foamed as thermocole.
- **PMMA (Perspex, Plexiglas)**: highly transparent. Used for lenses and aircraft windows.
- **Nylon 6,6**: condensation of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid. Tough, high tensile strength from H-bonding. Used for fibres, ropes, gears.

**Thermosetting resins**
- **Bakelite (phenol-formaldehyde)**: phenol + HCHO first give methylol phenols. With acid and excess phenol they give linear **novolac**; heating with **hexamethylenetetramine** cross-links it to bakelite. With base and excess HCHO the product is **resol**. Hard, rigid, an excellent electrical insulator. Used for switches, plugs, handles.
- **Urea-formaldehyde**: light-coloured, hard. Used for crockery and adhesives.
- **Epoxy resins**: bisphenol-A + epichlorohydrin, cured by amines. Used as adhesives (Araldite), coatings and composite matrices.
key_points: Preparation equation, properties and uses of PE (LDPE vs HDPE), PVC, PTFE, PS, PMMA, nylon 6,6
Bakelite: methylol phenol intermediates, novolac (acid, excess phenol) and resol (base, excess HCHO), hexamine curing
Urea-formaldehyde: mono- and dimethylol urea, then cross-linking; uses
Epoxy resin: bisphenol-A + epichlorohydrin; amine curing; adhesive and coating uses
Teflon properties linked to strong C-F bonds and a fluorine sheath round the chain
Nylon strength linked to inter-chain hydrogen bonding
formulas: $\mathrm{C_6H_5OH + HCHO \xrightarrow{H^+\ or\ OH^-} HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2OH}$ — o/p-methylol phenol (bakelite step 1)
traps: Writing bakelite as a direct one-step reaction: show methylol phenol, the novolac/resol stage, then cross-linking
Forgetting the role of hexamethylenetetramine (source of $\mathrm{CH_2}$ bridges to cure novolac)
Attributing Teflon's non-stick property to 'smoothness' instead of low surface energy from the C-F sheath
Swapping LDPE and HDPE conditions: high pressure gives LDPE (branched); Ziegler-Natta gives HDPE (linear)
topics.asked_as: 'Give the preparation, properties and uses of bakelite' (5 marks); 'Write short notes on any two: PVC, Teflon, nylon 6,6, epoxy resin' (3 marks each); 'Distinguish LDPE and HDPE' (3 marks); MCQs on uses and monomers.

questions.q: Teflon is used for non-stick cookware mainly because:
options: It is a good conductor of heat
Its strong C-F bonds and fluorine sheath give low surface energy and chemical inertness
questions.a: The C-F bond is very strong and the fluorine atoms form a tight sheath round the carbon chain. The surface has very low energy and reacts with almost nothing, so food does not stick and the coating survives cooking temperatures (melts about 327 °C).

questions.q: Novolac is converted into hard, cross-linked bakelite by heating with:
questions.a: Hexamethylenetetramine (hexamine) decomposes on heating to give formaldehyde and ammonia. The formaldehyde provides the extra $\mathrm{{-}CH_2{-}}$ bridges that cross-link the linear novolac chains into the 3-D bakelite network.

questions.q: Describe the preparation of bakelite with equations. Give its properties and uses.
questions.a:
**Raw materials**: phenol and formaldehyde, with an acid or alkaline catalyst.

**Step 1 (methylolation)**: formaldehyde attacks the o- and p-positions of phenol:
$\mathrm{C_6H_5OH + HCHO \rightarrow HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2OH}$ (o- and p-methylol phenol)

**Step 2 (condensation to novolac)**: with acid and excess phenol, methylol phenols condense with phenol, losing water, to give **linear** chains joined by $\mathrm{{-}CH_2{-}}$ bridges at the o/p-positions. This is **novolac**, a fusible, soluble thermoplastic resin. (With base and excess HCHO the product is the **resol** type.)

**Step 3 (curing)**: novolac is heated in a mould with **hexamethylenetetramine**. It supplies more $\mathrm{{-}CH_2{-}}$ bridges, and the chains cross-link at the remaining o/p-positions into a 3-D network: **bakelite** (infusible, insoluble).

**Properties**: hard, rigid, scratch resistant; excellent electrical insulator; resistant to heat, water and most chemicals; dark coloured.

**Uses**: electrical switches, plugs and switchboards; handles of cookers and kettles; telephone and radio cabinets; adhesive for plywood; ion-exchange resins (sulphonated form).

questions.q: Give the preparation, properties and uses of PVC.
questions.a:
**Preparation**: vinyl chloride is polymerised by the free-radical route using benzoyl peroxide or $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$ under pressure:
$\mathrm{n\,CH_2{=}CHCl \rightarrow {-}[CH_2{-}CHCl]_n{-}}$

**Properties**: colourless, rigid and fairly strong; resistant to water, acids, alkalis and weathering; poor heat stability, so stabilisers are added; becomes soft and flexible with plasticisers (dioctyl phthalate).

**Uses**: rigid PVC for water pipes, fittings and sheets; plasticised PVC for cable insulation, raincoats, floor tiles, hoses, shoe soles.

questions.q: Give the preparation and uses of nylon 6,6. Why is it strong?
questions.a:
**Preparation**: condensation of hexamethylenediamine with adipic acid (via nylon salt) at about 280 °C:
$\mathrm{n\,H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2 + n\,HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH \rightarrow {-}[NH(CH_2)_6NH{-}CO(CH_2)_4CO]_n{-} + 2n\,H_2O}$

The '6,6' means each monomer has 6 carbon atoms.

**Strength**: the amide groups (-CO-NH-) of neighbouring chains form **hydrogen bonds**, so the chains pack closely, are highly crystalline and have high tensile strength and toughness.

**Uses**: fibres for textiles, ropes, fishing nets, parachutes, tyre cord; moulded gears, bearings and bushes.

questions.q: Distinguish between LDPE and HDPE.
questions.a:
| LDPE | HDPE |
|---|---|
| Free-radical polymerisation at high pressure (about 1000-2000 atm), 150-250 °C, traces of $\mathrm{O_2}$/peroxide | Coordination (Ziegler-Natta) polymerisation at low pressure (a few atm), about 60-70 °C |
| Highly branched chains | Linear chains |
| Lower density (about 0.91-0.93 g/cm³), lower crystallinity | Higher density (about 0.94-0.97 g/cm³), higher crystallinity |
| Soft, flexible, lower melting point | Rigid, stronger, higher melting point |
| Films, carry bags, squeeze bottles | Pipes, crates, buckets, containers |

topics.why: Vulcanisation (why, how, what changes) is a fixed 3-5 mark question; Buna-S, Buna-N and neoprene preparations come as short notes.
topics.gist:
**Natural rubber** is *cis*-1,4-polyisoprene obtained from latex. Raw rubber has serious defects. It becomes soft and **sticky in summer** and **brittle in winter** (usable only about 10-60 °C), has low tensile strength, absorbs water, swells in oils and solvents, is attacked by oxidising agents and ozone, and shows **permanent set**: stretched chains slip and do not fully recover.

**Vulcanisation** (Goodyear, 1839) cures these defects. The rubber is heated with **sulphur** (about 3-5% for tyre rubber, about 30% or more for hard **ebonite**) at about 100-140 °C, usually with an **accelerator** (for example mercaptobenzothiazole) and an **activator** (ZnO). Sulphur forms **-S-S- cross-links** between chains at the double bonds and allylic positions. The links stop chains slipping, so the rubber becomes stronger (tensile strength rises roughly tenfold), more elastic, non-sticky, usable over about -40 to 100 °C, less soluble and more resistant to oxidation and abrasion. Too much sulphur makes it hard and non-elastic (ebonite).

**Synthetic rubbers** (elastomers):
- **Buna-S (SBR)**: butadiene + styrene (about 3:1). Used for tyres and shoe soles.
- **Buna-N (NBR)**: butadiene + acrylonitrile. **Oil resistant**, so used for oil seals and fuel hoses.
- **Neoprene**: polychloroprene. Resists oil, flame and weather; vulcanised with MgO/ZnO.
- **Butyl rubber**: isobutylene + a little isoprene. Very low gas permeability, so used for inner tubes.
- **Thiokol**: a polysulphide, oil- and solvent-resistant.
- **Silicone rubber**: stable over a very wide temperature range.
key_points: Natural rubber = cis-1,4-polyisoprene; list its drawbacks
Vulcanisation: S (3-5%), 100-140 °C, accelerator + ZnO; sulphur cross-links between chains
Property changes after vulcanisation: tensile strength, elasticity, temperature range, tackiness, solvent and oxidation resistance
Ebonite: high sulphur, hard, used as an insulator
Buna-S, Buna-N, neoprene, butyl, thiokol: monomers, equation and one use each
Elasticity explained by coiled chains straightening under stress and recoiling (entropy)
traps: Saying sulphur 'reacts with all the double bonds'; only a few cross-links form at a time, otherwise the product would be ebonite
Using natural rubber as the answer for oil hoses; Buna-N and neoprene are the oil-resistant ones
Writing chloroprene as vinyl chloride; chloroprene is 2-chloro-1,3-butadiene
Mentioning that neoprene is vulcanised with sulphur like natural rubber; it is usually cured with MgO/ZnO
Listing property changes without any cross-link structure; draw two chains joined by -S-S- bridges
topics.asked_as: 'What is vulcanisation? Explain with reaction and list the changes in properties' (5 marks); 'Write the preparation and uses of Buna-S / Buna-N / neoprene' (3 marks); 'What are the drawbacks of natural rubber?' (2 marks); MCQs on monomers and uses.

questions.q: Buna-N is preferred for oil seals and petrol hoses because it is:
options: Resistant to oils due to polar -CN groups
questions.a: Acrylonitrile units carry polar -CN groups, which make the rubber incompatible with non-polar hydrocarbons, so it does not swell or dissolve in oil and petrol.

questions.q: The monomer of neoprene is:
questions.a: Neoprene is polychloroprene: $\mathrm{n\,CH_2{=}CCl{-}CH{=}CH_2 \rightarrow {-}[CH_2{-}CCl{=}CH{-}CH_2]_n{-}}$.

questions.q: Inner tubes of tyres are best made of butyl rubber because it has:
questions.a: Butyl rubber (polyisobutylene with about 1-3% isoprene) has tightly packed chains with few double bonds, making it nearly impermeable to air, so it holds pressure in tubes.

questions.q: What is vulcanisation of rubber? Explain the process and the changes it produces in the properties of rubber.
questions.a:
**Vulcanisation** is heating raw rubber with sulphur (or another cross-linking agent) so that cross-links form between the polyisoprene chains.

**Process**: raw rubber is mixed with about 3-5% sulphur, an accelerator (for example mercaptobenzothiazole), ZnO and stearic acid as activator, plus fillers such as carbon black. It is heated at about 100-140 °C for a fixed time.

**Chemistry**: sulphur forms mono- and polysulphide bridges ($\mathrm{{-}S{-}}$, $\mathrm{{-}S{-}S{-}}$) between neighbouring chains at the double bonds / allylic $\mathrm{CH_2}$ groups:
$\mathrm{{\sim}CH_2{-}C(CH_3){=}CH{-}CH_2{\sim}}$ chains are linked through $\mathrm{{-}S_x{-}}$ bridges into a loose network.

**Changes in properties**:
| Raw rubber | Vulcanised rubber |
|---|---|
| Soft and sticky in summer, brittle in winter (about 10-60 °C) | Useful from about -40 to 100 °C |
| Low tensile strength | Tensile strength roughly ten times higher |
| Permanent set (chains slip) | High elasticity, returns to shape |
| Swells in oils and solvents | Much more resistant to solvents |
| Easily oxidised, poor abrasion resistance | Better resistance to oxidation and abrasion |
| High water absorption | Low water absorption, better insulator |

With about 30% or more sulphur the product is **ebonite**, hard and non-elastic, used as an electrical insulator.

questions.q: Give the preparation, properties and uses of Buna-S.
questions.a:
**Preparation**: emulsion copolymerisation of 1,3-butadiene (about 75%) with styrene (about 25%) using a peroxide initiator:
$\mathrm{n\,CH_2{=}CH{-}CH{=}CH_2 + n\,C_6H_5CH{=}CH_2 \rightarrow {-}[CH_2{-}CH{=}CH{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH(C_6H_5)]_n{-}}$

**Properties**: good abrasion resistance, strength and load-bearing capacity after vulcanisation; less elastic than natural rubber; swells in oils; oxidised by ozone.

**Uses**: motor tyres (the largest use), shoe soles, conveyor belts, floor tiles, cable insulation, gaskets.

questions.q: List the drawbacks of raw natural rubber.
questions.a:
1. Soft and sticky at high temperature, hard and brittle at low temperature (useful only about 10-60 °C).
2. Low tensile strength and poor abrasion resistance.
3. Large **permanent set**: on stretching, chains slip past each other and the rubber does not fully recover.
4. High water absorption.
5. Swells or dissolves in oils and organic solvents (petrol, benzene).
6. Easily attacked by oxidising agents, ozone and light (perishes).

Vulcanisation removes most of these defects.

questions.q: Write a short note on thiokol rubber.
questions.a:
**Thiokol** is a polysulphide rubber made by condensing ethylene dichloride with sodium tetrasulphide:
$\mathrm{n\,ClCH_2CH_2Cl + n\,Na_2S_4 \rightarrow {-}[CH_2CH_2{-}S_4]_n{-} + 2n\,NaCl}$

**Properties**: excellent resistance to oils, petrol and solvents; low gas permeability; resistant to ozone and weathering; poor mechanical strength and an unpleasant smell. It cannot be vulcanised with sulphur like natural rubber, but is cured with ZnO.

**Uses**: lining of hoses and tanks for petrol and oil, gaskets, sealants, and as a fuel binder in solid rocket propellants.

topics.why: It is a newer, descriptive topic usually asked as a short note or a definition with examples; it rarely carries a full long question.
topics.gist:
A **composite** is a material made of two or more chemically and physically distinct phases, combined so that the result has properties neither has alone. It has a continuous **matrix** (polymer, metal or ceramic) that binds the reinforcement, transfers load to it and protects it, and a dispersed **reinforcement** (fibres, particles, flakes) that carries most of the load and provides stiffness and strength.

Classification by reinforcement:
- **Fibre-reinforced**: glass fibre (GFRP), carbon fibre (CFRP), aramid (Kevlar) in epoxy or polyester matrices.
- **Particle-reinforced**: carbon black in rubber, concrete itself.
- **Structural**: laminates (plywood) and sandwich panels.

Polymer composites are light, have a high **strength-to-weight ratio**, resist corrosion and fatigue, and can be tailored to a job. Their drawbacks are high cost, anisotropy, difficult repair and poor recyclability. They are used in aircraft and helicopter parts, boat hulls, car bodies, wind-turbine blades, sports goods and bulletproof vests.

**Biomedical polymers** are polymers used in contact with the body. They must be **biocompatible**: non-toxic, non-carcinogenic, causing no clotting or immune rejection. They must also be sterilisable, chemically stable or degrade at a controlled rate, and have suitable mechanical properties. Examples:
- **PMMA**: bone cement, intraocular lenses, dentures.
- **UHMWPE**: hip and knee cups.
- **Silicone rubber**: implants, catheters.
- **PTFE and PET (Dacron)**: vascular grafts.
- **Polyurethanes**: heart-valve and artificial-heart parts.
- **pHEMA hydrogel**: soft contact lenses.
- **PLA/PGA**: biodegradable sutures and drug-delivery systems.
key_points: Definition of composite; functions of matrix and reinforcement
Classification: fibre-reinforced, particle-reinforced, structural (laminates, sandwich)
Common fibres: glass, carbon, aramid (Kevlar); matrices: epoxy, polyester
Advantages: high strength-to-weight, stiffness, corrosion and fatigue resistance; drawbacks: cost, anisotropy, recycling
Applications in aerospace, automobiles, marine, sports, construction
Requirements of a biomedical polymer (biocompatibility, sterilisability, stability or controlled degradation, mechanical match)
Five or six biomedical polymers with their specific use
traps: Calling an alloy or a copolymer a composite: a composite keeps distinct phases with an interface
Swapping the roles: the reinforcement carries the load, the matrix binds and transfers it
Listing biomedical polymers without saying what each is used for
Writing 'non-toxic' as the only requirement; biocompatibility also covers blood compatibility and no immune rejection
topics.asked_as: 'What are polymer composites? Classify them and give their applications' (3-5 marks); 'Write a short note on biomedical polymers' (3 marks); MCQs: 'Kevlar is ...', 'Which polymer is used for biodegradable sutures?'

questions.q: Kevlar, used in bulletproof vests, is:
questions.a: Kevlar is poly(p-phenylene terephthalamide), an aramid. Rigid aromatic chains and strong inter-chain hydrogen bonding give it very high tensile strength at low density.

questions.q: Which polymer is commonly used for absorbable (biodegradable) surgical sutures?
questions.a: PGA (and PLA, or their copolymers) are polyesters that hydrolyse in the body to glycolic or lactic acid, which is metabolised. The suture dissolves after the wound heals. PTFE, PVC and PS are not biodegradable.

questions.q: What is a composite material? Explain the roles of the matrix and the reinforcement.
Classify composites with one example of each class.
questions.a:
1. **Particle-reinforced**: reinforcement as roughly equiaxed particles. Examples: carbon black in tyre rubber; concrete (gravel and sand in cement); cermets.
2. **Fibre-reinforced**: continuous or chopped fibres in a matrix. Examples: glass-fibre reinforced plastic (GFRP) boat hulls; carbon-fibre/epoxy (CFRP) aircraft parts; Kevlar/epoxy.
3. **Structural composites**: layers of materials bonded together. Examples: laminates (plywood, laminated glass) and sandwich panels (honeycomb core between two thin face sheets).

They can also be classified by matrix: polymer-matrix (PMC), metal-matrix (MMC) and ceramic-matrix (CMC).

questions.q: State the advantages and applications of fibre-reinforced polymer composites.
What are biomedical polymers? State the requirements they must satisfy and give four examples with uses.
questions.a:
**Biomedical polymers** are polymers used in medical devices, implants, prostheses and drug delivery, in direct contact with living tissue or body fluids.

**Requirements**:
1. **Biocompatible**: non-toxic, non-carcinogenic, non-allergenic; no inflammation or immune rejection.
2. **Blood compatible** where relevant: should not cause clotting or damage blood cells.
3. Chemically stable in the body, or **biodegradable at a controlled rate** with harmless products.
4. Mechanical properties matched to the tissue (strength, flexibility, wear resistance).
5. Can be **sterilised** without degradation; easy to fabricate.

**Examples**:
- **PMMA**: bone cement, intraocular lenses, dentures.
- **UHMWPE**: acetabular cups of hip joints, knee-joint inserts.
- **Silicone rubber**: breast and facial implants, catheters, tubing.
- **PTFE / Dacron (PET)**: vascular grafts.
- **pHEMA**: soft contact lenses.
- **PLA / PGA**: absorbable sutures, drug-delivery matrices.

topics.topic: Manufacture of Portland cement (wet and dry)
topics.why: A long question on manufacture with the rotary kiln zones and reactions, often with the wet vs dry comparison, is the most likely cement question.
topics.gist:
**Raw materials**: a **calcareous** material that supplies lime (limestone, chalk, marl) and an **argillaceous** material that supplies silica, alumina and iron oxide (clay, shale), roughly in the ratio 3:1. A little **gypsum** is added at the end, and coal or oil is used as fuel.

**Steps**:
1. **Crushing and mixing**. In the **dry process** the raw materials are crushed, dried and ground to a fine powder (**raw meal**). In the **wet process** they are ground with about 35-40% water into a **slurry**, which mixes very uniformly.
2. **Burning in a rotary kiln**. The kiln is a long steel cylinder lined with firebricks (roughly 90-150 m long, 2.5-3.5 m diameter), slightly inclined and rotating slowly; fuel is fired from the lower end. The charge passes through three zones:
   - **Drying zone** (upper end, about 400 °C): water evaporates.
   - **Calcination zone** (about 700-1000 °C): $\mathrm{CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2}$.
   - **Clinkering (burning) zone** (about 1400-1500 °C; some texts quote 1500-1700 °C): lime combines with silica, alumina and iron oxide to form $\mathrm{C_3S}$, $\mathrm{C_2S}$, $\mathrm{C_3A}$ and $\mathrm{C_4AF}$. The product leaves as greyish-black balls called **clinker**.
3. **Cooling** the clinker.
4. **Grinding** the clinker with **2-3% gypsum**, which acts as a retarder against flash set.
5. **Storage and packing**.

The wet process gives a better-mixed product but uses much more fuel. Modern plants therefore mostly use the dry process with preheaters and precalciners.
key_points: Raw materials: calcareous + argillaceous, about 3:1; gypsum; fuel
Dry process: raw meal; wet process: slurry with about 35-40% water
Rotary kiln construction: long, inclined, slowly rotating, firebrick-lined; counter-current flow of charge and hot gases
Three zones with temperatures and reactions: drying, calcination, clinkering
Clinker compounds formed: $\mathrm{C_3S, C_2S, C_3A, C_4AF}$
Grinding with 2-3% gypsum to control setting
Wet vs dry comparison: mixing quality, fuel, kiln length, time, cost, raw material suitability
traps: Saying gypsum is added to the kiln; it is added while grinding the cooled clinker (it would decompose in the kiln)
Putting the calcination zone at the hottest end; the clinkering zone is nearest the burner
Claiming the wet process is cheaper; it uses more fuel to evaporate the water
Drawing the flow sheet without labelling the zones and their temperatures
topics.asked_as: 'Describe the manufacture of Portland cement by the wet process with a neat flow diagram and the reactions in the rotary kiln' (5-10 marks); 'Compare wet and dry processes' (3-5 marks); 'Why is gypsum added to cement?' (2 marks).

questions.q: Gypsum is added to Portland cement clinker to:
options: Act as a fuel in the kiln
questions.a: Gypsum reacts with $\mathrm{C_3A}$ to form insoluble calcium sulphoaluminate (ettringite) on the grains, slowing the very fast hydration of $\mathrm{C_3A}$. This prevents flash set and gives workable time (initial setting not less than 30 min).

questions.q: In the rotary kiln, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is mainly given off in the:
questions.a: In the calcination zone (about 700-1000 °C) limestone decomposes: $\mathrm{CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2}$.

questions.q: Most modern cement plants use the dry process mainly because it:
options: Gives a more homogeneous mix than the wet process
Uses much less fuel since no slurry water has to be evaporated
questions.a: In the wet process about 35-40% water must be evaporated in the kiln, which costs a lot of fuel. The dry process saves this energy and uses a shorter kiln. Mixing in the wet process is actually better, so A is wrong.

questions.q: Describe the manufacture of Portland cement by the wet process with a flow sheet and the chemical reactions in the rotary kiln.
questions.a:
**Raw materials**: calcareous (limestone, chalk) and argillaceous (clay, shale) in about 3:1; gypsum; coal dust or oil as fuel.

**1. Mixing**: limestone is crushed; clay is washed in a wash mill. They are ground together in a ball/tube mill with about 35-40% water to a uniform **slurry**, which is corrected for composition in storage tanks (correcting basins) and fed into the kiln.

**2. Burning in the rotary kiln**: the kiln is a steel tube lined with firebricks, about 90-150 m long and 2.5-3.5 m in diameter. It is inclined slightly and rotates slowly (about 1 rpm). Slurry enters at the upper end and hot gases from the burner at the lower end move up (**counter-current**).
- **Drying zone** (about 400 °C, upper part): water evaporates.
- **Calcination zone** (about 700-1000 °C): $\mathrm{CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\uparrow}$
- **Clinkering zone** (about 1400-1500 °C, lower part): lime combines with the acidic oxides; partial fusion gives clinker.
  - $\mathrm{2CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow 2CaO\cdot SiO_2}$ (dicalcium silicate)
  - $\mathrm{3CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot SiO_2}$ (tricalcium silicate)
  - $\mathrm{3CaO + Al_2O_3 \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3}$ (tricalcium aluminate)
  - $\mathrm{4CaO + Al_2O_3 + Fe_2O_3 \rightarrow 4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3}$ (tetracalcium aluminoferrite)

**3. Cooling**: hot clinker (greyish-black balls, a few mm to about 1 cm) is cooled in rotary or grate coolers; the hot air is reused for combustion.

**4. Grinding**: clinker is ground very fine in ball/tube mills with **2-3% gypsum** (retarder).

**5. Storage and packing** in silos and 50 kg bags.

**Flow sheet**: limestone crusher + clay wash mill → slurry tank (correction) → rotary kiln (drying → calcination → clinkering) → cooler → ball mill (+ gypsum) → silo → packing.

questions.q: Compare the wet and dry processes of cement manufacture.
questions.a:
| Point | Wet process | Dry process |
|---|---|---|
| Form of raw mix | Slurry with about 35-40% water | Dry powdered raw meal |
| Suitable raw material | Soft materials like chalk, clay | Hard materials like limestone, shale |
| Mixing and composition control | Very homogeneous; easy to correct | Less uniform (good with modern blending) |
| Fuel consumption | High (water must be evaporated) | Low |
| Kiln length | Longer | Shorter |
| Time | Slower | Faster |
| Cost of production | Higher | Lower |
| Quality of cement | Better and uniform | Somewhat inferior (traditionally) |
| Dust nuisance | Little | More dust, needs collectors |

questions.q: Why is the rotary kiln inclined and rotated? Why is the flow counter-current?
questions.a:
The **inclination** (a few degrees) and slow **rotation** make the charge tumble and move steadily from the upper (feed) end to the lower (burner) end. This mixes it continuously and exposes all particles to heat.

The flow is **counter-current**: the charge moves down while hot combustion gases move up. The hottest gases meet the material that needs the highest temperature (clinkering), and the cooler exit gases still dry and preheat the incoming feed. This gives maximum heat transfer and fuel economy.

topics.topic: Composition, setting and hardening of cement
topics.why: Setting and hardening with the hydration reactions of the four Bogue compounds is the most asked cement question, in short and long form.
topics.gist:
**Oxide composition** of OPC (typical): $\mathrm{CaO}$ 60-67%, $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ 17-25%, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ 3-8%, $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ 0.5-6%, $\mathrm{MgO}$ 0.1-4%, $\mathrm{SO_3}$ 1-3%, alkalis about 0.4-1.3%.

These oxides are present as four **Bogue compounds**:

| Compound | Short name | Approx. % | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tricalcium silicate $\mathrm{3CaO\cdot SiO_2}$ | $\mathrm{C_3S}$ (alite) | 40-50 | early strength (first 7 days); high heat |
| Dicalcium silicate $\mathrm{2CaO\cdot SiO_2}$ | $\mathrm{C_2S}$ (belite) | 20-30 | later strength (7-28 days and beyond); low heat |
| Tricalcium aluminate $\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3}$ | $\mathrm{C_3A}$ | 5-11 | initial setting (flash set without gypsum); most heat |
| Tetracalcium aluminoferrite $\mathrm{4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3}$ | $\mathrm{C_4AF}$ | 8-14 | contributes to setting; little strength; grey colour |

**Setting** is the loss of plasticity, as the paste stiffens in the first few hours. It is caused mainly by hydration of $\mathrm{C_3A}$ and $\mathrm{C_4AF}$, controlled by gypsum, which forms ettringite. **Hardening** is the gain of strength over days to months, caused by hydration of $\mathrm{C_3S}$ (fast) and $\mathrm{C_2S}$ (slow). The silicates give **tobermorite gel** (calcium silicate hydrate, C-S-H), which binds the mass, plus $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$, which keeps concrete alkaline. Each reaction gives out heat (heat of hydration), which matters in mass concrete. IS limits for OPC: initial setting time not less than 30 min, final setting time not more than 600 min.
key_points: Typical oxide composition of OPC with ranges
Four Bogue compounds: formula, short notation, percentage, function
Setting = stiffening (C3A, C4AF, gypsum); hardening = strength gain (C3S early, C2S late)
Hydration equations and heats: C3A about 880, C4AF about 420, C3S about 500, C2S about 250 kJ/kg (values as in Jain & Jain)
Role of gypsum: forms calcium sulphoaluminate (ettringite) and prevents flash set
Tobermorite gel (C-S-H) is the main binding phase; Ca(OH)2 makes concrete alkaline
Initial setting at least 30 min; final setting at most 600 min (10 h)
formulas: $\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3 + 6H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 6H_2O}$ + 880 kJ/kg — C3A hydration (initial set)
$\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3 + 3(CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O) + 26H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 3CaSO_4\cdot 32H_2O}$ — ettringite (gypsum retards; Jain & Jain write it with 31 $\mathrm{H_2O}$)
$\mathrm{4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3 + 7H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 6H_2O + CaO\cdot Fe_2O_3\cdot H_2O}$ + 420 kJ/kg — C4AF hydration
$\mathrm{2(2CaO\cdot SiO_2) + 4H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O + Ca(OH)_2}$ + 250 kJ/kg — C2S hydration (later strength)
traps: Treating setting and hardening as the same thing: setting is stiffening, hardening is strength gain
Giving C2S as the source of early strength; C3S gives early strength, C2S later strength
Unbalanced hydration equations: check the CaO and H2O count on both sides
Saying gypsum accelerates setting; it retards the C3A reaction
Forgetting that Ca(OH)2 is released by the silicates, which is why cement paste is alkaline (about pH 12.5)
topics.asked_as: 'Explain the setting and hardening of cement with chemical reactions' (5-10 marks); 'Give the composition of Portland cement and the role of each constituent' (5 marks); 'What is the function of gypsum in cement?' (2 marks); MCQs on which compound gives early strength or flash set.

questions.q: The early strength of cement (first 7 days) is mainly due to:
questions.a: $\mathrm{C_3S}$ hydrates quickly (within days), forming tobermorite gel and $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$, and gives most of the 7-day strength. $\mathrm{C_2S}$ hydrates slowly and gives the later strength.

questions.q: 'Flash set' of cement without gypsum is caused by:
questions.a: $\mathrm{C_3A}$ reacts almost instantly with water (and releases the most heat, about 880 kJ/kg), stiffening the paste within minutes. Gypsum prevents this by forming ettringite on the $\mathrm{C_3A}$ grains.

questions.q: Tobermorite gel formed during hardening of cement is:
questions.a: Tobermorite gel, $\mathrm{3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O}$ (C-S-H), comes from hydration of $\mathrm{C_3S}$ and $\mathrm{C_2S}$. Its huge surface area and binding power give hardened cement its strength.

questions.q: Explain the setting and hardening of Portland cement with chemical reactions.
questions.a:
When water is added, cement forms a plastic paste. It first **sets** (loses plasticity) and then **hardens** (gains strength) through hydration and hydrolysis of its compounds.

**A. Initial setting (first day)**
1. $\mathrm{C_3A}$ hydrates very rapidly:
$\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3 + 6H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 6H_2O}$ + 880 kJ/kg
This alone would cause flash set. **Gypsum** reacts with $\mathrm{C_3A}$ to give insoluble **calcium sulphoaluminate (ettringite)**:
$\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3 + 3(CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O) + 26H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 3CaSO_4\cdot 32H_2O}$
which coats the grains and retards further hydration, giving workable time.
2. $\mathrm{C_4AF}$ hydrates:
$\mathrm{4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3 + 7H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 6H_2O + CaO\cdot Fe_2O_3\cdot H_2O}$ + 420 kJ/kg

**B. Hardening (days to months)**
3. $\mathrm{C_3S}$ hydrates within about 7 days (early strength):
$\mathrm{2(3CaO\cdot SiO_2) + 6H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O + 3Ca(OH)_2}$ + 500 kJ/kg
4. $\mathrm{C_2S}$ hydrates slowly, from 7 to 28 days and beyond (later strength):
$\mathrm{2(2CaO\cdot SiO_2) + 4H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O + Ca(OH)_2}$ + 250 kJ/kg

The **tobermorite gel** (C-S-H) fills the spaces and binds the particles, and crystals of $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ and aluminate hydrates interlock, so the mass becomes hard and strong. The liberated $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ makes the paste alkaline.

(Heat values as given in Jain & Jain.)

questions.q: Give the approximate composition of Portland cement in terms of its four main compounds and state the role of each.
questions.a:
| Compound | Formula | % (approx.) | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tricalcium silicate (C3S) | $\mathrm{3CaO\cdot SiO_2}$ | 40-50 | Hydrates fast; early strength (up to 7 days); high heat of hydration |
| Dicalcium silicate (C2S) | $\mathrm{2CaO\cdot SiO_2}$ | 20-30 | Hydrates slowly; ultimate/later strength (7 days to a year); low heat; good chemical resistance |
| Tricalcium aluminate (C3A) | $\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3}$ | 5-11 | Initial setting; highest heat; prone to sulphate attack; controlled by gypsum |
| Tetracalcium aluminoferrite (C4AF) | $\mathrm{4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3}$ | 8-14 | Takes part in setting; acts as flux in the kiln; gives grey colour; little strength |

Minor: gypsum (2-3%) retards setting; free MgO and free lime above limits cause unsoundness (delayed expansion).

questions.q: A cement has 6% $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ and 3% $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$. Using Bogue's equations, estimate its $\mathrm{C_3A}$ and $\mathrm{C_4AF}$ content.
questions.a:
Bogue's equations (oxide mass %):

$\mathrm{C_3A} = 2.65\,(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}) - 1.69\,(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}) = 2.65(6) - 1.69(3) = 15.90 - 5.07 = 10.83\%$

$\mathrm{C_4AF} = 3.04\,(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}) = 3.04(3) = 9.12\%$

The $\mathrm{C_3A}$ value is in the normal OPC range (5-11%); this cement would not count as sulphate resisting, which needs $\mathrm{C_3A}$ below about 5%.

questions.q: Distinguish between setting and hardening of cement.
questions.a:
| Setting | Hardening |
|---|---|
| Stiffening of the paste: loss of plasticity | Development of strength |
| Takes place in the first few hours (initial at least 30 min, final at most 10 h) | Continues for days, months, even years |
| Mainly due to hydration of $\mathrm{C_3A}$ and $\mathrm{C_4AF}$, controlled by gypsum | Mainly due to hydration of $\mathrm{C_3S}$ (early) and $\mathrm{C_2S}$ (late) |
| Products: hydrated aluminates, ettringite | Products: tobermorite gel (C-S-H) and $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ |

topics.topic: Lime saturation factor and silica modulus
topics.why: It turns up as a small numerical or a 'significance' question; less frequent than water or fuel numericals, but easy marks when it appears.
topics.gist:
The raw mix must contain the **right amount of lime** relative to the acidic oxides. These ratios (moduli) are used to check that.

**Lime saturation factor (LSF)** compares the lime actually present with the maximum that silica, alumina and iron oxide can combine with in the kiln. IS 269 allows about **0.66-1.02** for OPC (0.80-1.02 for 43 and 53 grades).
- LSF too **high** (above 1.02): uncombined **free lime** remains. It hydrates slowly after the cement has set ($\mathrm{CaO + H_2O \rightarrow Ca(OH)_2}$, with expansion), causing cracking, called **unsoundness**.
- LSF too **low**: little $\mathrm{C_3S}$ forms, so early strength is poor and setting is slow.

**Silica modulus (silica ratio, SM)** = $\mathrm{SiO_2/(Al_2O_3 + Fe_2O_3)}$, usually about 2-3 (some texts quote 1.9-3.2 or up to 4). A higher SM means less liquid (flux) phase in the kiln. The mix is then harder to burn, sets and hardens more slowly, but gains more strength later. A lower SM means easier burning, quicker setting and lower strength.

**Alumina (iron) modulus (AM)** = $\mathrm{Al_2O_3/Fe_2O_3}$, typically about 1-2.5 (IS requires at least 0.66). A high AM means more $\mathrm{C_3A}$, so quick setting and high early heat.

**Hydraulic modulus** = $\mathrm{CaO/(SiO_2 + Al_2O_3 + Fe_2O_3)}$, about 1.7-2.3.

All these are computed directly from the oxide percentages.
key_points: LSF formula with the 0.7 SO3 correction; IS range about 0.66-1.02
High LSF gives free lime and unsoundness; low LSF gives low C3S and poor early strength
Silica modulus formula, usual range about 2-3, and effect of high or low values
Alumina modulus formula and effect on C3A and setting
Hydraulic modulus formula and range
Substitute oxide mass percentages directly; give the answer to 2-3 decimal places with a comment on acceptability
traps: Forgetting the $0.7\,\mathrm{SO_3}$ correction in the numerator when $\mathrm{SO_3}$ is given
Swapping the coefficients 2.8, 1.2, 0.65 between the oxides
Quoting a single 'textbook' range for silica modulus as if all books agree; ranges differ (about 2-3 is the safe statement)
Not commenting whether the computed value is within limits; the question usually expects that line
topics.asked_as: 'Calculate the lime saturation factor and silica modulus of a cement having the following composition ... and comment' (3-5 marks); 'What is LSF? What happens if it is too high?' (2 marks).

questions.q: A Portland cement has: CaO 63%, $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ 22%, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ 6%, $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ 3%, $\mathrm{SO_3}$ 2%. Calculate the LSF, silica modulus and alumina modulus and comment.
questions.a:
**LSF** $= \dfrac{\mathrm{CaO} - 0.7\,\mathrm{SO_3}}{2.8\,\mathrm{SiO_2} + 1.2\,\mathrm{Al_2O_3} + 0.65\,\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}} = \dfrac{63 - 0.7(2)}{2.8(22) + 1.2(6) + 0.65(3)} = \dfrac{61.6}{61.6 + 7.2 + 1.95} = \dfrac{61.6}{70.75} = 0.871$

**SM** $= \dfrac{22}{6 + 3} = 2.44$

**AM** $= \dfrac{6}{3} = 2.0$

**Comment**: LSF 0.87 is within 0.66-1.02 (and within 0.80-1.02 for higher grades), so no excess free lime: the cement should be sound. SM 2.44 and AM 2.0 are in the normal ranges, so burning and setting behaviour should be normal.

questions.q: A cement analyses CaO 65%, $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ 20%, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ 5.5%, $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ 3.5%, $\mathrm{SO_3}$ 2.5%. Find its LSF, silica modulus and hydraulic modulus.
questions.a:
**LSF** $= \dfrac{65 - 0.7(2.5)}{2.8(20) + 1.2(5.5) + 0.65(3.5)} = \dfrac{65 - 1.75}{56 + 6.6 + 2.275} = \dfrac{63.25}{64.875} = 0.975$

**SM** $= \dfrac{20}{5.5 + 3.5} = \dfrac{20}{9} = 2.22$

**HM** $= \dfrac{65}{20 + 5.5 + 3.5} = \dfrac{65}{29} = 2.24$

LSF 0.975 is close to but below the upper limit 1.02, so the cement is lime-rich: high $\mathrm{C_3S}$ and good early strength, but burning must be thorough to avoid free lime. SM and HM are within normal ranges.

questions.q: If the lime saturation factor of a raw mix is much greater than 1.02, the cement is likely to:
options: Contain free lime and be unsound
questions.a: Excess lime cannot all combine with the acidic oxides, so free CaO remains. It hydrates and expands after the cement has set, causing cracks (unsoundness).

questions.q: Silica modulus of cement is defined as:
questions.a: Silica modulus (silica ratio) = $\mathrm{SiO_2/(Al_2O_3 + Fe_2O_3)}$. $\mathrm{Al_2O_3/Fe_2O_3}$ is the alumina (iron) modulus.

questions.q: What is the significance of LSF and silica modulus in cement manufacture?
questions.a:
**LSF** tells whether the amount of lime matches what the silica, alumina and iron oxide can combine with.
- LSF above about 1.02: free lime remains, causing delayed expansion and cracking (unsoundness).
- LSF too low (below about 0.66): less $\mathrm{C_3S}$ forms, giving poor early strength and slow hardening.
So LSF is kept within 0.66-1.02 to get a sound cement with good strength.

**Silica modulus** controls the proportion of silicates to the flux (liquid-forming) oxides.
- High SM: little liquid phase in the kiln, so the mix is hard to burn; slow setting and hardening but high later strength.
- Low SM: more liquid phase, easier burning and quick setting, but lower ultimate strength and possible kiln ring formation.
It is usually kept at about 2-3.

questions.q: Increasing the alumina modulus ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3/Fe_2O_3}$) of cement will mainly:
questions.a: More alumina relative to iron oxide means more $\mathrm{C_3A}$ (by Bogue: $\mathrm{C_3A} = 2.65\,\mathrm{Al_2O_3} - 1.69\,\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$), giving quicker setting and higher early heat. A low AM gives sulphate-resisting, slower-setting cement.

topics.why: It mostly appears as a 2-3 mark short note or an MCQ on which cement suits which job.
topics.gist:
Special cements are OPC variants made by changing the compound balance, the fineness or the additions to suit a job.

- **Rapid hardening cement**: more $\mathrm{C_3S}$ and finer grinding. It **sets like OPC but gains strength faster** (3-day strength close to 7-day OPC). Used for road repairs and precast work.
- **Quick setting cement**: less gypsum and finer grinding. It **sets very fast** (initial about 5 min). Used for underwater work and grouting.
- **Low heat cement**: less $\mathrm{C_3A}$ and $\mathrm{C_3S}$, more $\mathrm{C_2S}$, so heat of hydration is low. Used for mass concrete in dams.
- **Sulphate resisting cement**: $\mathrm{C_3A}$ below about 5%. Used for foundations in sulphate-bearing soils and for marine work.
- **High alumina cement (ciment fondu)**: made by fusing bauxite and limestone, about 35-40% $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$. It hardens very rapidly, resists heat and sulphates, and is used for refractory linings. It loses strength over time in warm, wet conditions (conversion), so it is not used for structural concrete.
- **White cement**: $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ below about 1% (iron gives the grey colour), made with china clay and fired with oil or gas. Used for decorative work and tiles.
- **Portland pozzolana cement (PPC)**: OPC clinker + 15-35% fly ash or pozzolana. The pozzolana reacts with $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ to form extra C-S-H, giving low heat, more chemical resistance and higher later strength.
- **Portland slag cement**: OPC clinker + granulated blast-furnace slag.
- Others: coloured, waterproof and expansive cements.
key_points: Rapid hardening vs quick setting: strength rate vs setting time
Low heat cement for dams: low C3A, C3S; high C2S
Sulphate resisting: C3A below about 5%
High alumina cement: bauxite + lime, rapid hardening, refractory, conversion problem
White cement: very low Fe2O3
PPC and slag cement: industrial by-products, pozzolanic reaction with Ca(OH)2
formulas: $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2 + SiO_2\,(pozzolana) + H_2O \rightarrow C{-}S{-}H\ gel}$ — pozzolanic reaction (schematic)
traps: Treating rapid hardening and quick setting as the same; the first is about strength, the second about setting time
Saying low heat cement has more C3S; it has less C3S and C3A
Recommending high alumina cement for ordinary structural concrete; its strength drops on conversion
topics.asked_as: 'Write short notes on any two special cements' (3 marks each); 'Which cement would you use for a dam / sea-water structure / road repair and why?' (2 marks); MCQs.

questions.q: White cement differs from OPC mainly in having very low:
questions.a: Iron oxide (as $\mathrm{C_4AF}$) gives OPC its grey colour. White cement keeps $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ below about 1% by using china clay and pure limestone and firing with oil or gas instead of coal.

questions.q: Sulphate-resisting cement is made by keeping low:
questions.a: Sulphates attack the hydrated aluminate of $\mathrm{C_3A}$, forming expansive ettringite that cracks the concrete. Keeping $\mathrm{C_3A}$ below about 5% gives sulphate resistance.

questions.q: Which cement is preferred for the construction of a large dam? Why?
questions.a: **Low heat Portland cement.** In mass concrete the heat of hydration cannot escape, so the core gets much hotter than the surface. The temperature difference causes thermal cracking. Low heat cement has less $\mathrm{C_3A}$ and $\mathrm{C_3S}$ (the high-heat compounds) and more $\mathrm{C_2S}$, so it releases heat slowly and in smaller amounts, while still giving good long-term strength. (PPC is also used in dams for the same reason.)

questions.q: Write a short note on high alumina cement.
questions.a:
**Manufacture**: limestone (or chalk) and bauxite are fused together at about 1500-1600 °C, and the cooled product is ground. It contains about 35-40% $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ and a similar amount of CaO, mainly as calcium aluminate ($\mathrm{CaO\cdot Al_2O_3}$).

**Properties**: sets in normal time but **hardens very rapidly** (about 24-hour strength equal to 28-day OPC); high heat of hydration; highly resistant to sulphates, sea water and dilute acids; refractory (withstands high temperatures).

**Limitation**: in warm, moist conditions the hydrates convert to denser forms, increasing porosity and reducing strength (conversion). So it is not used for structural concrete.

**Uses**: refractory concrete and furnace linings, emergency repairs, sewers and chemical plants.

questions.q: Distinguish between rapid hardening cement and quick setting cement.
questions.a:
| Rapid hardening cement | Quick setting cement |
|---|---|
| Setting time about the same as OPC | Sets very quickly (initial about 5 min, final about 30 min) |
| Gains strength faster (higher $\mathrm{C_3S}$, finer grinding) | Achieved by reducing gypsum and fine grinding |
| Early strength high (3-day about equal to 7-day OPC) | Strength development is not specially rapid |
| Road repairs, precast units, cold weather work | Underwater construction, grouting, stopping leaks |

questions.q: What is Portland pozzolana cement? State its advantages.

topics.why: It is at most a short note in a chemistry paper; the useful exam link is corrosion of reinforcement, which ties into the corrosion unit.
topics.gist:
**Concrete** is a mixture of **cement** (binder), **fine aggregate** (sand), **coarse aggregate** (crushed stone or gravel) and **water**. The cement paste coats the aggregates and, on hydration, binds them into a stone-like mass. Sand fills the voids between the coarse particles. Coarse aggregate gives bulk, strength and resistance to shrinkage. Water is needed for hydration and workability.

Typical nominal mixes (cement : sand : aggregate) are 1:2:4 (M15) and 1:1.5:3 (M20). Strength depends mainly on the **water-cement ratio** (usually about 0.4-0.6): more water improves workability but leaves pores, which lowers strength and durability (Abrams' law). Concrete must be **cured**, that is kept moist (commonly for at least 7-14 days), so that hydration continues. Strength is tested at 28 days.

Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension (tensile strength about one-tenth). **RCC (reinforced cement concrete)** places steel bars in the tension zone. The combination works because steel and concrete have almost the **same coefficient of thermal expansion** (about $1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ per °C) and bond well. The highly alkaline pore solution (pH about 12.5-13) **passivates** the steel.

Durability problems:
- **Carbonation** ($\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O}$) lowers the pH to about 9.
- **Chloride ions** break the passive film.

Either way the rebar rusts. Rust occupies several times the volume of steel, so the concrete cracks and spalls. Sulphate attack and alkali-aggregate reaction also damage concrete. Prestressed concrete uses tensioned high-strength steel to pre-compress the member.
key_points: Ingredients of concrete and the function of each
Nominal mix ratios; water-cement ratio and its effect on strength
Curing and why it matters
Why RCC works: steel takes tension, similar thermal expansion, good bond, alkaline passivation
Corrosion of reinforcement: carbonation, chlorides, rust expansion, spalling
Prevention: adequate cover, low w/c ratio, good compaction, coated or galvanised bars, inhibitors, cathodic protection
Other deterioration: sulphate attack, alkali-aggregate reaction
formulas: $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O}$ — carbonation of concrete
traps: Saying more water always means stronger concrete; extra water lowers strength
Forgetting why steel does not rust in good concrete (alkaline passivation)
Calling concrete itself a chemical compound; it is a composite
topics.asked_as: 'Write a short note on concrete and RCC' (3 marks); 'Why does steel reinforcement corrode in old concrete? How is it prevented?' (3-5 marks); MCQs on w/c ratio and the thermal expansion match.

questions.q: Steel and concrete work well together in RCC mainly because:
options: They have nearly equal coefficients of thermal expansion
questions.a: Both expand by about $1.2\times10^{-5}$ per °C, so temperature changes do not set up stresses that break the bond. Concrete is weak, not strong, in tension, which is why steel is added.

questions.q: Carbonation of concrete reduces the pH of the pore solution from about 12.5 to about:
questions.a: $\mathrm{CO_2}$ converts $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ into $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, lowering the pH to about 9. At this pH the passive film on steel is no longer stable and the rebar can corrode.

questions.q: What is concrete? State the function of each ingredient.
questions.a:
**Concrete** is a composite building material made by mixing cement, fine aggregate, coarse aggregate and water in suitable proportions (for example 1:2:4) and allowing it to harden.

- **Cement**: the binder; on hydration it forms C-S-H gel that binds all particles.
- **Fine aggregate (sand)**: fills voids between coarse aggregate, reduces shrinkage, improves workability and density.
- **Coarse aggregate (stone chips, gravel)**: provides bulk, compressive strength and dimensional stability at low cost.
- **Water**: needed for hydration of cement and to make the mix workable. Its amount (w/c ratio) controls strength.
- Optional **admixtures**: plasticisers, accelerators, retarders, air-entraining agents.

questions.q: How does the water-cement ratio affect the strength of concrete?
questions.a: Only about 0.25-0.3 of water (by weight of cement) is needed chemically for hydration; the rest is added for workability. Excess water evaporates and leaves **capillary pores**, which reduce density, strength and durability and increase permeability. According to **Abrams' law**, strength falls as the w/c ratio rises: $S = A/B^{w/c}$. So the lowest w/c ratio that still gives a workable, well-compacted mix (usually about 0.4-0.5) should be used.

questions.q: Why does the steel reinforcement in RCC corrode after some years? Suggest methods of prevention.
questions.a:
**Why steel is normally safe**: the pore solution of concrete is highly alkaline (pH about 12.5-13, due to $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$), and steel forms a passive oxide film in it.

**Causes of corrosion**:
1. **Carbonation**: atmospheric $\mathrm{CO_2}$ diffuses in, $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O}$, so the pH drops to about 9 and the passive film is lost.
2. **Chlorides** (sea water, de-icing salts, contaminated sand) break down the passive film locally even at high pH, causing pitting.
3. Moisture and oxygen through cracks and a thin cover then allow electrochemical corrosion: anode $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$; cathode $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
4. **Rust occupies several times the volume** of the original steel, so it creates internal pressure, cracking and spalling of the cover, which lets in more water.

**Prevention**: adequate concrete cover; low w/c ratio and good compaction (dense, impermeable concrete); proper curing; chloride-free materials; epoxy-coated or galvanised bars; corrosion inhibitors (for example calcium nitrite); surface sealants; cathodic protection for marine structures; blended cements (PPC, slag) for low permeability.

questions.q: What is curing of concrete and why is it necessary?
questions.a:
**Curing** is keeping freshly placed concrete moist and at a suitable temperature (by ponding, wet gunny bags, sprinkling or curing compounds) for a period, commonly at least 7-14 days.

It is necessary because hydration of cement, especially of $\mathrm{C_2S}$, continues for weeks and needs water. If the concrete dries early, hydration stops, strength stays low, and plastic shrinkage cracks and a porous, dusty surface form. Proper curing gives full strength, durability and impermeability.

topics.why: The electrochemical theory of corrosion (anodic and cathodic reactions, hydrogen evolution vs oxygen absorption, rust formation) is the most predictable question of the unit.
topics.gist:
**Corrosion** is the gradual destruction of a metal by chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment. It is the reverse of extraction: the metal goes back to a stable compound such as an oxide, carbonate or sulphide.

**1. Dry (chemical) corrosion** is direct attack by gases or dry environments, with no electrolyte. The main type is **oxidation corrosion**: $\mathrm{2M \rightarrow 2M^{n+} + 2ne^-}$, $\mathrm{\tfrac{n}{2}O_2 + 2ne^- \rightarrow nO^{2-}}$, giving the oxide $\mathrm{M_2O_n}$ on the surface. What happens next depends on the oxide film:
- **stable, non-porous** (Al, Cr): protective;
- **porous or cracked** (alkali and alkaline earth metals): corrosion continues;
- **volatile** ($\mathrm{MoO_3}$): the surface is always exposed;
- **unstable** (Ag, Au, Pt oxides): decomposes back to metal.

The **Pilling-Bedworth ratio** (oxide volume / metal volume) predicts this. Other dry types are attack by $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$ and $\mathrm{SO_2}$, and liquid-metal corrosion.

**2. Wet (electrochemical) corrosion** happens when a conducting liquid is present, or the metal is moist. Tiny **anodic** and **cathodic** areas form on the metal.
- At the anode the metal dissolves: $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$.
- At the cathode either **hydrogen is evolved** (acidic, oxygen-free medium) or **oxygen is absorbed** (neutral or alkaline aerated water).

$\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ diffuse and meet, giving $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_2}$, which oxidises to rust, $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}$. The metal is eaten away at the **anode**, but rust usually deposits **near the cathode** or between the two.
key_points: Definition of corrosion; why metals corrode (thermodynamically unstable state)
Dry corrosion: oxidation mechanism, nature of oxide film (stable, porous, volatile, unstable)
Pilling-Bedworth ratio: below 1 porous, about 1-2 protective, much above 2 spalls
Wet corrosion: anodic dissolution; cathodic hydrogen evolution (acidic) vs oxygen absorption (neutral or alkaline)
Rust formation equations; rust is $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}$ (with $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ in limited oxygen)
Corrosion occurs at the anode; product deposits nearer the cathode
Table: dry vs wet corrosion
formulas: $\mathrm{PBR} = \dfrac{V_{oxide}}{V_{metal}} = \dfrac{M_{oxide}\,\rho_{metal}}{n\,M_{metal}\,\rho_{oxide}}$ — Pilling-Bedworth ratio ($n$ = metal atoms per oxide formula)
traps: Writing the cathodic reaction for neutral water as $\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2}$; in aerated neutral water it is oxygen absorption
Saying rust forms at the anode; the metal dissolves at the anode, rust deposits near the cathode
Stating that a higher PBR is always better; above about 2 the film cracks and flakes off
Calling dry corrosion 'slow' and wet corrosion 'fast' as a rule; the real difference is the presence of an electrolyte
Not balancing the electrons between anodic and cathodic half-reactions in the overall equation
topics.asked_as: 'Explain the electrochemical theory of corrosion with hydrogen evolution and oxygen absorption mechanisms' (5-10 marks); 'Differentiate dry and wet corrosion' (3-5 marks); 'What is the Pilling-Bedworth rule?' (2-3 marks); MCQs on cathodic reactions.

questions.q: In iron corroding in neutral aerated water, the main cathodic reaction is:
questions.a: In neutral, aerated solutions $\mathrm{H^+}$ is scarce, so dissolved oxygen takes the electrons (oxygen absorption), giving $\mathrm{OH^-}$. Hydrogen evolution is the cathodic reaction in acidic, oxygen-free media. Option A is the anodic reaction.

questions.q: A metal whose Pilling-Bedworth ratio is less than 1 (for example Mg, Na, K) forms an oxide film that is:
questions.a: PBR below 1 means the oxide occupies less volume than the metal it replaces, so it cannot cover the surface; it is porous and oxygen keeps reaching the metal. PBR about 1-2 gives a protective film (Al, Cr); much above 2 the film cracks and spalls.

questions.q: Explain the electrochemical theory of wet corrosion. Describe the hydrogen evolution and oxygen absorption mechanisms with equations.
questions.a:
**Theory**: when a metal is in contact with an electrolyte (moisture, salt solution), small **anodic and cathodic areas** form because of heterogeneity (impurities, stresses, differences in aeration or concentration). Electrons flow through the metal from anode to cathode, ions move through the electrolyte, and the metal at the anode dissolves.

**Anodic reaction** (oxidation; always metal dissolution):
$\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$

**Cathodic reaction** depends on the medium:

**(a) Hydrogen evolution**: acidic, oxygen-free media (for example iron in acid, industrial wastes). Electrons are taken by $\mathrm{H^+}$:
$\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2\uparrow}$
Overall: $\mathrm{Fe + 2H^+ \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + H_2}$. Usually there is a **large anodic area and small cathodic area**, giving fairly uniform dissolution.

**(b) Oxygen absorption**: neutral or alkaline aqueous media with dissolved oxygen (for example iron in sea water or moist air). For example, a small crack in an oxide film is the anode and the large surrounding surface is the cathode:
$\mathrm{\tfrac{1}{2}O_2 + H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow 2OH^-}$
$\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ diffuse and meet:
$\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2}$
With excess oxygen: $\mathrm{4Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4Fe(OH)_3}$, which dehydrates to yellow-brown rust $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}$. With limited oxygen, black magnetite $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ forms.

Note: the metal is destroyed at the **anode**, but rust deposits **near the cathode** where $\mathrm{OH^-}$ is produced. The small anode / large cathode arrangement makes the attack intense (pitting).

questions.q: Differentiate between dry (chemical) and wet (electrochemical) corrosion.
questions.a:
| Dry (chemical) corrosion | Wet (electrochemical) corrosion |
|---|---|
| Occurs in the absence of moisture/electrolyte | Needs a conducting liquid or moisture |
| Direct chemical attack by gases ($\mathrm{O_2}$, $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$) | Formation of a large number of tiny galvanic cells |
| No separate anode and cathode | Separate anodic and cathodic areas |
| Corrosion product forms at the place of attack | Corrosion at the anode; product deposits near the cathode |
| Usually uniform | Often localised (pitting, crevice) |
| Explained by absorption/oxidation mechanism (film growth) | Explained by electrochemical theory |
| Example: oxidation of metals at high temperature | Example: rusting of iron in moist air or sea water |

questions.q: Calculate the Pilling-Bedworth ratio for aluminium and predict whether its oxide is protective. (Al = 26.98, $\rho_{Al}$ = 2.70 g/cm³; $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ = 101.96, $\rho$ = 3.95 g/cm³)
questions.a:
$\mathrm{PBR} = \dfrac{M_{oxide}\,\rho_{metal}}{n\,M_{metal}\,\rho_{oxide}}$, with $n = 2$ Al atoms per $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$.

$\mathrm{PBR} = \dfrac{101.96 \times 2.70}{2 \times 26.98 \times 3.95} = \dfrac{275.3}{213.1} = 1.29$

Since $1 < 1.29 < 2$, the oxide occupies slightly more volume than the metal, covers it completely without excessive stress, and is **protective and non-porous**. This is why aluminium resists atmospheric corrosion.

questions.q: Iron dissolves at the anode, yet rust is often found away from the point of attack, near the cathode. Explain.
questions.a: At the anode $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$; the $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ ions, being small and mobile, diffuse into the electrolyte. At the cathode, oxygen absorption produces $\mathrm{OH^-}$ ($\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$). $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ moves faster than $\mathrm{OH^-}$, so the ions meet nearer the cathode, where $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_2}$ precipitates and is oxidised to rust. So the metal loss (pit) is at the anode, while the rust deposit is at or near the cathode.

topics.why: Galvanic corrosion with an example and differential aeration (with the half-immersed zinc rod or waterline example) are standard 3-5 mark questions.
key_points: Galvanic corrosion: two dissimilar metals + electrical contact + electrolyte; the more active metal corrodes
Factors: potential difference, area ratio (small anode / large cathode is worst), conductivity of electrolyte
Examples: steel screws in copper plate, Zn-Fe, brass fittings on steel pipes
Prevention of galvanic corrosion: insulation, metals close in series, large anode, avoid painting the anode only
Concentration cell: one metal, different electrolyte concentration or aeration
Differential aeration: the less-oxygenated part is the anode; zinc rod / waterline / crevice examples
EMF of a concentration cell from the Nernst equation
formulas: $E = \dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log\dfrac{C_2}{C_1}$ — metal-ion concentration cell at 25 °C ($C_2 > C_1$; dilute side is the anode)
traps: Saying the more aerated region corrodes; in differential aeration the oxygen-poor region is the anode
Ignoring the area effect: a small anode with a large cathode corrodes fastest
Painting only the anodic metal in a couple; any scratch then gives a tiny anode facing a huge cathode
Calling concentration cell corrosion 'galvanic corrosion'; it needs only one metal
