topics.asked_as: 'Explain galvanic corrosion with an example. How can it be minimised?' (3-5 marks); 'What is differential aeration corrosion? Explain with a suitable example and diagram' (5 marks); 'Distinguish galvanic and concentration cell corrosion' (3 marks); MCQs on which part corrodes.

questions.q: In differential aeration corrosion, the part of the metal that corrodes is the one:
questions.a: The poorly aerated region has a lower potential and becomes the anode ($\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + ne^-}$), while the well-aerated region acts as the cathode where $\mathrm{O_2}$ is reduced. So corrosion occurs where oxygen is less.

questions.q: Steel bolts are used to fasten a large copper plate in sea water. What happens?
options: Both corrode at the same rate
questions.a: Steel is more active than copper, so the bolts become the anode. Because the bolt area (anode) is small and the copper area (cathode) is large, the current density at the bolts is very high and they corrode rapidly.

questions.q: Calculate the EMF of the concentration cell $\mathrm{Cu|Cu^{2+}(0.01\,M)\,||\,Cu^{2+}(1\,M)|Cu}$ at 25 °C. Which electrode corrodes?
questions.a:
$E = \dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log\dfrac{C_2}{C_1} = \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{0.01} = 0.02955 \times 2 = 0.0591$ V

The copper in contact with the **dilute (0.01 M)** solution is the anode and corrodes ($\mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-}$), tending to equalise the concentrations. Copper is deposited at the electrode in 1 M solution.

questions.q: What is differential aeration corrosion? Explain with a suitable example.
questions.a:
**Differential aeration corrosion** is a concentration cell corrosion that occurs when different parts of the **same metal** are exposed to different concentrations of oxygen (air). The **less-aerated part becomes the anode** and corrodes; the more-aerated part becomes the cathode.

**Example: a zinc (or iron) rod partly immersed in dilute NaCl solution.**
- The part near the surface is in contact with water rich in dissolved oxygen, so it acts as the **cathode**: $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
- The part deeper in the solution, with less oxygen, acts as the **anode**: $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$.
- Electrons flow through the rod from the immersed part to the part near the surface; $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ form $\mathrm{Zn(OH)_2}$.
- So the rod corrodes just **below the waterline**, while the part near the surface is protected.

**Diagram**: beaker with NaCl solution; rod with the upper immersed portion labelled 'more $\mathrm{O_2}$: cathode' and the lower portion labelled 'less $\mathrm{O_2}$: anode, corrosion'; arrows for electron flow.

**Other examples**: waterline corrosion of tanks and ships, corrosion under dirt or a water drop, crevice corrosion under washers and bolts, pipelines passing through clay (poorly aerated) and sand (well aerated).

questions.q: Explain why a small anodic area with a large cathodic area leads to severe corrosion.
questions.a:
In a corrosion cell the total electrons released at the anode must equal those consumed at the cathode. A large cathode can consume electrons (reduce $\mathrm{O_2}$ or $\mathrm{H^+}$) at a high total rate, so it demands a large current. This whole current must come from the small anode, so the **current density at the anode is very high**, and the metal there dissolves rapidly and deeply (pitting).

Example: a small scratch in a tin coating on iron (iron is the small anode, tin the large cathode), or steel rivets on a copper sheet. Therefore the anodic area should be kept large, and if only one metal can be painted, the cathode should be painted.

questions.q: Distinguish between galvanic corrosion and concentration cell corrosion.
questions.a:
| Galvanic corrosion | Concentration cell corrosion |
|---|---|
| Two **different metals** in electrical contact | A **single metal** |
| Driving force: difference in electrode potential of the metals | Driving force: difference in concentration (of $\mathrm{O_2}$ or metal ions) of the electrolyte |
| The more active metal is the anode | The less-aerated (or more dilute) region is the anode |
| Examples: Zn-Cu couple, steel bolts in copper sheet | Waterline corrosion, half-immersed zinc rod, crevice corrosion |
| Prevented by insulating the metals or choosing metals close in the galvanic series | Prevented by uniform aeration, avoiding crevices, keeping surfaces clean |

topics.why: It is usually a 2-3 mark definition with examples, or appears inside questions on the galvanic series and stainless steel.
topics.gist:
**Passivity** is the phenomenon in which a metal or alloy shows **much higher corrosion resistance than its position in the electrochemical series predicts**. It happens because the metal forms a very thin (of the order of nanometres), invisible, highly adherent, non-porous and **self-healing** oxide film that separates it from the environment.

Examples:
- **Al, Cr, Ti, Ni, Co** and **stainless steel**, which needs at least about 11-12% Cr to form a $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ film;
- **iron in concentrated nitric acid**: iron dissolves rapidly in dilute $\mathrm{HNO_3}$, but conc. $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ makes it passive, and passive iron then does not even displace copper from $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$.

Aluminium, very active by its $E^\circ$ (-1.66 V), is used for utensils, window frames and aircraft because its $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ film protects it. If scratched, the film re-forms at once in air (self-healing). This is why active-looking metals like Al and Ti sit near the noble end of the galvanic series.

Passivity is **lost** in the presence of **chloride ions** (sea water) and reducing conditions. Chloride breaks the film locally, so passive metals such as stainless steel suffer **pitting** and crevice corrosion in sea water. Passivity is used deliberately in **anodic protection** (keeping a metal at a potential where it stays passive) and in **anodising** of aluminium. The potential at which a passive metal becomes active again is called the **Flade potential**.
key_points: Definition of passivity and the nature of the passive film (thin, adherent, non-porous, self-healing)
Examples: Al, Cr, Ti, Ni, stainless steel, Fe in conc. $\mathrm{HNO_3}$
Why Al and Ti are corrosion resistant despite very negative $E^\circ$
Stainless steel: about 11-12% Cr minimum, $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ film
Breakdown of passivity by $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ and reducing conditions, leading to pitting
Applications: anodising, anodic protection; Flade potential (optional)
traps: Defining passivity as 'a metal that does not react at all'; it is a protective film, and it can break down
Saying chloride strengthens the passive film; chloride destroys it
Claiming Al is less reactive than Zn by nature; it is more reactive by $E^\circ$ and only behaves as more noble because of passivity
topics.asked_as: 'What is passivity? Explain with examples' (2-3 marks); 'Why is aluminium used for utensils though it is an active metal?' (2 marks); 'Why does stainless steel corrode in sea water?' (2-3 marks); MCQs.

questions.q: Iron becomes passive when dipped in:
questions.a: Concentrated $\mathrm{HNO_3}$, a strong oxidiser, forms a thin protective oxide film on iron. After this the iron is passive and does not dissolve or displace copper from $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$. Dilute $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ dissolves iron.

questions.q: The passivity of stainless steel is most readily destroyed by:
questions.a: Chloride ions penetrate and break the $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ film at weak spots, starting pitting and crevice corrosion, which is why stainless steel pits in sea water. Oxygen and chromates help maintain passivity.

questions.q: Define passivity. Give examples.
questions.a:
**Passivity** is the condition in which a metal or alloy becomes chemically inactive (resists corrosion) far more than expected from its position in the electrochemical series. It is due to a very thin, invisible, adherent, non-porous and self-healing protective oxide film on its surface.

**Examples**: Al, Cr, Ti, Ni and Co in air; stainless steel (owing to $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$); iron after treatment with concentrated $\mathrm{HNO_3}$.

questions.q: Aluminium has a highly negative standard electrode potential (-1.66 V), yet it is widely used for utensils, window frames and aircraft. Explain.
questions.a: On exposure to air, aluminium immediately forms a thin, compact, adherent and non-porous film of $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ ($\mathrm{4Al + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Al_2O_3}$). Its Pilling-Bedworth ratio is about 1.3, so it fully covers the metal. The film cuts off contact between the metal and oxygen or moisture, so further corrosion stops: aluminium becomes **passive**. If the film is scratched, it re-forms at once (self-healing). Its thermodynamic tendency to corrode is high, but the kinetic barrier of the film makes it practically corrosion-resistant. Anodising thickens this film further.

questions.q: Why does stainless steel need a minimum chromium content, and why does it still pit in sea water?
questions.a:
Stainless steel resists corrosion because chromium forms a continuous passive film of $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ on the surface. Only when Cr is at least about 11-12% (10.5% by standard definitions) is there enough chromium at every point to form a **continuous, self-healing** film; below this the film is patchy and the steel rusts like ordinary steel.

In sea water, **chloride ions** adsorb on the film and break it down locally. The tiny exposed spot becomes an **anode** surrounded by a huge passive **cathode** surface, so the attack is concentrated and deep (pitting). Metal chlorides hydrolyse in the pit and make it acidic, so the pit keeps growing. Molybdenum-containing grades (316) resist this better.

questions.q: Passivity is used deliberately in which of the following?
questions.a: Anodising makes aluminium the anode in an oxidising electrolyte (for example $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ or chromic acid) to thicken its natural $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ passive film. Galvanising and sacrificial anodes rely on a more active metal corroding instead.

topics.topic: Soil, pitting, intergranular, waterline and stress corrosion
topics.why: 'Write short notes on pitting / waterline / stress corrosion' with cause, mechanism, example and diagram is among the most frequent short-note questions.
topics.gist:
These are **localised** forms of corrosion; learn cause, mechanism, example and prevention for each.

- **Soil corrosion**: attack on buried pipes, cables and tank bottoms. It depends on moisture, **aeration** (clay is the anode, sand the cathode), pH, salts (low resistivity) and **sulphate-reducing bacteria**, which form FeS. Prevented by coatings, cathodic protection and backfill.
- **Pitting corrosion**: intense attack at small spots, forming deep pits. A broken film, scratch, or deposit that shields a spot from oxygen creates a **small anode with a large cathode**. Typical of stainless steel and Al in chloride media; a pipe can be perforated with little weight loss.
- **Intergranular corrosion**: attack **along grain boundaries**. In sensitised stainless steel (heated at about 500-800 °C, for example near welds, called **weld decay**), chromium carbide precipitates at the boundaries. The adjacent zone is depleted in Cr, loses passivity, and corrodes. Prevented by low-carbon grades (304L), stabilising with Ti or Nb, and solution annealing.
- **Waterline corrosion**: in tanks and ship hulls partly filled with water, the metal **just below the waterline** (less oxygen) is the anode and the metal at the waterline is the cathode. Prevented with antifouling paints and cathodic protection.
- **Stress corrosion cracking (SCC)**: cracking caused by the **combined action of tensile stress and a specific corrosive environment**. Stressed regions are anodic. Examples: **season cracking** of cold-worked brass in ammonia; **caustic embrittlement** of boiler steel in NaOH; chloride SCC of stainless steel. Prevented by stress-relief annealing and inhibitors.
key_points: Soil corrosion: moisture, aeration, pH, salts, resistivity, SRB; prevention
Pitting: localised, small anode / large cathode, differential aeration under deposits, chloride breakdown of films
Intergranular: grain-boundary attack; sensitisation of stainless steel by $\mathrm{Cr_{23}C_6}$ precipitation; weld decay; prevention
Waterline: zone just below the water surface is anodic; antifouling paints
Stress corrosion: tensile stress + specific environment; season cracking of brass, caustic embrittlement, chloride SCC
One labelled diagram each for pitting and waterline corrosion
formulas: $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + S^{2-} \rightarrow FeS}$ — black iron sulphide deposit
$\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$ (inside pit, anode); $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$ (surrounding surface, cathode) — pitting
traps: Placing waterline corrosion above the waterline; it is maximum just below it
Explaining weld decay as 'the weld metal is impure'; the cause is Cr depletion next to grain-boundary carbides
Describing stress corrosion as purely mechanical; it needs both stress and a specific corrodent
Writing pitting with no mention of the small anode / large cathode ratio
topics.asked_as: 'Write short notes on (any two): pitting, intergranular, waterline, stress corrosion' (3 marks each, often with a diagram); 'Explain soil corrosion and the factors affecting it' (3-5 marks); 'What is caustic embrittlement / season cracking?' (2-3 marks).

questions.q: Season cracking of brass is a form of stress corrosion caused by:
questions.a: Cold-worked brass with residual tensile stress cracks along grain boundaries in atmospheres containing traces of ammonia or amines (they form soluble copper/zinc ammine complexes). It was first noticed in cartridge cases stored in stables during the monsoon season.

questions.q: Weld decay in austenitic stainless steel is caused by:
options: Precipitation of chromium carbide at grain boundaries
Formation of a thick oxide film
questions.a: Near a weld the steel is held at about 500-800 °C, so carbon combines with chromium to form chromium carbide ($\mathrm{Cr_{23}C_6}$) at grain boundaries. The adjacent region falls below about 12% Cr, loses passivity and corrodes: intergranular corrosion.

questions.q: In a steel water tank, waterline corrosion is most severe:
options: At the bottom of the tank
questions.a: The metal at the waterline is in contact with highly aerated water and is the cathode. The region just below it receives less oxygen and becomes the anode, so it corrodes, forming a band of attack just below the water level.

questions.q: Explain pitting corrosion with its mechanism. How can it be prevented?
questions.a:
**Pitting corrosion** is a highly localised attack that produces small but deep cavities (pits) on a metal surface while the rest of the surface is almost unaffected.

**Causes**: local breakdown of a protective or passive film (by $\mathrm{Cl^-}$), scratches, surface inclusions, or deposits (dust, sand, a water drop) that shield a spot from oxygen.

**Mechanism** (differential aeration): consider a drop of water or a speck of dirt on steel. The metal under the deposit receives less oxygen and becomes the **anode**; the large surrounding area, well supplied with oxygen, is the **cathode**.
- Anode (inside pit): $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$
- Cathode (around): $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$
Because the anode is **small and the cathode large**, the current density in the pit is very high and the pit deepens rapidly. Hydrolysis of metal ions inside the pit ($\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 2H_2O \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2 + 2H^+}$) makes it acidic, and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ migrates in, so the process is **autocatalytic**. Rust forms a cap over the mouth of the pit.

**Diagram**: metal surface with a deposit; pit beneath labelled anode; surrounding surface labelled cathode with $\mathrm{O_2}$ arrows; rust ring.

**Prevention**: smooth, clean surfaces free of deposits; avoid stagnant water; use alloys resistant to pitting (Mo-containing stainless steel); cathodic protection; inhibitors; remove chlorides.

questions.q: What is stress corrosion? Explain with examples and prevention.
questions.a:
**Stress corrosion cracking (SCC)** is the cracking of a metal under the **combined action of a tensile stress** (applied or residual from cold working, welding or heat treatment) **and a specific corrosive environment**. Neither alone would cause the failure.

**Mechanism**: the stressed regions (grain boundaries, crack tips) are more energetic and act as **anodes**, while the unstressed bulk is cathodic. Attack is concentrated along a narrow path, and the stress keeps the crack tip open and active, so a fine crack grows, often along grain boundaries, until sudden failure.

**Examples**:
1. **Season cracking** of cold-worked brass in ammonia-containing atmospheres.
2. **Caustic embrittlement** of boiler steel: concentrated NaOH accumulates at stressed rivets and joints and attacks the steel at grain boundaries.
3. **Chloride stress corrosion** of austenitic stainless steel in hot chloride solutions.

**Prevention**: stress-relief annealing after fabrication; avoid sharp corners and stress raisers in design; remove the specific corrodent (for example add $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ or phosphates to boiler water against caustic embrittlement); use inhibitors; cathodic protection; choose resistant alloys.

questions.q: Explain soil corrosion and list the factors affecting it.
questions.a:
**Soil corrosion** is the corrosion of buried metal structures (pipelines, cables, tank bottoms, poles) by the soil, which acts as an electrolyte.

**Factors**:
1. **Moisture content**: water is needed as electrolyte; wet soils are more corrosive.
2. **Aeration / oxygen**: a pipe passing through clay (poorly aerated, anode) and sand (well aerated, cathode) suffers differential aeration corrosion.
3. **pH**: acidic soils (peat, cinders, industrial waste) are highly corrosive.
4. **Dissolved salts and resistivity**: chlorides and sulphates lower resistivity and increase corrosion.
5. **Microbial activity**: anaerobic **sulphate-reducing bacteria** (Desulfovibrio) reduce $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ to $\mathrm{S^{2-}}$, depolarising the cathode and forming black FeS: $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-} + 8H^+ + 8e^- \rightarrow S^{2-} + 4H_2O}$; $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + S^{2-} \rightarrow FeS}$.
6. **Stray currents** from DC sources (electric railways).

**Prevention**: coal-tar or bitumen coatings and wrapping, cathodic protection, a non-corrosive backfill around the pipe, insulating joints.

questions.q: What is intergranular corrosion? How can it be prevented in stainless steel?

topics.why: It is asked as 'distinguish the electrochemical series and the galvanic series' or as an MCQ on the Zn/Al and Ti anomalies.
topics.gist:
The **electrochemical series (ECS)** lists **pure metals** by their **standard reduction potentials**, measured against the SHE under standard conditions (1 M ions, 25 °C). It is thermodynamic and does not account for oxide films.

The **galvanic series** lists **metals and alloys** in the order of their actual corrosion potentials measured in a **specific real environment**, usually **sea water**. It includes the effect of protective films, so the same alloy can appear twice: stainless steel *active* and *passive*.

A typical galvanic series in sea water, from active (anodic, corrodes) to noble (cathodic, protected):

Mg, Mg alloys → Zn → Al and Al alloys → Cd → mild steel, cast iron → stainless steel (active) → Pb → Sn → brass → Cu → bronze → Ni (passive) → stainless steel (passive) → Ag → Ti → graphite → Au → Pt

**Anomalies** that examiners ask about:
- In ECS, **Al** ($E^\circ = -1.66$ V) is more active than **Zn** (-0.76 V), but in the galvanic series Zn is more active because Al is passivated by $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$.
- **Ti** is very active in ECS (about -1.63 V) but near the noble end of the galvanic series because of its passive $\mathrm{TiO_2}$ film.

**Use**: for design, the galvanic series is the more practical guide. When two metals must be joined, they should lie **close together** in it. The farther apart they are, the faster the more active one corrodes.
key_points: Definition of galvanic series: metals and alloys ranked by potential in a given environment (sea water)
Order from active to noble, with Mg, Zn, Al at the active end and Pt, Au, graphite, Ti at the noble end
ECS vs galvanic series: pure metals vs alloys too; standard vs real conditions; thermodynamic vs practical; films ignored vs included
Anomalies: Zn above Al; Ti and passive stainless steel at the noble end
Use in selecting metal pairs: the greater the separation, the stronger the galvanic attack on the active metal
traps: Treating the galvanic series as identical to the ECS
Forgetting that the galvanic series depends on the environment: a ranking in sea water may not hold in acid
Placing stainless steel in only one position; active and passive forms are listed separately
topics.asked_as: 'What is galvanic series? How does it differ from electrochemical series?' (3-5 marks); 'Why is zinc more anodic than aluminium in sea water?' (2 marks); MCQs on which metal of a pair corrodes.

questions.q: In the galvanic series (sea water), which of the following is the most active (anodic)?
questions.a: In sea water, zinc lies above aluminium because aluminium's passive $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ film raises its practical potential. Copper and titanium are near the noble end. (In the ECS, Al would be more active than Zn.)

questions.q: Which pair would cause the most severe galvanic corrosion if coupled in sea water?
questions.a: Magnesium (most active) and copper (fairly noble) are far apart in the galvanic series, so the potential difference is large and the magnesium would corrode rapidly. The other pairs are close neighbours.

questions.q: Differentiate between the electrochemical series and the galvanic series.
questions.a:
| Electrochemical series | Galvanic series |
|---|---|
| Ranks **pure metals** (and non-metals) by standard reduction potential | Ranks **metals and alloys** by corrosion potential |
| Measured against SHE at standard conditions (1 M ions, 25 °C) | Measured in a specific real environment, usually sea water |
| Thermodynamic; predicts relative displacement tendency | Practical; predicts actual galvanic corrosion behaviour |
| Ignores oxide films and passivity | Includes the effect of protective films; a metal can appear in active and passive forms |
| A metal has one fixed position | Position varies with the environment |
| Example: Al ($-1.66$ V) above Zn ($-0.76$ V) | Zn above Al; Ti near the noble end |

questions.q: Why is aluminium placed below (more noble than) zinc in the galvanic series, although it is above zinc in the electrochemical series?
questions.a: The ECS uses standard potentials of bare metal surfaces, where Al ($E^\circ = -1.66$ V) is more active than Zn ($-0.76$ V). In real environments such as sea water, aluminium is covered by a thin, adherent, passive film of $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$, which raises its effective potential and slows its dissolution. The galvanic series is based on such measured potentials, so passivated Al shows up as more noble than Zn.

questions.q: How is the galvanic series useful to a design engineer?
questions.a:
1. It shows which metal of a coupled pair will corrode (the one nearer the active end) under real service conditions.
2. It guides the choice of metals for joints: they should lie close together in the series to minimise galvanic corrosion.
3. When dissimilar metals must be used, it shows which part needs insulation, which to make larger (the anode), and which to coat.
4. It helps select sacrificial anodes: Mg, Zn and Al alloys lie at the active end and protect steel.

questions.q: A galvanic series is always referred to:
options: Standard hydrogen electrode at 1 M concentration
A particular environment such as sea water
questions.a: The galvanic series is an empirical ranking measured in a specified environment, most commonly sea water. The standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions defines the electrochemical series.

topics.why: 'Discuss the factors affecting the rate of corrosion' is a classic 5-10 mark essay question, and individual factors (area ratio, pH, overvoltage) come as reasoning questions.
topics.gist:
Two groups: the **metal** and the **environment**.

**A. Nature of the metal**
1. **Position in the galvanic series**: the more active the metal, and the farther apart two coupled metals are, the faster the corrosion.
2. **Overvoltage**: a high hydrogen overvoltage on the metal slows corrosion. Pure Zn dissolves slowly in dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, but adding $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$ deposits Cu, which has a low overvoltage, and corrosion speeds up.
3. **Relative areas of anode and cathode**: a small anode with a large cathode gives severe corrosion.
4. **Purity**: impurities set up local cells.
5. **Physical state**: fine grains and stressed or cold-worked regions are anodic.
6. **Nature of the surface film**: whether it is protective, as judged by the Pilling-Bedworth ratio.
7. **Passivity**.
8. **Solubility and volatility of the corrosion product**: soluble or volatile products keep the surface exposed.

**B. Nature of the environment**
1. **Temperature**: the rate generally rises with temperature.
2. **Humidity**: above a **critical humidity** (roughly 60-70% for iron in polluted air) atmospheric corrosion rises sharply.
3. **Impurities in the atmosphere**: $\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$ and salt spray.
4. **Suspended particles**: hygroscopic or conducting dust.
5. **pH**: for iron, the rate is high below about pH 4, roughly constant between about 4 and 10 (controlled by $\mathrm{O_2}$ diffusion), and low above about 10 (passivation). Amphoteric Zn and Al are also attacked in strong alkali.
6. **Oxygen concentration and differential aeration**.
7. **Conductivity of the electrolyte**: sea water is much more corrosive than fresh water.
key_points: Metal factors: galvanic position, overvoltage, area ratio, purity, physical state, oxide film, passivity, solubility/volatility of products
Environment factors: temperature, humidity, atmospheric impurities, suspended particles, pH, oxygen and differential aeration, conductivity
Overvoltage example: pure Zn vs Zn + $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$ in dilute acid
Effect of pH on iron corrosion (three regions)
Critical humidity concept
Corrosion rate from weight-loss data in mm/y or mpy
formulas: $\mathrm{CR\ (mm/y)} = \dfrac{87.6\,W}{D\,A\,T}$ — W in mg, D in g/cm³, A in cm², T in h
$\mathrm{CR\ (mpy)} = \dfrac{534\,W}{D\,A\,T}$ — W in mg, D in g/cm³, A in in², T in h
traps: Writing only a list of factors with no explanation or example; essay marks come from the reasoning
Saying higher overvoltage increases corrosion; it decreases it
Claiming corrosion of iron always increases with pH; it falls in strongly alkaline solution
Mixing up units in corrosion-rate formulas (mg vs g, cm² vs in²)
topics.asked_as: 'Discuss the factors which influence the rate of corrosion' (5-10 marks); 'Explain the effect of (i) relative area of anode and cathode (ii) pH (iii) overvoltage on corrosion' (2-3 marks each); occasionally a weight-loss corrosion rate numerical.

questions.q: Corrosion of a metal is most rapid when:
options: Anodic area is large and cathodic area is small
Anodic area is small and cathodic area is large
Anodic and cathodic areas are equal
questions.a: The large cathode demands a large electron current, which must all come from the small anode. The current density at the anode is therefore very high and it corrodes rapidly.

questions.q: Pure zinc dissolves only slowly in dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, but the rate rises sharply when a little $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$ is added. This is because:
options: Deposited copper provides cathodic sites of low hydrogen overvoltage
Copper forms a passive film on zinc
questions.a: Zinc displaces Cu, which deposits on its surface. Hydrogen is evolved easily on Cu (low overvoltage) and with difficulty on Zn (high overvoltage), so local Zn-Cu cells form with an efficient cathode, and zinc dissolves much faster.

questions.q: Discuss the factors influencing the rate of corrosion.
questions.a:
**A. Nature of the metal**
1. **Position in galvanic series**: metals higher (more active) corrode faster; in a couple, the greater the potential difference, the faster the active metal corrodes.
2. **Overvoltage**: a high hydrogen overvoltage on the metal (cathodic sites) slows the cathodic reaction and hence corrosion. Example: pure Zn in dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ is slow; with $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$ added, it is fast.
3. **Relative areas of anode and cathode**: rate is proportional to cathode area / anode area; a small anode with a large cathode means severe attack.
4. **Purity of metal**: impurities form local galvanic cells; 99.999% Zn corrodes far less than commercial Zn.
5. **Physical state**: fine-grained, stressed or cold-worked areas are anodic.
6. **Nature of surface film**: PBR below 1 gives a porous, non-protective film; about 1-2 gives a protective one.
7. **Passivity**: Al, Cr, Ti and stainless steel resist corrosion because of passive films.
8. **Solubility and volatility of corrosion products**: soluble or volatile products ($\mathrm{MoO_3}$) expose fresh metal; insoluble ones may protect.

**B. Nature of the environment**
1. **Temperature**: higher temperature speeds diffusion and reaction, so a higher rate (except where it drives out dissolved $\mathrm{O_2}$ from open systems).
2. **Humidity**: above the critical humidity (roughly 60-70% for iron) a moisture film forms an electrolyte and the rate rises sharply.
3. **Impurities in the atmosphere**: $\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$ (industrial areas) and NaCl spray (coastal areas) increase acidity and conductivity.
4. **Suspended particles**: hygroscopic salts or charcoal particles absorb moisture or act as cathodes.
5. **pH**: acidic media (pH below about 4) are highly corrosive to iron; between about 4 and 10 the rate is nearly constant (limited by $\mathrm{O_2}$ diffusion); above about 10 iron passivates. Amphoteric Al, Zn and Pb also corrode in strong alkali.
6. **Oxygen concentration**: more $\mathrm{O_2}$ speeds oxygen-absorption corrosion; differential aeration causes local attack.
7. **Conductance of the medium**: sea water and saline soils (high conductance) are more corrosive than fresh water or dry sandy soil.

questions.q: A mild steel coupon of exposed area 100 cm² loses 250 mg in 1 week (168 h) in a test solution. If the density of steel is 7.86 g/cm³, calculate the corrosion rate in mm/year.
questions.a:
$\mathrm{CR\ (mm/y)} = \dfrac{87.6\,W}{D\,A\,T}$, with W in mg, D in g/cm³, A in cm², T in h.

$\mathrm{CR} = \dfrac{87.6 \times 250}{7.86 \times 100 \times 168} = \dfrac{21{,}900}{1{,}32{,}048} = 0.166$ mm/year

(About 0.17 mm/y: a moderate rate for mild steel.)

questions.q: Explain the effect of pH on the corrosion of iron.
questions.a:
- **pH below about 4 (acidic)**: the hydrogen evolution reaction ($\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2}$) is fast and the oxide film dissolves, so corrosion is rapid and rises as pH falls.
- **pH about 4-10**: a porous ferrous hydroxide layer covers the surface; the rate is nearly independent of pH and is controlled by diffusion of dissolved oxygen to the surface.
- **pH above about 10 (alkaline)**: iron becomes passive (a protective oxide film forms), so the rate drops. (In very concentrated hot alkali iron can again be attacked, which is a factor in caustic embrittlement.)

For amphoteric metals like Zn, Al and Pb, corrosion is high at both low and high pH.

questions.q: Corrosion of iron in the atmosphere increases sharply above a certain value of relative humidity. This is called:
questions.a: Above the critical humidity (roughly 60-70% for iron, lower in polluted air) a continuous moisture film forms on the surface and acts as an electrolyte, so electrochemical corrosion becomes rapid.

traps: Saying the protected structure is made the anode in cathodic protection; it is made the cathode
Confusing cathodic protection with anodic protection (the latter keeps a passivating metal in its passive range)

questions.q: Which metal is commonly used as a sacrificial anode to protect a buried steel pipeline?
questions.a: Magnesium is far more active than iron in the galvanic series, so when connected to the pipe it becomes the anode and corrodes, while the steel pipe becomes the cathode and is protected. Cu, Pb and Sn are nobler than iron and would accelerate its corrosion.

questions.q: Sodium chromate added to cooling water acts as:
questions.a: Chromate ions react with metal ions formed at the anodic sites to form an insoluble protective film (passivation), suppressing the anodic reaction. Chromates, phosphates, tungstates and nitrites are anodic inhibitors.

questions.q: What is cathodic protection? Explain the sacrificial anode and impressed current methods and compare them.
questions.a:
**Principle**: the metal to be protected is forced to behave as the **cathode** of a corrosion cell by supplying electrons to it from an external source, so the anodic reaction ($\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + ne^-}$) cannot take place on it.

**1. Sacrificial anodic protection**
- The structure (steel pipeline, ship hull, tank) is connected by an insulated wire to a block of a **more active metal**: Mg, Zn or Al alloys.
- The active metal becomes the anode and corrodes ($\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$); the electrons flow to the structure, which becomes the cathode and is protected.
- Exhausted anodes are replaced periodically.
- *Applications*: buried pipelines and cables, ship hulls and boats, Mg rods in domestic water heaters, marine structures.
- *Diagram*: buried pipe connected by wire to a Mg block in backfill; arrow showing electron flow from Mg to pipe.

**2. Impressed current cathodic protection**
- A **DC source** (rectifier) is connected with its negative terminal to the structure and its positive terminal to an **insoluble anode** (graphite, high-silicon iron, platinised Ti, scrap iron).
- The anode is buried in a **backfill** of coke breeze, gypsum and bentonite to improve electrical contact and conductivity.
- The impressed current opposes the corrosion current and makes the structure cathodic.
- *Applications*: long buried pipelines, underground tanks, water tanks, offshore platforms, condensers.

**Comparison**:
| Sacrificial anode | Impressed current |
|---|---|
| No external power needed | Needs a continuous DC supply |
| Anode metal is consumed; must be replaced | Anode is inert; long life |
| Low driving voltage; suits small structures and low-resistivity soils | Can be adjusted; suits large structures and high-resistivity soils |
| Low installation cost, little maintenance | Higher installation and running cost |
| No interference with neighbouring structures | Stray currents may affect nearby structures |

questions.q: Write a short note on corrosion inhibitors.
questions.a:
**Corrosion inhibitors** are substances which, when added in small amounts to the corrosive medium, reduce the rate of corrosion.

**1. Anodic inhibitors**: chromates, phosphates, tungstates, molybdates, nitrites. They react with the metal ions formed at anodic sites to form an insoluble protective film (or passivate the anode). *Caution*: if too little is added, a few anodic spots remain unprotected; these tiny anodes facing large cathodes suffer intense pitting.

**2. Cathodic inhibitors**:
- In **acidic** media (cathodic reaction is $\mathrm{H_2}$ evolution): organic amines, mercaptans, thiourea and heavy-metal (As, Sb) salts adsorb on cathodic sites or raise the hydrogen overvoltage, slowing the cathodic reaction.
- In **neutral** media (cathodic reaction is $\mathrm{O_2}$ absorption): oxygen scavengers such as $\mathrm{Na_2SO_3}$ ($\mathrm{2Na_2SO_3 + O_2 \rightarrow 2Na_2SO_4}$) and hydrazine ($\mathrm{N_2H_4 + O_2 \rightarrow N_2 + 2H_2O}$), or Mg, Zn or Ni salts that precipitate insoluble hydroxides on the cathode.

**3. Vapour-phase inhibitors**: volatile compounds such as dicyclohexylammonium nitrite and benzotriazole, used in packing machinery and equipment in closed spaces.

**Uses**: boiler and cooling water, acid pickling baths, oil-well equipment, radiators.

questions.q: How can proper design and selection of material help in controlling corrosion?
questions.a:
1. Avoid contact of **dissimilar metals**; if unavoidable, choose metals close in the galvanic series and **insulate** the joint.
2. Keep the **anodic area large** compared with the cathodic area (for example use rivets of a nobler metal than the plate, not the reverse).
3. Avoid **crevices, sharp corners and recesses** where water and dirt collect; prefer welded joints to riveted or bolted ones.
4. Design for **free drainage** and air circulation so that water does not stagnate; tanks should have sloping bottoms and drain valves.
5. Avoid uneven stresses; **stress-relieve** fabricated parts.
6. Use **pure metals or corrosion-resistant alloys** (stainless steel, Cu-Ni) in aggressive media.
7. Make provision for easy **inspection, painting and replacement** of parts likely to corrode.

questions.q: In impressed-current cathodic protection, the structure to be protected is connected to:
options: The positive terminal of the DC source
The negative terminal of the DC source
questions.a: Electrons are pushed into the structure from the negative terminal, making it the cathode. The positive terminal goes to the inert anode (graphite, high-silicon iron) in backfill.

questions.q: What is meant by deaeration and deactivation in corrosion control?
questions.a:
Both remove dissolved **oxygen**, which drives the cathodic reaction ($\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$) in neutral water.

- **Deaeration**: physical removal of dissolved gases by heating the water, applying vacuum, or bubbling inert gas (mechanical deaerators in boiler feed systems).
- **Deactivation**: chemical removal of dissolved oxygen by adding substances that react with it:
  $\mathrm{2Na_2SO_3 + O_2 \rightarrow 2Na_2SO_4}$
  $\mathrm{N_2H_4 + O_2 \rightarrow N_2 + 2H_2O}$
  Hydrazine is preferred in high-pressure boilers because its products are not salts.

topics.why: 'Distinguish anodic and cathodic coatings' and 'galvanising vs tinning' are regular 3-5 mark questions, with the scratched-coating reasoning as a favourite.
topics.gist:
Every coating is a **barrier**; a metallic one also has an electrochemical role that decides what happens at a scratch.

- **Anodic coating**: the coating metal is **more active** than the base metal, as with Zn, Al or Cd on steel. If the coating is scratched, the coating becomes the anode and corrodes, and the exposed steel is the cathode and stays protected (**sacrificial** action). Protection continues until the coating is used up. Example: **galvanising**.
- **Cathodic coating**: the coating metal is **more noble** than the base metal, as with Sn, Cu, Ni, Cr or Ag on steel. It protects only while it is **continuous**. At a scratch the exposed iron becomes a **small anode** against a **large cathode** of tin, so corrosion is faster than on bare steel. Example: **tinning**.

**Galvanising**: steel is cleaned, pickled in dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, washed, fluxed with $\mathrm{ZnCl_2 + NH_4Cl}$ and dipped in molten zinc (about 425-450 °C), and the excess is removed by rollers. It is used for sheets, pipes, wires and buckets, but **not for food containers**, because zinc dissolves in food acids to give toxic compounds.

**Tinning**: steel is pickled, fluxed with $\mathrm{ZnCl_2}$ and passed through molten tin (about 232-250 °C) and palm oil. Tin is non-toxic and resists food acids, so it is used for food cans.

Other metal-coating methods: electroplating, spraying, cladding, and cementation (sherardizing Zn, calorizing Al, chromizing Cr). Non-metallic coatings include **anodising** (thick $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ on Al), **phosphating**, **chromating**, and organic coatings: paints, varnishes, enamels and lacquers.
key_points: Anodic coating: more active metal (Zn, Al, Cd on Fe); sacrificial protection even when scratched
Cathodic coating: more noble metal (Sn, Cu, Ni, Cr on Fe); protects only when intact; a scratch speeds corrosion of the base

questions.q: Galvanising is the coating of iron or steel with:
questions.a: Galvanising is the coating of a thin layer of zinc, usually by dipping the cleaned article in molten zinc at about 425-450 °C. Coating with tin is tinning; with Al by diffusion is calorizing.

questions.q: When the coating on tinned iron is scratched and exposed to moist air:
options: Iron corrodes rapidly at the scratch
A passive film forms on iron
questions.a: Tin is more noble than iron, so at the scratch iron becomes a small anode surrounded by a large tin cathode. Iron therefore corrodes faster than if it were uncoated. Tin is a cathodic coating.

questions.q: Food containers are tinned rather than galvanised because:
options: Zinc reacts with food acids to form poisonous compounds
Tin is more active than zinc
Galvanised coatings cannot be applied to thin sheets
questions.a: Zinc is attacked by the organic acids in food (citric, acetic) and forms toxic zinc salts. Tin is non-toxic and quite resistant to food acids, so tinning is used for food cans despite its poorer protection when scratched.

questions.q: Distinguish between anodic and cathodic coatings with examples.
questions.a:
| Anodic coating | Cathodic coating |
|---|---|
| Coating metal is **more active** (anodic) than the base metal | Coating metal is **more noble** (cathodic) than the base metal |
| Examples: Zn, Al, Cd on steel | Examples: Sn, Cu, Ni, Cr, Ag on steel |
| Protects the base metal **sacrificially** | Protects only as a **barrier** |
| If scratched, the coating corrodes and the base metal is still protected | If scratched, the base metal becomes a small anode and corrodes rapidly |
| Coating is gradually consumed | Coating itself is not attacked while intact |
| Typical process: galvanising | Typical process: tinning, electroplating of Ni/Cr |
| Not suitable for food (Zn) | Tin suitable for food containers |

questions.q: Compare galvanising and tinning, including the process for each.
questions.a:
**Galvanising (process)**: the iron article is degreased, pickled in dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ at about 60-90 °C to remove rust and scale, washed, dried, dipped in a flux of $\mathrm{ZnCl_2}$ + $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$, then dipped in molten zinc at about 425-450 °C. Excess zinc is removed by passing between rollers and the article is cooled (annealed).

**Tinning (process)**: the article is pickled in dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, passed through a $\mathrm{ZnCl_2}$ flux, then through molten tin (about 232-250 °C), and then through rollers immersed in palm oil to remove excess tin and prevent oxidation of the hot tin surface.

| Galvanising | Tinning |
|---|---|
| Coating of Zn | Coating of Sn |
| Zn is anodic to Fe: protects even when scratched | Sn is cathodic to Fe: protects only when intact |
| Bath about 425-450 °C | Bath about 232-250 °C |
| Zn is attacked by acids/food: not for food containers | Sn is non-toxic: used for food cans |
| Uses: roofing sheets, pipes, wires, buckets, nails | Uses: food and beverage cans, copper utensils (kalai), refrigerator parts |
| Coating is thicker and cheaper per unit protection | Coating is thinner, costlier |

questions.q: Write short notes on (a) electroplating (b) sherardizing.
questions.a:
**(a) Electroplating**: deposition of a coating metal on the base metal by electrolysis. The cleaned article is made the **cathode**, the coating metal (or an inert material) is the **anode**, and the electrolyte is a salt solution of the coating metal (for example $\mathrm{NiSO_4}$ for nickel, $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$ for copper, chromic acid for chromium). On passing DC, metal ions are reduced and deposited on the article: $\mathrm{Ni^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Ni}$. Additives (brighteners, levellers) and control of current density, temperature and pH give a uniform, adherent, bright deposit. Used for Ni-Cr plating of cycles and taps, Au/Ag on jewellery, Zn/Cd on fasteners.

**(b) Sherardizing**: a **cementation** (diffusion) process. Cleaned steel articles are packed with **zinc dust** (with a little ZnO) in a slowly rotating drum and heated to about 350-450 °C for a few hours. Zinc diffuses into the surface, forming a hard, uniform Zn-Fe alloy layer. It is used for small articles such as screws, bolts, nuts and washers, where it gives an even coating without clogging threads. (Similar processes: **calorizing** with Al and **chromizing** with Cr.)
